title: AAP volume 14 issue 3 Cover and Front matter
Advances in Archaeological Labor Management
abstract: Critical scholarship on the state of archaeological labor has boomed and bloomed in recent years, demonstrating systemic harms, inequities, and patterns of exclusion in archaeological work. This body of historical and contemporary analysis has documented low wages, poor working conditions, and efforts to separate the intellectual work from the physical work of archaeology, resulting in diminished recognition and compensation for those performing supposedly “unskilled” labor. Research and reflections on archaeological labor have also demonstrated that such exploitation and marginalization especially affect archaeological workers of marked, nondominant, intersectional identities. With the problems of archaeological labor increasingly clear, this themed issue turns our attention to what can be done to improve working conditions for archaeologists in various sectors and geographic contexts. Recognizing the hierarchies and power structures in the field that position some individuals, groups, and institutions to take effective action to ensure more decent work for all who labor in archaeology, the authors in this issue articulate particular interventions that might be made by the people and institutions most ideally positioned to make change that leads to better labor conditions for all archaeologists and therefore to better archaeology. Here, I outline the robust global scholarship on archaeological labor to situate this themed issue and provide a trail map through the articles gathered here, which aim to ignite sparks for advancing labor management in archaeology.

title: Toward a Regulation of Archaeological Labor in Spain: Up against a Brick Wall for 40 Years
authors: Jaime Almansa-Sánchez; F. Rafael Varón-Hernández; Carlos Caballero-Casado; Ángel Astorqui
abstract: Since the first attempts to organize as a collective in the mid-1980s, with the surge of the new management models in a democratic and decentralized Spain, both archaeology and labor have changed considerably. Although many old battles to recognize the profession are still alive, other initiatives have strengthened the archaeological ecosystem in the country. Addressing the structural challenges of work precarity in archaeology is on the horizon. Temporary contracts, low salaries, lack of legal and administrative recognition, and deficiencies in basic rights (for example, in health and safety) are some of the problems we have been facing for decades, and now we are closer to counteracting them. This article will review (1) the recent history of Spanish archaeology and the formation of the current archaeological ecosystem, (2) collective action to improve working conditions in Spanish archaeology over the last decades, (3) the latest actions from the Spanish State Platform of Professional Archaeologists to overcome obstacles, and (4) the dream of a common front in Europe (and beyond) to create the profession we want to have. Although sometimes this struggle is frustrating, a retrospective view of the events and the achievements gained over the years brings hope for the future and some significant steps forward.

title: In the Shadows of Colonialism: Archaeological Labor Practices in (Post-)Colonial Zimbabwe
abstract: Archaeological practice is structured through labor, shaping who participates in fieldwork, who interprets findings, and who produces knowledge. Recent scholarship on archaeological labor in Egypt, Palestine, Turkey, Mexico, Europe, and North America shows that labor regimes are not merely logistical arrangements but constitutive elements of archaeological epistemology, shaping how evidence is generated, interpreted, and circulated. This article examines the historical formation and persistence of archaeological labor practices in Zimbabwe. It traces how colonial archaeology established racialized divisions between African workers and European experts and how these have only been partially reconfigured after independence. Drawing on colonial and postcolonial excavation reports, published scholarship, and recent field practices in Zimbabwe, the analysis shows that postindependence archaeology has not fully dismantled divisions between those who generate field data and those who retain interpretive and authorship authority. The article argues that these labor arrangements reproduce epistemic injustice, limiting whose knowledge counts within archaeological narratives. It proposes a framework for reorganizing archaeological labor through recognition of intellectual labor, inclusive decision-making, transparent authorship and acknowledgment, and embedded capacity building. The article places Zimbabwean archaeology in global debates on labor, expertise, and decolonization, demonstrating that transforming archaeological practice requires reconfiguring labor as a site of knowledge production.

title: Toward More Inclusive Fieldwork: Labor, Knowledge, and Structural Constraints in Chinese Archaeology
abstract: Archaeological fieldwork in China commonly relies on short-term labor recruited from nearby villages, forming a long-standing mode of collaboration between state-employed staff and local workers. Drawing on sustained field engagement and interviews at the Chengcun City Site of the Han Dynasty, this research examines how locally recruited workers enter, sustain, and experience participation in archaeological practice. Community members often begin archaeological work during agricultural off-seasons and may accumulate decades of experience. Their trajectories vary: some obtain institutional posts, others return to farming, and many continue in project-based employment. These trajectories indicate that funding structures shape employment continuity and welfare access, while skills developed through long-term practice do not always translate into formal professional status. Archaeological labor constitutes a key mechanism in producing excavation knowledge, shaping professional roles, and structuring heritage governance in everyday practice. Viewed through labor trajectories, archaeological professionalization appears uneven, shaped by institutional arrangements, rural livelihood strategies, and localized opportunities. Based on the Chengcun case, this research points to broader dynamics: large-scale projects rely on localized labor regimes while maintaining differentiated forms of recognition and authority. Reconsidering archaeology through labor offers a perspective on knowledge production, participation, and governance.

title: From Workers to Companions: Confronting the Contradictions in Neoliberal Social Relationships in Peruvian Archaeology
authors: Henry Tantaleán; Carito Tavera Medina; José Roman; Juan Manuel Quispe-Baquedano; Sayury Sanandres; Isaac Santiago; Julio Bendezú-Sarmiento
abstract: In the practice of archaeological research in Peru, a set of economic, political, and ethical contradictions can be recognized in the relationships between archaeologists, excavation technicians, and other groups. It has been observed that our social relationships in fieldwork and other archaeological practice spaces reproduce the principles of the free market, individual competition, and labor exploitation. However, a medium-term archaeological project, the Chicama Archaeological Program (PRACH), has been established on the northern coast of Peru, confronting those contradictions to transform socioeconomic relationships in the discipline. Over time, crew members and participants in this program have transformed their ways of being, transcending the conventional boundaries of mere workers. Despite the pervasive influence of the laws of the market on our social fabric, a conscious political stance has emerged as a counterforce, aiming to overcome the alienating effects of neoliberalism. Thus, our crew prioritizes cooperation, solidarity, and care over competition, individualism, selfishness, and immediate and utilitarian relationships. A host of challenges must be confronted, but the motivation for this effort lies in adopting an alternative, novel, and conscious approach to the inequalities generated by conventional forms of interpersonal interaction, especially in our archaeological practice.

title: Beyond the Trenches: Rethinking Archaeological Labor through Ritual, Relational, and Community Archaeologies in the Central Andean Highlands
abstract: Archaeological labor in the Andes unfolds not only in field trenches and labs but also in the social and cosmological landscapes where sites remain powerful actors affecting daily community life. Drawing on collaborative fieldwork in the Huaylas and Cosma River Basins of the Cordillera Negra Mountains, Ancash, Peru, this article reflects on how archaeological work is shaped by theoretical framing, traditional field methods, and the relationships between descendant communities and the archaeological sites they live around that influence daily fieldwork. We argue for an expanded definition of archaeological labor that encompasses ceremonial, emotional, and relational work alongside excavation and analysis and share strategies in hiring, organization, and training. These include daily routines that make space for ritual practice, decision-making frameworks that treat local knowledge as actionable, and project planning that honors contractual and cultural obligations. By including these community-framed practices in the methodology, we call for culturally engaged archaeological labor that recognizes how communities, researchers, and sites co-produce knowledge and working conditions, thereby building a safer, more inclusive, and more equitable work environment.

title: Working against Silence: Nahua Scholarly Labor, Digital Precarity, and the Politics of Archaeological Sovereignty—The MONARO Project in Veracruz, Mexico
abstract: Archaeology faces a turning point as digital technologies transform who performs archaeological labor and under what conditions. Although inequities affecting students, technicians, and Indigenous collaborators have been increasingly acknowledged, less attention has been paid to the political economy that structures these forms of work. Drawing on collaborative research with Nahua communities in Mixtla de Altamirano, Veracruz, this article examines how transcription, translation, deep mapping, and digital annotation of oral narratives constitute archaeological labor—despite being excluded from Mexico’s state-defined model of “legitimate” archaeology. Community projects operate under digital precarity, relying on fragile infrastructures, unstable electricity, and unpaid labor. These conditions reveal structural inequalities in archaeological practice and raise urgent questions about data governance. We propose strategies for repurpose digital tools and AI toward more inclusive practices through ethical protocols, community training, and infrastructures grounded in archival sovereignty. The article proposes a grounded framework for rethinking archaeological labor, digital infrastructures, and collaboration in community-based contexts.

title: Is Archaeological Data Labor Sustainable? Only through Ethical and Policy Reforms, Open Data Emphases on Public Engagement, and Indigenous Data Sovereignty
authors: Joshua J. Wells; Neha Gupta; Kelsey Noack Myers
abstract: The proliferation of information and communication technologies in US archaeology has created myriad expectations for professional labor throughout the life cycle of data. Technological adoption has outpaced the development of professional and ethical frameworks, leaving archaeological data labor unsustainable in our under-resourced discipline. This article reviews traditional Western paradigms underpinning legal and intellectual property models that have shaped archaeological data standards and contribute to problematic outcomes for archaeological data labor, alienate publics from primary data of publicly mandated heritage preservation, disregard Indigenous Data Sovereignty, and enable the extractive commodification of heritage for AI enterprises. To address these tensions, archaeologists must reshape data labor and its products by centering public goods and Indigenous rights in all aspects of their work. As scientific and cultural professionals, archaeologists should embrace best practices in data ecosystems to create, guide, and enforce governance principles that inform and promote labor sustainability and accountability. This article illuminates the current state of archaeological data labor across the discipline through a critical review of policies, legislation, and ethics surrounding data governance (e.g., CARE, FAIR, and the US OPEN Government Data Act) and describes how archaeologists can integrate these efforts into technological initiatives across the full spectrum of archaeological practice.

title: Unmanned Aerial Systems and an Archaeology of Accessibility
abstract: Archaeology is in the midst of a technological revolution, particularly for data collection, first championed by light detection and ranging (lidar) in the early 2000s and now with widespread applications of unmanned aerial systems (UAS)-deployed remote sensing. While the importance of remote sensing for data collection and heritage conservation is known, less work has acknowledged the implications of remote sensing for field safety, particularly for disabled researchers. UAS offer a unique opportunity to explore circumstances that may affect mobility in the field and how advances in archaeological science can transform fieldwork by improving accessibility for disabled archaeologists. I argue that UAS can—and should—be improved to promote accessibility in archaeological fieldwork, due to their promotion of field safety, increased planning of daily tasks, and broader applications to community-engaged research. These interventions should be applied to the larger field of archaeology to improve labor management for researchers in all sectors of practice.

title: Daily Provisions: Tracing a Longue Durée of Feeding Archaeological Workers and Paths of Sustenance for the Future
abstract: Providing sustenance for archaeological workers has been a logistical and social challenge from the earliest stages of the discipline. Food preparation involved a constellation of workers, from gardeners to ingredient purchasers, and from cooks and chefs, who were often teams of locals who catered to and fought against preferences around taste, sustenance, and nutrition for a regionally and internationally diverse group of people. By analyzing food provision lists, material culture, and archival correspondence pertaining to excavations of Coahuila, Mexico (1947) and Piedras Negras, Guatemala (1931–1946), I seek to trace a regional cross section of mid-twentieth-century food preparation for archaeological workers. I chose to analyze these sites because of the robustness of the archival record and the similarities of their time periods. When taken together, they can provide a more detailed account of North American archaeologists working between the 1930s and 1940s south of the US border, yielding insight into this era of archaeological labor management. Food preparation and dining habits are ways in which hierarchical and segregated labor management manifest in archaeology. By juxtaposing these examples with contemporary archaeological sources, I argue that we can radically question the inheritance of quotidian structures of archaeological practice.

title: Putting the People before the Work: Creating Healthy Working Environments in CRM
abstract: Cultural resource management (CRM) in the United States is an industry that thrives (or falters) on tight budgets and short deadlines. To steadily secure a reliable stream of projects from major clients (and to support the limited budgets of smaller clients), CRM firms are often forced to work with bare-bones funding, requiring them to demand a great deal of effort from their field and office personnel to stay within budget and on schedule. When the projects themselves can easily become the main focus, above the needs of the staff, an unhealthy working environment, lack of work–life balance, burnout, and resentment toward management can result. In this article, I reflect on my own leadership experiences and present a model that outlines best practices for CRM leadership professionals to follow to grow and maintain their businesses through the genuine and consistent support of staff members. I recommend three basic components to creating a healthy working environment in CRM: (1) policies and procedures that clearly outline staff safety, approaches to work–life balance, and field and lab protocols; (2) a “practice what you preach” approach to leadership; and (3) access to professional development opportunities for all staff, regardless of their job level or experience.

title: Mentoring as Career Infrastructure: Building Sustainable Pathways in Archaeological Practice
abstract: Sustaining a career in archaeology, particularly one in cultural resources management (CRM), requires more than technical expertise or academic credentialing. Career opportunities have expanded beyond traditional pathways, but the scaffolding that supports professionals across every career stage has not kept pace. Mentoring, in the form of knowledge sharing, advocacy, and intentional networking, can make the difference between leaving the field or thriving in it. This article contends that mentoring is essential career infrastructure, as fundamental to career sustainability as field school training or thesis research. Drawing on experience mentoring more than 75 students, colleagues, and job seekers, this discussion demonstrates how thoughtful mentoring fosters professional development, promotes access, and helps mentees navigate the complex intersections of client work, personal research interests, and public engagement. This article also introduces the concepts of sponsorship—the active promotion of mentees for advancement—and network weaving, the deliberate cultivation of professional connections across broader scales, as critical tools for career readiness, resilience, and inclusion. Case studies illustrate how these practices unlock doors to leadership, expand skill sets, and may help slow attrition. The article concludes with actionable and scalable recommendations for CRM organizations seeking to build the mentoring infrastructure that archaeological careers require.

title: Building Intentional Leadership and Management Approaches in Archaeology
abstract: Archaeologists have a history of borrowing tools, theories, and practices from other disciplines. Yet, despite a large body of literature and calls for our discipline to establish more inclusive and safe workplaces, few archaeologists have studied or utilized scholarship addressing best practices in leadership and management practices. This article argues that engaging with this scholarship could be an effective way to improve our leadership and management approaches. It does so by exploring three components of this literature: a values-based workplace culture, a coaching-oriented leadership, and project management methods. It also provides examples from the author’s experience in implementing these practices in museum and higher-education settings. By adopting more intentional approaches to our work by looking at the wide array of research that has studied how organizations operate and succeed, archaeologists have the opportunity to produce safer, more effective, and more inclusive workplaces and more effective research outcomes.

title: Fun Labor Is Still Labor: Archaeological Consulting in the Games Industry
abstract: Overview Games have the potential to engage a wider public with archaeology, but popular products also continue to perpetuate misconceptions about the past. One potential solution is for archaeologists, heritage professionals, and historians to act as consultants in the process of game design. However, there has been little published about what consultation involves, particularly with the understanding that games with archaeological themes often rely heavily on colonial narratives, as well as stereotypes that affect descendant communities. In this digital review, I draw on my experiences as an archaeologist and cultural consultant within the tabletop games industry to highlight how representation, expertise, and positionality are considerations for any scholar who is solicited for consultation on a commercial product. I also address the unpaid, underpaid, and emotional labor that lurks within an industry reliant on personal passions and work characterized as fun. I conclude with recommendations that focus on reducing harm in the present while playing with the past.

title: Unmanned Aerial Systems and an Archaeology of Accessibility – ERRATUM
Clarifying Stratigraphic Terminology in Paleolithic Archaeology Using Natural Language Processing
abstract: Archaeological context is a foundational concept, yet its definition remains ambiguous and inconsistent. Traditionally, lithostratigraphic frameworks rooted in geology have long dominated, but recent computational and spatial approaches increasingly redefine stratigraphic units. This shift raises a critical challenge: the lack of clear and consistent terminology for defining stratigraphic units. To explore this issue, we applied natural language processing (NLP) to a broad corpus of Paleolithic literature, focusing on the use of key terms such as “layer,” “level,” “occupation,” and “horizon.” Using SciBERT (Scientific BERT; BERT = Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) to generate contextual embeddings, we compared their semantic distributions with a control set of distinct terms (lithic, bone, flake, charcoal). The control set produced stable, separable clusters, whereas contextual terms showed extensive semantic overlap and instability, reflecting their interchangeable and inconsistent use. These results underscore that the problem is not only linguistic but theoretical: without clear terminological baselines, new methodological advances risk conflating analytical tools with interpretive outcomes. We argue that terminological precision is essential for comparability across sites and for cumulative research. NLP offers a replicable framework for auditing and clarifying terminology, contributing to greater rigor and interoperability in archaeological interpretation.

title: Incorporating Existing Archaeological Collections into Cultural Resource Management Mitigation
authors: Sarah Herr; Elizabeth Bollwerk; S. Terry Childs; A. Gwynn Henderson; Heather L. Olson; Lori Thompson
abstract: Excavation is strongly embedded in cultural resource management (CRM) in the United States as the preferred mitigation of impacts of development, maintenance, or management projects on federal land, funded by federal money, or constructed under federal permits. The law allows more diversity in mitigation than is typically practiced. Consciously integrating the assessment, rehabilitation, research, and interpretation of existing collections of artifacts and associated records into projects conducted in compliance with government regulations is a responsible and public-serving approach to preserving heritage. Case studies from Virginia, New Mexico, Georgia, Rhode Island, and Arizona provide a basis for critically evaluating the challenges and possibilities of this work. Because archaeologists may have less experience reusing existing collections in compliance, the article describes how to assess when such work is an appropriate mitigation and how to identify existing collections, conduct the due diligence involved, and integrate collections work into preservation programs and projects planned within a consultation framework. It also notes that incorporating existing collections can be an effective element of state-, Tribal-, and local-, as well as federal-level compliance. The article concludes by identifying the structures that are in place to support this work and where additional training and resources will be needed.

title: Navigating the AI Revolution in the Era of Community-Accountable Archaeological Praxis
authors: Melanie G. Cootsona; Mario Alberto Castillo; Jun Sunseri
abstract: This article explores how generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs) such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, can be mobilized to support collaborative and community-accountable archaeological practice. We situate this exploration within the growing conversation about the use and utility of generative AI in archaeological practice and a discussion about the capabilities of LLMs. Through three case studies—Picuris Pueblo’s legacy collections documentation; the transcription of early twentieth-century archival materials in San Ildefonso Tultepec, Querétaro; and the digitization of the Mountain Messenger —we evaluate the potentials and pitfalls of LLMs in supporting document transcription, organization, and analysis within community-led research contexts. Our findings suggest that, when used transparently and under community direction, LLMs can potentially increase efficiency and accessibility in data processing, expand opportunities for capacity building, and promote citizen-science approaches to heritage stewardship. However, we also identify critical challenges, including data sovereignty, environmental concerns, inequitable access to digital infrastructure, and the persistent need for human oversight to ensure accuracy and accountability.

title: Integrating Remote Sensing and Indigenous Knowledge: A Community-Commanded Approach to Heritage Management in the Atacama Desert
authors: Cristian González Rodríguez; Guillermo González Chinga; Valentina Figueroa; Manuel Prieto; Jacinta Arthur; Christian Espíndola; Ariadna Cifuentes; Camilo Sanzana; Natalia La Mura; Pía Sapiains; Cristian Varela; Cristian Games; Larry Games
abstract: This article presents the Zapar project, a community-commanded initiative developed in collaboration with the Atacameño Community of Toconao (northern Chile), which repositions remote sensing (RS) technologies through Indigenous governance and ethical frameworks. By embedding the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance—Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, and Ethics—into every stage of the workflow, the project transforms RS from an extractive documentation tool into a participatory, culturally grounded practice. UAV-based photogrammetry, spatial modeling, and virtual documentation were codesigned with community members to support Indigenous-led heritage management, memory activation, and territorial governance. Beyond technical innovation, this project offers a procedural, epistemological, and ethical-governance advance in archaeological practice. Procedurally, it demonstrates how the CARE Principles can guide RS workflows through shared authority and iterative validation (1) epistemologically, by integrating Indigenous narratives that redefine site interpretation; and (2) ethically, by ensuring data sovereignty and long-term stewardship of digital heritage within the community. The Zapar project therefore provides a replicable framework for decolonizing digital archaeology, demonstrating that technological innovation can coexist with Indigenous leadership, collaborative ethics, and sustainable heritage governance.

title: Slow, Digital, Immersive, Accessible: A Crip Studies–Centered Framework for Inclusive Archaeological Practice
abstract: Archaeological practice has historically privileged fieldwork-intensive methodologies that systematically exclude practitioners whose bodies, minds, or life circumstances diverge from disciplinary norms. Drawing on crip theory and intersectional disability studies, this article uses the Homo archaeologus archetype—an often idealized archaeologist characterized by able-bodiedness, neurotypicality, cisgender identity, and physical presence in the field—which functions as both professional stereotype and gatekeeping mechanism. I argue that moving beyond accommodation-based approaches toward accessibility-centered design transforms not only who can participate in archaeology but what the discipline can know. This article proposes a four-pillar framework for inclusive archaeological practice: (1) Slow , restructuring temporal rhythms to prioritize deliberation over efficiency; (2) Digital , integrating computational methods as core archaeology rather than post-fieldwork analysis; (3) Immersive , employing technologies such as photogrammetry and virtual reality (VR) to multiply modes of engagement with archaeological contexts; and (4) Accessible , designing projects from the outset for diverse participation rather than retrofitting accommodations afterward. Through case studies from archaeological projects, I show that these pillars, in one form or another, are already operational in contemporary practice and that recognizing marginalized practitioners as methodological innovators—rather than problems requiring accommodation—strengthens archaeological rigor while expanding epistemic possibilities. This framework reframes accessibility not as an optional enhancement but as a fundamental methodology that benefits all practitioners while centering those historically excluded from disciplinary legitimacy.

title: Unearthing Indigenous Seed Collections: The State of Ethnobotanical Holdings in US Museums and University Repositories
authors: Charlotte Dawson; Jewel Cummins; Matthew J. Rowe; Stephanie Russo Carroll; Jane Anderson; Michael Kotutwa Johnson
abstract: Indigenous communities and scholars are calling for archaeologists and museum professionals to critically assess stewardship of Indigenous agricultural seeds and ethnobotanical collections housed in museums and other institutions and the rematriation of these important cultural items. Indigenous seeds retain cultural and religious significance along with diverse genetic information that could help revitalize Indigenous agriculture systems. Many seeds remain viable, making them especially vulnerable to appropriation and patenting by industrial agriculture corporations searching for climate-resilient seed varieties. We present results of a survey of US museums and universities to determine the prevalence of Indigenous seeds held in collections and to evaluate practices surrounding cataloging, care, storage, and researcher and descendant-community access. Results demonstrate that significant amounts of Indigenous seed stock are currently stored in museums and other institutional repositories, often due to ethnobotanical collecting in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries as well as ongoing archaeological activities from the twentieth century onward. Additionally, based on our findings, we suggest that failure to adequately steward these materials represents a significant risk for further disenfranchisement of Indigenous people from their cultural heritage. We propose pathways to enhance protections of Indigenous seeds and plant materials throughout acquisition and curation processes.

title: Decolonizing the Spear-Thrower: New Perspectives on Propulsor Projectile Technologies from the Northwest Coast of North America
authors: Adam N. Rorabaugh; James Brown; Sarah Campbell
abstract: Historically, much of the archaeological research on spear-throwers has been in the context of comparison with bow and arrow technologies, revealing a colonialist preoccupation with technologies more familiar to Europeans while exoticizing other projectile delivery systems. The commonly used term “atl-atl” from Nahuatl is culturally specific, which at best obscures the existence of multiple regional traditions and independent innovation and development and at worst perpetuates antiquarian exoticism. Other archaeological research, especially experimental work, has focused on understanding the mechanics and physics of using spear-throwers. Although much of this research has had the explicit goal of understanding the functional trade-offs between spear-throwers and bows—and is therefore affected by the implicit colonialist bias—the research also has contributed to a better understanding of spear-thrower design and effectiveness and, most recently, has contributed to reevaluating gender relationships with these technologies. We propose (1) engagement of descendant communities on projectile terminology and (2) a schema that situates propulsor projectiles in the wider context of projectile delivery systems. These steps focus on propulsor technologies as an important dynamic system deserving of its own story in terms of how it was developed, introduced, and refined in local contexts.

title: A Review of the Turkwel Tradition: Cultural Variability and Social Change in the First Millennium CE East Africa
abstract: Collating all available information, literature, data, and research history on the Turkwel tradition and the material, narratives, and interpretations that have been linked to it, the paper reviews the similarities, differences, and nuances of the assemblages and sites associated with the 1st millennium CE tradition found across South Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, and Uganda. It discusses issues and shortcomings in how we treat the distinctive grooved pottery as a fossil directeur , but also highlights the area-specific localizations in material culture, production processes, and subsistence that make this tradition so variable. Through the analysis focused on ceramics, it also proposes a division of Turkwel into two phases and a northern and southern facies, links the former typological isolate to South Sudan’s Lokabulo tradition, and points to new avenues of research that could shed light on social dynamics in the 1st millennium CE and the Pastoral Neolithic-Pastoral Iron Age transition. The review proposes to treat the Turkwel tradition and its peoples as bricoleurs, adopting and appropriating new and existing practices and ideas into their culture. The trait might be a symptom of broader socio-cultural and technological developments happening in East Africa at the time that contributed to a flurry of new ceramic wares and which indicates new attitudes towards the “materialization” of identity.

title: Auditory Affordances of Game Pass Shelter (South Africa): Implications for Performative Practices and Multisensory Engagement with San Rock Art
authors: Neemias Santos da Rosa; Lidia Alvarez-Morales; Diego Moreno-Iglesias; Ghilraen Laue; Margarita Díaz-Andreu
abstract: Sensory research on San rock art has often focused on whether acoustic effects influenced the selection of places to be painted or engraved. This article addresses the issue from a different perspective by examining the auditory affordances of Game Pass shelter, one of the most iconic rock art sites in southern Africa. Using impulse-response measurements adapted from room acoustics, we analyzed reverberation, clarity, definition, and sound strength within the shelter. The results show that Game Pass is acoustically "dry," with low reverberation and local reinforcement of direct sound through early reflections. Rather than producing spectacular sonic effects, the site offers conditions in which sounds involved in performative practices could remain clear while gaining presence at specific listening positions. Although these measurements do not demonstrate that specific performances took place at the shelter, they indicate the kinds of sonic practices Game Pass could have supported. More generally, the study suggests that the acoustic significance of painted shelters may lie less in unusual phenomena than in how their auditory affordances facilitate performances involving sound and contribute to multisensory engagement with rock art.

title: Breaking Borders: The Medieval Archaeology of the Ethiopian-Somaliland Borderland
authors: Jorge de Torres Rodríguez; Jorge Rouco Collazo; Valeria Leticia Franco Salvi; Manuel Antonio Franco Fernández; Mohamed Abdi Allamagen; Carolina Cornax Gómez; Mario Llorente García; Mesfin Getachew; Adrián de la Torre García; Juan Montegú; Worku Derara; Álvaro Minguito Palomares; Khalid Abdilahi Abdi
abstract: This article examines the impact of colonial borders on the interpretation of medieval archaeology in the Horn of Africa, focusing on the region now divided between Ethiopia and Somaliland. The boundary established in the 1930s fragmented what had historically been an integrated cultural and economic landscape, leading to uneven research trajectories and hindering the reconstruction of historical processes whose scope transcended modern political limits. Through an archaeological project conducted between 2022 and 2025 in the Aw Bare and Harawo woredas of Ethiopia’s Somali Region, nineteen sites—fifteen previously unknown for the academic literature—were identified and documented, allowing for a reassessment of medieval Muslim settlement patterns between the thirteenth and seventeenth centuries. The results reveal a hierarchical sedentary occupation, ranging from major urban centers such as Aw Bare and Aw Boba to medium-sized villages, small hamlets, and isolated dwellings, alongside defensive structures and specialized cemeteries. Excavations at Aiyanle produced a detailed stratigraphic sequence, imported materials, and radiocarbon dates that place the site’s peak during the rule of the Barr Saʿd al-Dīn Sultanate, followed by a decline associated with its collapse in the late sixteenth century. In parallel, substantial evidence of nomadic occupation was recorded, including ritual aggregation sites, cemeteries, and craft-related activity areas. Together, these data reveal a densely occupied and highly complex landscape in which sedentary and nomadic communities interacted dynamically. The findings also challenge interpretations shaped by contemporary borders and offer new insights into territorial organization, economic strategies, and religious practices in the medieval Muslim Horn of Africa.

title: Lithic Techno-economics and OSL Chronology of the Later Stone Age at Chessungalane, Save River Valley, Mozambique
authors: Osama Samawi; Jeffrey I. Rose; Li Li; Ana Gomes; Daniel Martins; Elena Skosey-LaLonde; Gina M. Buckley; Ilona Benedetti; J. Michael Daniels; Jan-Pieter Buylaert; Jonathan A. Haws; Juma Nacuti Turquia; May Murungi; Michael M. Benedetti; Milena Carvalho; Milton Chirindza; Mussa Raja; Profina Júlio Mondlane; Sarah Marie Foley; Takalani A. Dubayi; Telma João Sipaneque; Nuno Bicho
abstract: Nestled between East and Southern Africa, the Stone Age archaeology of Mozambique offers important insights into Later Stone Age (LSA) behavioral variability across a region pivotal to understanding human adaptations. Here, we present results from technological analysis, refitting and optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating of the newly discovered site of Chessungalane (CHE) in south-central Mozambique. OSL dates indicate occupation spanning ~ 23–7 ka, corresponding to the early LSA through Wilton periods. Technological analysis of lithic artifacts, refitting, and raw material survey reveals differential technological investment strategies employed by LSA groups. Chert was introduced during last occupation phase for systematic bladelet production through complex reduction sequences, likely due to its scarcity and superior knapping qualities. In contrast, quartz and quartzite were procured during all the occupation phases for simple flake production via shorter, simpler reduction sequences, reflecting their local abundance and fracture constraints. Preliminary comparison with contemporaneous LSA sequences from the broader region suggests that CHE followed a distinct technological trajectory, with bladelet production appearing significantly later in time, highlighting the importance of regional variability in shaping LSA technological behavior. The results demonstrate a strong relationship between raw material availability, quality, and technological investment, and contribute critical new data to the largely undocumented LSA record of Mozambique.

title: Bored Discs of Stone and Rain Control in Kaingo Game Reserve, Limpopo Province, South Africa
authors: Lyn Wadley; Ghilraen Laue; Wim Biemond
abstract: Bored disc fragments of quartzitic sandstone were excavated from Welgevonden Rock Shelter and collected from the surface of the talus slope of Dwaalhoek 11 Rock Shelter on Kaingo Game Reserve in the Waterberg. The fragments represent stages of manufacture, breakage, and occasional recycling as grinders. Naturally flat slabs were knapped, often bifacially, to shape discs. Then, small, rounded hollows were pecked to thin the center of both disc faces. Finally, a central hole was pecked and/or punched, probably using a short, narrow stone reamer. Large, sharp-edged discs may have been hafted axes. Small bored discs resemble stone spindle whorls used by Iron Age farmers, but they were probably imitations for ritual purposes. Eiland facies ceramic sherds were also excavated. Since farmers did not live in rock shelters, it seems likely that makers of Eiland ceramics used Welgevonden for working with rain. The performance of drilling discs to make spindle whorls may have been part of the ritual. A rock art motif at a nearby site suggests that the area was also used by Bushmen for working with rain. Conceptually, threads are important for Bushmen and for Iron Age farmers, and both groups link them to rain. Threads spun on spindle whorls are woven into fine cotton for Iron Age chiefs, who are charged with producing rain for their subjects. When Bushman rain specialists trance, they climb threads to access the sky. Here, or from water pits, they use threads to lead rain animals to slaughter.

Chronology and Funerary Practices Associated with Antennae Tumuli in Western Sahara
authors: Joaquim Soler; Helena Ventura; Isaac Rufí; Neus Coromina; Jordi Revelles; Maria Saña; Laura Moll; Narcís Soler
abstract: This study presents the results of the archaeological excavation of an antennae tumulus in Western Sahara, conducted at Wadi Lawash el Telli. While earlier research across the region had established a broad typological and chronological framework for prehistoric stone funerary monuments, the function and chronology of antennae tumuli had remained undocumented. Two AMS radiocarbon dates place the burial between 4417 and 4100 cal BP, providing the first absolute chronology for this type of monument in the Atlantic Sahara. These results position antennae tumuli at the end of the Late Neolithic sequence of stone funerary constructions, contemporaneous with crescent-shaped tumuli. Beyond confirming their funerary function, this study helps address the scarcity of chronological and cultural data relevant to understanding the development of prehistoric mortuary traditions in the region and offers new perspectives for future comparative studies across the Sahara.

title: An Unknown Roman Temple in Cyprus? Reading the Architectural Fragments from Latsithkia (District Limassol, Cyprus)
authors: Anna Urszula Kordas; Szymon Popławski; Monika Rekowska; Aleksandra Brzozowska-Jawornicka
abstract: Although Classical Greek religious traditions were well established in Cyprus, Greek-style temples appear to have been relatively rare. Newly documented and analyzed architectural fragments from the Latsithkia area, preserved in the museums of Episkopi and Limassol, suggest that a previously unknown temple may have existed in the chora of Kourion (Cyprus). The aims of this article are to present the architectural fragments with their stylistic and structural analysis and to explore the potential identification and location of the building from which they may have originated, while emphasizing the tentative nature of the reconstruction and the need for further field investigation. Based on the material presented, it may be inferred that the architectural fragments from the Latsithkia area once adorned a temple-like structure dating to the end of the first century CE that was constructed at the site of their discovery. The potential identification of a Greek-style temple from the Early Roman period in Latsithkia calls for a reassessment of architectural developments in Cyprus, possibly suggesting new Roman investment in extra muros sanctuaries.

title: Shopping Local and Trusted Traders: Identifying Production Zones and Trade Routes of Northern Italian Terra Sigillata Using Similarity Indices
abstract: Italian Terra Sigillata (ITS) was one of the most widely traded fine wares in the Roman world, seeing distribution across the Mediterranean and beyond. Northern Italian Terra Sigillata (NITS) has rarely been included in wider debates surrounding ITS, with its zones of production, consumption, and trade routes still matters of speculation. To better understand how NITS was produced and traded during the first century BCE and first century CE, an assemblage of 1,844 legible stamps on NITS from 24 sites in Northern Italy was analyzed using the Morisita-Horn Index of similarity. The similarity analysis generated two geographic clusters of sites containing similar NITS stamp assemblages, suggesting that two distinct production zones existed. Further analysis of the stamp assemblages within each cluster demonstrates limited chronological overlap between the two, implying they correspond to different phases of production. This pattern is corroborated by unstamped assemblages. Mapping the distribution of workshop output from each cluster also suggests that this ware was traded over short and long distances by different mechanisms. Within Northern Italy, it was primarily consumed a short distance from where it was produced, with little regional circulation. In contrast, output from both identified production zones had similar long-distance distribution to sites in the Balkans.

title: Asking Different Questions: 3D Scanning and the Refinement of the Typological Method in Hadrianic Portraiture
abstract: This study aims to identify imperial portraits through contextual and iconographic markers rather than from physiognomy and hairstyle. Modern scholarship categorizes portraits into types based on facial features and hair arrangements, applying standards facilitated by photography, a mid 19th-century invention that fundamentally altered expectations with regard to physical resemblance. The approach implies that ancient viewers recognized emperors through a facial likeness and fixed hairstyle. Using 3D scanning of seven Hadrianic-period sculptural portraits, analysis of provincial coinage, and a text by Arrian, we demonstrate that this methodology, while productive for identifying some relationships, does not fully describe how Roman imperial imagery functioned. Arrian explicitly states that schema (form/iconography) and location mattered more than a physical resemblance. Similarly, provincial coins of Hadrian display a range of physiognomic variations, thereby leaving the inscriptions and imperial context to indicate identity. Digital technology offers new tools in this regard: superimposition reveals that while some portraits demonstrate direct copying, others assigned to the same purported “type” share loose patterns. The evidence indicates a flexible system in which imperial symbolism and context took precedence over physiognomic likeness, with significant implications for how we identify portraits and understand Roman visual communication.

title: Divus Hadrianus, Divus Constantius Chlorus, and the Apotheosis of Hercules: The Tondo Reliefs of the Arch of Constantine
abstract: The second-century CE relief tondi now on the fourth-century CE Arch of Constantine are anomalous both in subject matter and in format. Among these eight reliefs, the scenes of the lion hunt and of the sacrifice to Hercules differ strikingly from the others, as well as from conventional iconography. The sacrifice to Hercules shows the image of the hero as an apparition in the heavens rather than a statue on a pedestal, a composition that perhaps calls attention to the unique status of Hercules as a mortal who won immortality through his noble deeds, just as worthy Roman emperors received apotheosis. The original patron of the tondi, probably Antoninus Pius, may have sought to justify the controversial deification of his predecessor Hadrian. The later reuse of the reliefs on the arch to honor Constantine similarly invoked the deification of his father, Constantius Chlorus, in support of Constantine’s claim to power.

title: Castellaraccio di Monteverdi (Civitella Paganico, Grosseto): A Deserted Medieval Village of the Ardenghesca
authors: Alessandro Sebastiani; Alessandro Carabia; Cleo Barbafiera; Massimo De Benetti; Marta De Pari; Matteo Penco; Luisa Russo; Alessandra Serra
abstract: This article presents the results of six years of archaeological excavations at Castellaraccio di Monteverdi, a minor fortified settlement in the middle valley of the Ombrone River in southern Tuscany. Previously known almost exclusively through 12th- and 13th-century CE documentary sources, the site now provides a tightly dated archaeological sequence that permits a reassessment of the foundation, function, and abandonment of a short-lived hilltop center within a contested territorial landscape. Excavations conducted by the IMPERO Project document episodic use of the hilltop in the Hellenistic period and possibly the early Middle Ages, with no evidence of structural or demographic continuity. The data place the formal establishment of the castle between the late 11th and early 12th centuries CE, followed by architectural investment, spatial reorganization, and economic specialization focused on storage and infrastructural control, including a bridge across the Ombrone River. Stratigraphic, architectural, and environmental evidence show that Castellaraccio was not a marginal or failed settlement but a selectively invested seigneurial site rendered redundant by planned territorial reorganization, particularly the foundation of the borgo franco of Paganico in 1292. Sporadic 14th-century reuse complicates narratives of abrupt abandonment and highlights archaeology’s role in reassessing models of incastellamento in medieval Tuscany.1

title: Mycenaeans in Messenia: Princes of Pylos, from Kalamata to Los Angeles and Athens
abstract: New discoveries from Mycenaean Pylos in southwest Greece were the focus of an exhibition inaugurated in early 2025 at the Archaeological Museum of Messenia (Kalamata). This exhibition traveled to the J. Paul Getty Museum Villa in Los Angeles in June of the same year for an expanded display, before returning to Greece in 2026 to be on view at the Hellenic National Archaeological Museum in Athens. The exhibition was unusual for its generous display of recently excavated material from tombs near the Palace of Nestor at Pylos. These tombs complemented selections from 10 Bronze Age sites in Messenia that preceded and were absorbed into Nestor’s kingdom. Together with a catalogue of essays and illustrations, the exhibition integrated archaeological excavation with digital documentation, historical and art historical interpretation, and scientific analysis of human remains. The results offer lasting lessons on the prehistoric Aegean (Bronze Age Greece).

title: Alexandreia Troas in the Hellenistic Period: War, Finance, and Civic Identity
abstract: This monograph is a significant contribution concerning Hellenistic kingdoms' effects on cities' and local communities' responses.Focusing on Alexandreia Troas in the Troad of western Asia Minor, Ellis-Evans shows how numismatic evidence can provide a more nuanced understanding of kings' urban foundations.Strabo, who cites Demetrius of Skepsis, says that Antigonus Monophthalmus first created Antigoneia Troas through a synoikism (ca.311-306 BCE) and that Lysimachus renamed it Alexandreia Troas (301 BCE).Typically, it has been assumed that the six communities discussed by Strabo (Skepsis, Kebren, Neandreia, Kolonai, Larisa, and Hamaxitos) were part of the original foundation.Dependent settlements, however, would not have been allowed to mint their own coins.Through die studies and redating of certain series of coinage, Ellis-Evans demonstrates that the physical size, imperial relations, and civic identity of Alexandreia Troas fluctuated over time.The book is organized into two parts: Part I has 11 chapters that provide the historical narrative of Alexandreia from its Hellenistic foundation until its life under the Roman emperor Commodus; part II is the numismatic catalogue.Chapter 1, the introduction, outlines the city's important location near the Hellespont and makes the case for using numismatic evidence since the site was spoliated and most surviving epigraphic and archaeological evidence comes from the Augustan colony.Chapter 2 presents the synoikism, which is the foundation for the rest of the book.Strabo only definitively says that Kebren and Skepsis were part of the original synoikism, and he notes that Lysimachus removed Skepsis (Strabo 13.1.26,33, 47, 52).Ellis-Evans suggests that the initial foundation included four settlements (Skepsis, Kebren, Neandreia, and Kolonai).Alexandreia adopted the grazing horse from Neandreia's coinage by 300 BCE, and Neandreia was not occupied past the late fourth century BCE.No evidence for an independent Kolonai makes its participation likely.Hamaxitos and Larisa appear not to be part of the foundation, since contemporary decrees of Hamaxitos and Antigoneia exist, and Larisa Alexandreia Troas in the Hellenistic Period: War, Finance, and Civic Identity

Beyond loom weights: Contextualising crescent-shaped objects as administrative instruments in Late Bronze Age Konya Karahöyük (south-central Anatolia)
abstract: Crescent-shaped objects (CSOs) are common in the Bronze Age archaeological contexts of Anatolia. Particularly for the Middle Bronze Age, these objects were routinely interpreted as loom weights for textile production. While arguments exist for different uses of CSOs, such as identity markers, receipts for goods, fishing net weights or pottery handles, incomplete data from a fully recovered archaeological context prevent further assertions for the Late Bronze Age. This article presents new data from the Late Bronze Age I (ca 16th century BCE) strata of the south-central Anatolian site of Konya Karahöyük, suggesting an alternative use for CSOs. Konya Karahöyük is a major Bronze Age hub in the Konya plain, with numerous examples of CSOs dating to the Old Assyrian Colony (OAC) period uncovered in previous excavations conducted at the site from 1953 to 1992. The new round of excavations, which started in 2022, yielded a significant collection providing an opportunity to reinterpret the functions of these objects. The CSOs found in association with pithoi and sealings in a grain and wine storage and preparation context offer evidence of CSOs used as administrative devices. We suggest that CSOs of the 16th-century BCE levels of Konya Karahöyük were utilised as a part of an administrative kit, conceivably accustomed to control time or check the capacity of grain and liquid containers. In the Late Bronze Age, a period marked by the advancement of centralised administrative systems, this new layer of evidence suggests that CSOs may have served a function distinct from their traditionally accepted role as loom weights, which dominates Middle Bronze Age interpretations.

title: Ephebeia in southern Asia Minor: A new funerary inscription of an ephebos candidate from Antalya
abstract: This article presents a funerary inscription dated to the late second and early third centuries AD. It is currently held in the Antalya Necropolis Museum, but its exact provenance remains unknown. The text is carved on a richly decorated round altar, beneath a relief depicting a young man wearing a chiton and holding a torch in his left hand. The inscription identifies him as Glaukos, a foster child who died at the age of 17 during the enkrisis , the examination for admission to the ephebeia . This newly presented text provides two important new insights into the ephebeia of the Roman Imperial period. Firstly, it appears to be the first inscription to mention the age of admission. Secondly, it shows that candidates from gymnasium groups also underwent the enkrisis . The article further discusses the striking similarities between athletic and gymnasium training practices, which are also evident in the age limit for admission and torch races, and proposes a revised definition of enkrisis. Additionally, the article compiles and analyses inscriptions indicating the presence of epheboi and torch races in the regions of southern Asia Minor likely associated with this inscription: Lycia, Pamphylia and Pisidia. Lastly, the study examines the rationale for seeking the inscription’s most probable provenance in eastern Lycia or western Pamphylia.

title: The divine Mount Koeros: A new nomos inscription of Antiochus I of Commagene
authors: Mehmet Alkan; Charles V. Crowther; Margherita Facella; Kahraman Yağız
abstract: In October 2021 the presence of ancient remains on a ridge below the 2000m summit of Kımıl Dağı in the Gerger district of Adıyaman province was reported to Adıyaman Museum. Investigations by archaeologists from the Museum revealed the existence of a previously unreported sanctuary belonging to the ruler cult of Antiochus I of Commagene. Two substantial limestone stelai recovered from the site have now been brought to the Perrhe Archaeological Park. One of the stelai carries a relief showing Antiochus shaking hands with a divine figure seated on a mountain peak. A long inscription recording the establishment of the sanctuary and a sacred law regulating its associated cult begins on the reverse face of the relief stele and continues onto a separate block and both faces of a second stele. In this article we provide a first publication and analysis of the inscription, and in the light of the information provided by it reconsider the significance of the relief. The novel features presented by the relief and the inscription raise new questions about the development of Antiochus’ ruler cult and the weight of local religious tradition in shaping its form which are explored in the concluding sections of the article.

title: A late antique bath complex with an honorific statue display on the Tetrapylon Street at Aphrodisias
authors: Joshua J. Thomas; Duru Yağmur Başaran; Ine Jacobs
abstract: An imposing masonry structure with an arched statue niche in its façade overlooks the key north–south avenue in Aphrodisias known as the Tetrapylon Street. While this structure has traditionally been dated to the Early Imperial period, recent archaeological investigation has offered new insights concerning its chronology and function. This paper presents the results of this research. It is shown here that the structure was originally part of a larger bathing complex constructed when the entire Tetrapylon Street was renewed following a destructive earthquake of the later fifth century AD. Two components of the statue monument displayed in the building’s niched façade are also identified and discussed. Originally made in the first century AD, both components seem to have been recycled and reworked to commemorate a new benefactor involved in the late-fifth-century construction programme. They therefore provide a striking new case study that fits into the growing scholarly discourse on the long lives of ancient monuments in late antique Anatolia.

title: Architectural arrangements of the bouleuterion terrace in Metropolis to honour the city’s euergetai and their clues as to the location of the Agora
abstract: In the course of archaeological excavations at Metropolis between 1999 and 2004 when the hall of the city council (boule) was unearthed, an important inscription now referred to as the ‘Apollonios Decree’ was discovered on the bouleuterion terrace. This inscription decrees that a statue honouring Apollonios is to be erected ‘in that part of the Agora where it will be the most conspicuous’. Ongoing excavations have revealed a concentration of sculptures in the same area, further strengthening the hypothesis that the Agora was located on the bouleuterion terrace. The present study was undertaken to better understand and interpret the functions of this part of the site based on the findings of excavations on the northern side of the bouleuterion in 2018. It also aims to ascertain if this is the area referred to in inscriptions as the place where public benefactors (euergetai) were honoured with boule-decreed statues, to determine if the statue dedicated to Apollonios of Metropolis was indeed located here, and to propose a possible location for the as-yet unidentified Metropolitan agora.

title: ‘May your entry here be in peace’: Christian epigraphy and iconography in late antique northern Mesopotamia
abstract: This article explores late antique material evidence of Christianity in northern Mesopotamia, focusing on epigraphic and iconographic sources to trace its gradual integration into Roman society. Organised into two main sections, the study synthesises recent scholarship to contextualise these developments within the region’s commercial, military and cultural frameworks. Particular attention is given to addressing the imbalances in historical and archaeological visibility between urban centres and rural areas, drawing on findings from intensified research in northern Mesopotamia over the past two decades. The text provides a previously missing compilation of the region’s known late antique Christian inscriptions, paintings, carvings and mosaics. It discusses key themes, such as the interplay between Syriac and Greek as epigraphic languages, featuring the predominance of Greek inscriptions in cities like Edessa, Tella and Nṣībīn, alongside a gradual rise in Syriac epigraphy in rural areas by the sixth century. It also examines linguistic and symbolic markers of Christianisation, including the increasing use of crosses, monotheistic declarations and the adaptation of pre-existing visual motifs into Christian iconography. Finally, by integrating GIS data, the study delves into religious transformation’s spatial and socio-cultural dimensions in late antique northern Mesopotamia.

title: A Greco-Turkish Alexander the Great: The Karamanli Phyllada from 1843
abstract: The worldwide reception of Alexander the Great is remarkable, although the Turkish-speaking Greek Orthodox population of the Ottoman Empire is critically understudied in this context. This article addresses this shortfall by looking into a publication in Karamanlidika from 1843. It also analyses the largely unexplored Karamanli print culture in the first half of the 19th century. Published in Constantinople, this 336-page book is a translation into Karamanlidika of the Greek Phyllada tou Megalexandrou , translated by Agapios Papazoglou. Over 1,000 copies were pre-ordered by subscribers, with most of his audience being from Cappacodia and having Karamanli names. A few subscribers came from present-day Bulgaria and had mostly Slavic names and a handful from Cappadocia had Armenian names.Women and Muslims/Turks are manifestly absent from the list. This article employs historical methods, as well as textual and intertextual tools of research to investigate a book that falls within the worldwide legacy of Alexander the Great, and that was translated and published with a view to enlightening its audience, imbuing it with the virtues of logic and morality intended to make them better people and better Christians.

title: Architectural terracotta fragments from Sinope: Aeolian influences on the Archaic Architecture of the city
abstract: Eight architectural terracotta fragments uncovered during the 2021 excavations at Sinop are the focus of this study. These fragments, comprising lateral simae with revetment plaques and raking simae, are of importance, as they provide new insights into Archaic-period architecture and workshop practices in the city. The painted L-shaped lateral simae, with revetment plaques decorated with triangles, rectangles, bead-and-reel moulding and tongue pattern, and the probably painted raking simae, adorned with triangles and rectangles, exhibit close typological and functional parallels with architectural terracottas from Larisa in the Aeolis region. This suggests that the architectural terracottas used in a building constructed at Sinope may have been produced by a workshop based in the Aeolian region. These fragments, which can be dated to the last quarter of the sixth century BC, make it possible to form an idea of the appearance of the earliest roof of Sinope decorated with architectural terracotta elements identified to date.

title: A political history of the Pergamene theatre: Actors, kings and audience
abstract: This article investigates the political history of the Pergamene theatre with respect to developments in Greek theatre architecture and performance during the Hellenistic Age. Pergamon’s late Hellenistic theatre presents two distinctive features: a semicircular orkhēstra prefiguring Roman design, and a two-story wooden proskēnion that could be dismantled after performances. The article contextualises these features within broader Greek theatrical developments from the fifth to the second century BCE. By reconstructing various theatrical events – from dithyrambs to dramas and assembly meetings – the paper analyses how different scenic layouts articulated power relationships among actors, kings and audiences. The analysis reveals how scenic configurations were progressively refined from the Classical to the Hellenistic age in favour of individual actors and political leaders over the khoros and community representatives. The paper examines how Pergamon’s distinctive scenic layout embodied the socio-political dynamics of the Attalid autocracy while maintaining connections to Greek democratic theatrical traditions.

title: From the looting of Toprakkale (Van) to the rise of Tophane (Istanbul): What the red glossy pottery reveals
abstract: Urartian red glossy ceramics and Ottoman Tophane pipes share a striking similarity in colour and surface gloss. Yet the question of whether this resemblance has a common basis has remained unresolved. This article explores the origins of this similarity. It appears to have its origins in the looting of Toprakkale and the subsequent transfer of artefacts to Istanbul. The looting of Toprakkale (Van) – the royal residence of the Urartian Kingdom in the seventh century BCE – began in earnest in the 1800s, during which numerous archaeological artefacts were illicitly transported to Istanbul and subsequently dispersed to museums worldwide. Among these artefacts, the distinctively bright red pottery of Urartu attracted the attention of Istanbul’s elite and, it appears, eventually came to the notice of the craftsmen producing Tophane pipes. The Tophane craftsmen apparently studied these pieces – remarkable for their colour and luminosity – and ultimately sourced comparable raw materials from the Lake Van region. In doing so, the Tophane workshops developed a distinctive ceramic style inspired by Urartu, employing a slip preparation closely analogous to Urartian production methods, and catering to the tastes of the Ottoman elite.

title: Negotiating antiquities: Institutionalisation of French archaeological research in Anatolia (1890–1930)
abstract: This article examines the process that led to the establishment of the French Archaeological Institute in Istanbul in 1930, situating it within the broader context of French cultural diplomacy and inter-imperial competition in the late Ottoman Empire and early Turkish Republic, as well as the scientific curiosity towards Anatolian and Turkish Islamic antiquities. The article argues that the creation of the institute was not a predetermined outcome but rather the product of a protracted negotiation involving French and Ottoman/Turkish governmental, diplomatic and scholarly actors. These negotiations were shaped by shifting political contexts, conflicting institutional agendas and the broader redefinition of Franco-Turkish relations following World War I and the Allied occupation of Constantinople. By tracing the evolving proposals for the establishment of an institute from the late 19th century through the 1920s, and by focusing on key figures such as Albert Gabriel, the study highlights how scholarly interests and cultural diplomacy were entangled with political sovereignty and national identity. The institutional negotiations examined here reveal not only the challenges of maintaining cultural influence in a changing geopolitical landscape but also provide a window into the broader dynamics of scholarly diplomacy, negotiation and institutional formation in the early 20th century.

title: EARLY BRONZE AGE SEAL IMPRESSIONS FROM THERASIA: NEW EVIDENCE FOR SEAL USE IN THE CYCLADES AND THE EMERGENCE OF SCRIPT IN AN AEGEAN CONTEXT
authors: Kostas Sbonias; Iris Tzachili; Georgia S. Kordatzaki
abstract: This paper contributes to the understanding of Early Bronze Age sealing practices in the Cyclades, focusing on recent findings from the settlement site of Koimisis on Therasia. It discusses two seal impressions stamped on a jar handle from an Early Cycladic II context. One aligns with the broader Aegean glyptic tradition, while the second could represent the earliest evidence associated with developments tied to the broader context of script formation in the Aegean. The study analyses the context of the find, the iconography and the style of the seal impressions, and explores the associations and meaning of the signs. Additionally, the petrographic analysis of the pottery fragment provides insights into the vase’s origin and the broader interpretative context of the impressions.

title: EXPLORING POTTERY PRODUCTION AT PROTOPALATIAL TO POSTPALATIAL PALAIKASTRO (EAST CRETE) THROUGH INTEGRATED PETROGRAPHIC AND ELEMENTAL ANALYSIS
authors: John Gait; Noémi S. Müller; Evangelia Kiriatzi; Carl Knappett
abstract: This paper presents an archaeological material science study of pottery production and use at the Bronze Age Minoan town of Palaikastro, east Crete, from Middle Minoan IIA to Late Minoan IIIA2 ( c. 1850 to 1300 BC), through petrographic analysis of thin sections and wavelength dispersive X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy. The compositions of 288 archaeological samples are compared with geological references collected from the site and its adjacent hinterland. The results of this study indicate that throughout this period the majority of the archaeological pottery assemblage was probably produced using materials from a small number of geological outcrops local to the town; however, the manner in which these resources were utilised changed significantly over time, particularly between the Proto- and Neopalatial periods.

title: EAST OF KNOSSOS, WEST OF MALIA. CHANGING SETTLEMENT PATTERNS BETWEEN TWO MAJOR MINOAN POLITIES
abstract: The goal of this study is the presentation and evaluation of settlement patterns in the region between the Minoan palatial centres of Knossos and Malia, mainly on the north coast of Heraklion, during the second millennium BCE. The approach is based on new archaeological data from large- and small-scale rescue excavations and supervised digging activities in the context of public or private construction projects. Existing archaeological knowledge of this particular region is also taken into consideration. Following a chronological sequence, a Prepalatial (Middle Minoan [MM] IA) long wall, which is located 250 m south of the hill of Paliochora at Amnissos and belongs to a wider architectural planning of access control from the coast of Amnissos to the hinterland, is presented along with a contemporary rural installation in Stalida. An extensive settlement in the area of the Amirandes Hotel in Kato Gouves is dated mainly to the Protopalatial period and shows close affinities with Malia. Of the same date and cultural orientation is the extensive occupation near Agriana, which continues to exist in the early Neopalatial period. The Minoan settlement at Kastri in Chersonesos is dated to MM IIIB, while an earlier Protopalatial phase was also identified. A number of other sites in the district of Gouves are dated to Late Minoan (LM) III. A unique example of continuous habitation from LM IB to LM IIIB was excavated near the local primary school in Gournes. The decrease of sites in MM IIIB–LM IA and the scarcity of LM IB settlements, in contrast to the density of Protopalatial installations, confirm the centralisation of the habitation model during the late Neopalatial period, probably due to the expansionist policy of Knossos. However, the balance of power of the two palatial centres over the region under discussion shifted through time, with Malia having control of most of the area during the Protopalatial period and Knossos expanding its influence during the Prepalatial, Neopalatial and Final Palatial periods.
