title: Assessment of the threatened geoglyphs of Alto Caramucho, in the Atacama Desert, using new technologies
authors: Gonzalo Pimentel G.; Luis Pérez R.; Mariana Ugarte F.; Juan Gili H.; Javier Arévalo L.; Rodrigo Mendoza; Manuel Pérez-Carrasco; Marcela Sepúlveda
abstract: Photographed over more than two decades, alterations to the Alto Caramucho geoglyphs in the Atacama Desert show the unfolding of a heritage disaster. This article presents research that integrates new digital technologies (photogrammetry and artificial intelligence) for the evaluation and documentation of the deterioration of the geoglyphs.

title: Cultural landscapes reveal 5700 years of human–environment interaction on Curaçao
authors: Christina M. Giovas; Claudia T. Kraan; Kelsey M. Lowe; Michiel Kappers; Amy Ann Victorina; Christine Conlan; Shira Yoshimi Maezumi
abstract: From 2022–2025, the Curaçao Cultural Landscape Project conducted archaeological and palaeoecological investigations of Rif Sint Marie and Jan Thiel, Curaçao, to reconstruct long-term landscape history. Results reveal a 5700-year settlement history, strategic adaptations enacted by diverse cultural groups and the legacy of past human activities within the contemporary landscape.

title: Forced resettlement as an imperial strategy: evidence from the Ligures Baebiani in Roman Samnium
abstract: Forced population resettlement constituted a strategic instrument in the territorial expansion of the Roman Empire. Survey and geophysical data from Macchia di Circello (Campania) offer novel evidence on the settlement of a forcibly relocated community, the Ligures Baebiani, transferred from Liguria to Samnium in the second century BC.

title: Memory of the kings of Bia/Urartu: inscribed royal bowls from Western Asia
authors: Annarita Stefania Bonfanti; Roberto Dan; Nzhdeh Yeranyan; Astgh Poghosyan
abstract: Through autoptic examination, macrophotography and comparative palaeography, this study identifies changes in sign forms, engraving techniques and associated iconography in a corpus of Urartian inscribed bronze bowls. Evolving scribal practices, and the transformation of monumental cuneiform into portable media, highlight the role of inscribed metal vessels in expressing Urartian kingship.

title: Mousterian occupations in Dalmatia, Croatia: early dates suggested by optically stimulated luminescence
authors: Ivor Karavanić; Slobodan Miko; Marko Banda; Giovanni Boschian; Rory Becker; Fred H. Smith
abstract: New dates from Mujina pećina, obtained through optically stimulated luminescence (OSL), provide the earliest radiometric dates yet recorded from an archaeological site in Dalmatia, Croatia. Associated Mousterian artefacts indicate that humans were present in this part of the Adriatic region c . 30 000 years earlier than previously believed.

title: Pleistocene occupations of Northern Khorasan: first evidence from Esfarayen Plain, north-eastern Iranian Plateau
authors: Ali Sadraei; Mahya Azar; Javad Khodadoust
abstract: Field surveys in the Esfarayen Plain, north-eastern Iran, documented evidence of hominin occupations at 24 localities in Northern Khorasan. These findings help transform our understanding of Palaeolithic populations in north-eastern Iran and underscore the importance of this region in the dispersal of hominins into the interior of Asia.

title: Revisiting Hazar Merd Cave: 100 years after Dorothy Garrod’s excavations
authors: Saman Heydari-Guran; Nemat Hariri; Saber Ahmed Saber; Faramarz Azizi; Stefano Benazzi; Francesco Berna; Hashim Hama Abdulla
abstract: First excavated in 1928 by Dorothy Garrod, Hazar Merd represents the earliest documented Palaeolithic site in the Zagros Mountains and a landmark in regional archaeological research. Nearly a century later, renewed investigations are refining the site’s stratigraphy and cultural sequence, providing a more nuanced understanding of its long-term occupation.

title: Visualising uses of the past: an art contest with the Guaiquerí of Margarita Island, Venezuela
abstract: In 2021, submissions to an art contest on Margarita Island, Venezuela, showcased Guaiquerí identity. Archaeology was largely absent from the artworks, but areas for meaningful future contributions connecting with existing identity narratives were identified. Intangible heritage, especially the Virgen del Valle and fishing, emerges as central to Indigenous identity formation.

title: Xiaeryamakebu: life and death on the Tibetan Plateau in the late second millennium BCE
authors: Meng Guo; Jinhui Xiang; Wei Du; Feihu Wang; Zhen Wang; Zhanwang Liu; Yahui Qiu; Yongming Xiao; Honghai Chen
abstract: Excavations at Xiaeryamakebu, located in the Qaidam Basin of north-west China, have uncovered a large Bronze Age settlement that includes residences and cemeteries. The site provides crucial insights into the Nuomuhong culture, its mortuary practices and local adaptation to the Tibetan Plateau.

title: Silk and sacrifice at Sanxingdui: early evidence of silk use in ancient Shu, south-west China
authors: Jianbo Guo; Ruochen Ge; Qiutong Cai; Jingyu Tian; Lu Yang
abstract: Organic materials are rare but important components of the archaeological record. Here, the authors analyse textile residues adhering to artefacts excavated at Sanxingdui in Sichuan Province, China, a site associated with the ancient Shu culture. Through combined consideration of fibre characteristics, colouring practices, weaving structures and excavation contexts, the authors argue that, by the Late Shang period (1300–1046 BC), silk was in large-scale use at the site and, together with bronze, jade and ivory artefacts, was an important component of the Sanxingdui sacrificial system. The findings help situate ancient Shu within the broader trajectory of early Chinese silk traditions.

title: Iberian copper and Bronze Age Europe: Late Bronze Age mining and supply at Las Minillas (Badajoz, Spain)
authors: Juan Latorre-Ruiz; Mark A. Hunt Ortiz; Zofia Anna Stos-Gale; Aurélien Burlot; Jacobo Vázquez-Paz; Miguel Ángel de Dios Pérez; Manuel Grueso-Montero; Mikael Fauvelle; Marta Díaz-Guardamino; Johan Ling
abstract: Despite abundant copper deposits, the deep history of copper mining in Iberia has not been as extensively studied as in other European ore-rich areas. Here, the authors present new radiocarbon dates that demonstrate Late Bronze Age copper mining at Las Minillas, near Granja de Torrehermosa (southern Spain). Extensive mining infrastructure and abundant stone tools further identify Las Minillas as one of the largest Late Bronze Age copper-mining complex securely dated in Spain. The authors argue for a re-evaluation of links between southern Iberia and other European copper-producing and consuming regions, highlighting its potential as a major Late Bronze Age copper-producing hub.

title: Current challenges to archaeology in the United States: a story in three crises
abstract: Archaeology in the United States is facing unprecedented challenges.Changes to federal legislation on cultural heritage protections, attacks on museums and higher education institutions, divestment from research funding agencies and mass layoffs within government departments have created a perfect storm of daily challenges in the teaching and practice of archaeology in tandem with concern for the future of the discipline.While the Trump administration is not targeting archaeology per se, the current precarious status is a confluence of three crises that are having an outsized impact on our field.I hope in the following to illuminate these crises, some of which rarely make it into the national or international news cycles.

title: China’s 2025 ‘Top 10 Archaeological Discoveries’
authors: A. Mark Pollard; Wei Wang; Ruiliang Liu
abstract: Although China has a long tradition of historical writing, antiquarian scholarship and collecting, archaeology as a modern discipline is comparatively young, and yet the scale and volume of modern fieldwork in China probably now outstrip those in any other country.Every year for more than 30 years, the archaeology sector in China has selected 10 archaeological sites as its 'Top 10 Archaeological Discoveries in China', popularly known as the 'Oscars of Chinese Archaeology'.Founded in 1990 as an initiative between the Chinese Archaeological Society and the bi-weekly newspaper China Cultural Relics News (中国文物报), the selection process was upgraded in 2009 to be supervised by the National Cultural Heritage Administration (an administrative agency affiliated with the Ministry of Culture and Tourism of the People's Republic of China), establishing it as a highly authoritative industry benchmark.In 2019, the selection regulations were revised, and the approval process was further standardised.Projects can be either archaeological research programmes or excavations conducted during infrastructure construction, and they are nominated by the organisations themselves.Decisions are announced annually in April, covering the previous calendar year.Our aim here is to bring this internationally important competition to a wider audience through a description of the selection process and a summary of this year's 10 sites, rather than to provide comments on the final selection.A panel of more than 100 council members of the Chinese Archaeological Society assess the applications and create a short list of 20 projects, which are then evaluated by a committee of around 21 senior archaeologists.This process requires excavation team leaders to deliver a 15-minute presentation followed by a Q&A session; these are now livestreamed across multiple national and social-media platforms, allowing the public to follow professional archaeological debate in real time.The scale of this engagement can be considerable: when the final-selection process moved entirely online in 2020, the livestream attracted 22.78 million cumulative views by the morning of the second day, after a full day and a half of project presentations, subsequently exceeding 40 million views following the final announcement.This openness not only strengthens professional scrutiny and accountability, but also turns the selection into a major annual event for public engagement, stimulating wider interest in archaeological research and heritage protection in China.Importantly, the nomination process often precedes the publication in formal or traditional channels for major excavations, so it is an extremely useful way of keeping abreast of the most recent finds for both Chinese and international scholars.

title: Crafting power in Kush: faience production and state control in the Napatan region
authors: Rennan Lemos; Kathryn Howley; Siobhan Shinn; Shadia Abdu Rabo
abstract: Sanam Temple lies in the heart of Napata, the capital of the Kushite Empire in the first millennium BCE. Excavations at the temple (2018–2020) have revealed the remains of a mid-seventh-century BCE faience-production workshop, comprising three firing pits, two mudbrick basins and various faience objects, numerous beads, small shells and wasters found in compacted ashy layers. Here, the authors argue that this evidence provides insight not only into manufacturing techniques and restricted access to goods, but also into aspects of state control in Napatan Nubia, expanding our understanding of the Kushite state in Iron Age north-east Africa.

title: Ceramic petrography in Early Òṣogbo: craft technology, regional exchanges and social convergence
abstract: Excavations at Early Òṣogbo, a frontier market town in south-western Nigeria occupied c . AD 1590–1725, recovered ceramics associated with the Ọ̀ṣun, Ọ̀yọ́ and Ifẹ̀ traditions. To understand how these styles converged, the authors undertook thin-section petrographic analysis of 43 ceramic samples to examine clay composition. The results, they argue, show that potters across a 150km-long region consistently used micaceous kaolinitic clays from alluvial corridors. These clays, low in porosity and resistant to thermal stress, were well-suited for production of culinary wares and smoking pipes. Their use demonstrates knowledge circulation and technological borrowing through political expansion, mobility and trade networks.

title: Eating under Christian rule: isotopic evidence for food access and resilience among a medieval Muslim minority in Iberia
authors: Patxi Pérez-Ramallo; Jesús Sesma Sesma; Olatz Villanueva Zubizarreta; Patrick Roberts
abstract: Muslim minorities are documented as taxpayers or legal subjects in medieval Europe, but rarely as individuals or households. This study examines carbon and nitrogen stable isotopes from 120 individuals buried at Torre Monreal, Tudela (Navarre, Spain) between the late eleventh and fifteenth centuries to build a picture of everyday food access in an Islamic community under Christian rule. The results, the authors argue, show a long-term reorganisation of diet that reflects historical narratives on the legal accessibility and market availability of freshwater and terrestrial resources, and are presented here as evidence for adaptive food practices rather than dietary assimilation.

title: Castaways at the end of the world: ongoing archaeological research at Franklin Bay, Isla de los Estados
authors: Nicolas C. Ciarlo; Carlos G. Landa; Alejandra Raies; Sebastian L. Avila; Roberto Ulloa; Atilio Francisco J. Zangrando
abstract: Ongoing archaeological research at Lacroix Inlet, in Franklin Bay on Isla de los Estados, part of the Atlantic-Pacific sailing route since the early seventeenth century, has provided new information on shipwreck remains and a temporary camp possibly linked with the schooner brig Espora (1873) of the renowned Argentine sailor Luis Piedra Buena.

title: Polyvalent approaches to ancient Egyptian religion beyond the Eurocentric lens

Łysa Góra in north-eastern Poland: a key Early Iron Age site on the ‘Amber Route’
authors: Bartłomiej Kaczyński; Andrzej Maciałowicz; Wojciech Janusz Borkowski; Cezary Sobczak; Michał Aniszewski
abstract: Excavations at the site of Łysa Góra in north-eastern Poland have revealed La Tène artefacts such as a Berru -type helmet. Functioning as a fortified settlement, production centre and ritual site, Łysa Góra was a key hub on the amber trade route, facilitating long-distance exchange and interaction.

title: Social dynamics of toxic metal industry in medieval Europe: Peak District lead production, AD 600–1500
authors: Christopher P. Loveluck; Hannah J. O’Regan; Anna Bloxam; Catrin Fear; Jane Evans; Simon Chenery; Carolyn Chenery; Colin Merrony; Fiona E. Moore; Angela Darlington
abstract: The Derbyshire Peak District in central England was one of the largest lead-producing regions in medieval Europe, yet the early history of production is obscure. Here, the authors use tooth-enamel-based lead concentrations accumulated in childhood in three cemeteries, linked to radiocarbon dates, to identify the development of post-Roman lead smelting from the mid-seventh century, with large-scale production and contamination around key mines, including Castleton, by the mid-eighth century AD. Intra- and inter-site comparisons of lead concentrations hint at the social dynamics of producer communities that may provide a benchmark for identifying lead- and silver-producing communities in medieval Europe more widely.

title: Upper Palaeolithic mariners? Evaluating experimental evidence for intentional early seafaring
abstract: Brought to popular consciousness by Thor Heyerdahl in the 1940s, the role of seafaring in human migration has been intensely debated. Aiming to stimulate discussion around the ways in which experimental archaeology is used to support such grand narratives, the authors of this debate critically assess a recent claim for Upper Palaeolithic seafaring in the Japanese archipelago. Here, they argue that creating a boat for which there is no archaeological evidence with generic tools that were not widely available in the region risks a confounding circularity of logic.

title: Excavating a possible Christianisation mission: the medieval stronghold in Pyrzyce
authors: Andrzej Janowski; Kamila Baraniecka-Olszewska; Aleksander Paroń
abstract: Historical accounts of Otto of Bamberg’s twelfth-century Christianisation mission in Pyrzyce, Poland, have inspired archaeological excavations, which in turn influenced anthropological research into contemporary religious imagery. Archaeological investigations at Pyrzyce’s early medieval stronghold thus inform broader scholarly recognition of the past religious landscape and its present transformation.

title: Bringing past into present: Transitions, truth and reckoning with unmarked residential school graves
authors: Clinton N. Westman; Micaela Champagne; Terence Clark; Scott Hamilton; Nicholas Laluk; Andrew Martindale; Lindsay Martel Montgomery; H. Max Pospisil; Sarah Shulist; Kisha Supernant; Winona Wheeler
abstract: This conversation began as a roundtable at the 2023 joint meeting of the American Anthropological Association and the Canadian Anthropology Society in Toronto. The roundtable was part of the Executive Program and was intended as a follow-up to Kisha Supernant’s keynote presentation, which was entitled ‘Truth before transition. Reimagining anthropology as restorative justice.’ Considering the sensitive nature of the topic, we responded to a selection of written questions from the audience rather than taking open questions. The discussion was webcast, then transcribed and redacted. This article includes a portion of the question period as well as a contextual introduction that was not part of the initial conversation.

title: Beyond metrics of resilience and survival in Mediterranean landscape archaeologies
abstract: In recent years, alongside increasing interest in collapse narratives, Mediterranean landscape archaeologists have turned to resilience theory and concepts like sustainability to examine the complexity of social responses to environmental stress and to counter a predominant focus on catastrophism and decline. Yet the revamping of systems theory has its pitfalls, most notably in its reductionist language, its sidelining of human agency and its privileging of normative claims of success or failure. In this paper I build on cross-disciplinary critiques of resilience to highlight problems with metrics of stability or vulnerability, macrohistorical functionalism, patchy material chronologies and the obscuring of social dynamics. I argue that research on past human–environment relationships needs more attention to landscape time and smaller-scale practices, and advocate studying the political dimensions that structured how past communities created and managed liveable conditions in uneven ways.

title: Destruction as creation: modes of intra-active becoming in a created and built world
abstract: This provocation seeks to stimulate discussion by highlighting an alternative way of looking at the actions of destruction and creation, not as opposing forces but as an ongoing process of transformation. Destruction encompasses a variety of material and symbolic transformations, which go hand in hand with the creation of new possibilities. Therefore, destruction is not an antagonism to creation but – following Karen Barad’s agential realism – a mode of intra-active becoming. Far from being a theory in its own right, this paper presents a perspective that opens up the possibility of encountering archaeological discourses of destruction and creation from a posthumanist lens.

title: Towards an ecology of medieval mining towns: linking social and environmental changes
abstract: This paper proposes an ecological framework for understanding medieval mining towns as dynamic socio-ecological systems shaped by flows of matter, energy, capital and information. Drawing on concepts from human and political ecology, it examines how mining, technology and power structures interacted to produce feedback loops and tipping points that transformed both society and the environment. A case study of Kutná Hora (Czechia) illustrates these mechanisms, showing how the discovery of silver triggered cycles of population growth, technological innovation and capital accumulation, whilst also causing deforestation, pollution and social stratification. The study highlights how medieval mining towns functioned as adaptive, self-organizing systems embedded in global economic networks, revealing early forms of extractive capitalism and environmental change. This ecological perspective offers a heuristic model for analysing historical urban environments and their long-term sustainability, bridging archaeology, history and environmental science.

title: Institutional economics and the Viking Age: a response to Anders Ögren et al.
authors: Terri L. Barnes; Geoffrey M. Hodgson
abstract: An ‘institutional turn’ has been detected in archaeology, with several scholars drawing from institutional economics to help explain various economic and political developments, including in the Viking Age. Generally, institutional analysis encompasses both political and cultural change, casting light on underlying rule systems, motivations, and mechanisms. This note responds to an article in Archaeological Dialogues by Anders Ögren et al., which argues for the application of the new institutional economics to viking studies, but focuses largely on one author, Douglass North, from that tradition. North’s views evolved, and in some respects he moved closer to the ideas of Thorstein Veblen, who was part of the original institutional economics. Overall, we need to draw more widely from institutional economics, including from inspiring earlier contributions.

title: The fungal lives of ruins: paths forward for a mushroom archaeology
abstract: Recent literature within archaeology and heritage studies has highlighted the need for multispecies and more-than-human approaches that go beyond human exceptionalism in the past and within the remains of the past in the present. Responding to these developments, this paper highlights a previously underrepresented group of cohabitants within human societies and their ruins – fungi. The paper demonstrates the need to account for fungi in archaeology, given that fungi can be both decomposers (living off traces of the past) and symbionts (forging connections for healthier multispecies ecologies). As such, four principles for ‘a mushroom archaeology’ are proposed by drawing on the work done within the ongoing ‘fungal turn’ in social sciences, humanities and the popular imagination. As an example of how this can be done, recent archaeological work on German World War II era ruins in northeastern Norway is drawn into dialogue with ongoing research with a local citizen science group that has begun surveying the unique fungal ecologies of these post-conflict remains. In the process, this paper demonstrates how focusing on fungi reveals a previously overlooked archaeological data source and underscores the need to notice the emergent more-than-human subterranean ecologies created in the wake of human use and ruination that underpin life in the present and future.

title: The Paradoxes That Create the Space for Treating Archaeological Heritage as a Target in War
abstract: This article aims to put considerations of threats of damage and destruction to cultural heritage in periods of conflict into a wider context, looking at the nature of war itself as a cultural form. Taking a long-term perspective derived from other work on conflict archaeology, it will start from the premise that a concern for the fate of ‘things’ (however ancient) is a particular pathology of modernity and it is this pathology that creates the conditions under which objects of cultural value are chosen for attention by aggressors and for particular protection by defenders. We shall address war as a realm where violent destruction—of people and places—is the paramount aim, and thereby the equation of people with objects representative of those people becomes an essential part of the discourse of war-making: this in part explains how cultural objects become targets. There is more to war than destruction however: it is an aspect frequently overlooked that wars also create new things—among them new classes of people, new artefacts, new landscapes and new forms of cultural expression. The aftermath of wars also allows things that were destroyed to be remade and re-modelled. As a cultural activity, war is both destructive and creative. Taking this deliberately provocative approach raises important issues about contemporary attitudes to the destruction of heritage and its protection in wartime.

title: Antiracism in Online Archaeology Teaching: An Effort in Educational Reckoning
abstract: Drawing from a collaborative teaching and design partnership, the authors present Knowing the Past , a four-course online specialization on the Coursera platform designed to introduce archaeology through an antiracist lens. By integrating decolonial content and antiracist teaching practices in an online open global learning environment, the case study offers a model for how universities can take concrete, reparative steps through what and how they teach. The example also integrates antiracist theory into course design, through carefully chosen content and structured activities. This teaching approach illustrates how instructional design can extend STEM educational reckoning into global learning spaces when approached as a form of ethical praxis.

title: BRI volume 56 Cover and Back matter
BRI volume 56 Cover and Front matter
Editorial
Intellectual Property in Developer-Funded Archaeology Projects in Britain from the Roman Period
authors: Sadie Watson; Francesca Mazzilli; Kayt Hawkins
abstract: As the leading journal for studies of Roman Britain for over 50 years, Britannia has proved a successful publishing outlet for papers that have arisen from the UK developer-funded archaeology sector. This level of interest should encourage the sector to submit more papers to Britannia , but it could also encourage influential journals to improve inclusivity in the publishing traditions of the sector, which are discussed in terms of a widespread failure to acknowledge intellectual property and expertise and to encourage wider involvement in analysis and publishing. The authors use three case studies from their own areas of work to illustrate current problems surrounding authorship, leadership and gendered practice. We then propose ways in which these issues could be tackled.

title: What Happened Next? Hadrian’s Wall, the expeditio Britannica and the Fate of the Ninth Legion
abstract: Building on two recent contributions to this journal, this paper investigates the possible connections between Hadrian’s tour of the north-western provinces in a.d . 121–23, the expeditio Britannica , the disappearance of the Ninth Legion, the Hadrianic fire of London and the cessation of work at several sites along Hadrian’s Wall. These events are discussed as independent elements, their date ranges each narrowed to what is normally expected. The convergence of evidence invites a fresh examination of the possibility that a major security crisis erupted following the imperial visit of a.d . 122. Potential causes and consequences are briefly explored, including the apparent suppression of this ignominious episode.

title: The Antonine Wall Distance Slabs: A Critical Overview
authors: William S. Hanson; Roger S. O. Tomlin
abstract: This paper seeks to summarise and critique aspects of our understanding of the famous monumental building inscriptions from the Antonine Wall, traditionally known as the distance slabs. It addresses the following themes: uniqueness; positioning; audience and message; disposal; units of measurement; records of distance; allocation of labour; order of construction; advance preparation; and location of the eastern terminus. It draws attention to some misconceptions and misinterpretations, and offers some new insights.

title: Approaching Connectivity and Community Through Rural Crafts in Early Roman Cambridgeshire: The Case of the Lower Ouse Valley Potteries
abstract: Recent excavations on the A14 Cambridge-to-Huntingdon Road Improvement Scheme have revealed that pottery-making was an important aspect of the economies of early Roman rural communities living in the densely settled landscape of southern Cambridgeshire, UK. This paper discusses the seven known ‘Lower Ouse Valley’ pottery-making sites as reflective of local rural economy and social interaction, highlighting the different scales at which there is evidence for social networks being in play in the constitution of this newly discovered pottery industry. It is argued that the density of rural settlement in this area helped facilitate the emergence of a coherent but informally defined ceramic tradition, embodied as a system of technical knowledge shared predominantly between neighbours and as features of non-specialised social interactions.

title: Heating Londinium : Dating Relief-patterned Box-flue Tiles and Other Wall Cavity Traditions in Roman London’s Baths and Heated Buildings
abstract: In recent years a redating of relief-patterned tiles has been proposed, which argues against an established Flavian to Antonine chronology in favour of an earlier and much shorter Claudio-Neronian chronology. This paper tests the chronological underpinning of this important hypothesis by revisiting the dating for relief-patterned tiles in Roman London, which has produced by far the largest corpus of these tiles from any settlement in Roman Britain. The results provide considerable support for the traditional chronology, but do not necessarily rule out an earlier start date for this keying technique or the continued use of these tiles beyond the second century. The technique may have initially been used by certain tile makers supplying building projects that were largely outside London.

title: Pervasive Ritual at Wroxeter: The Evidence of the Buried Ceramics from the Bushe-Fox Excavations 1912–14
authors: Cameron Moffett; Jane Evans; Fiona Seeley
abstract: The excavations at Wroxeter conducted by J.P. Bushe-Fox examined a zone of the Roman city very different to the public baths and macellum complex extensively investigated in the later twentieth century. Bushe-Fox’s work in Insula 8 is the best and largest sample of Wroxeter’s residential buildings investigated to date; the focus of this paper is the large number of complete ceramic vessels included in the pits and wells he excavated. Recognition of the act of burying complete vessels, and of that practice as a meaningful tradition in antiquity, has developed over the last 25 years. Revisiting the Bushe-Fox excavations has provided a large body of new evidence for the practising of domestic rituals at Wroxeter.

title: Intramural Human Remains from Roman Towns in Britain: A Case Study from Late Iron Age and Roman Silchester
abstract: Intramural adult human remains, whether articulated or disarticulated, from Roman towns in Britain are uncommon. There is evidence for some remains to have been deliberately curated and/or treated post mortem in a particular way before final deposition. This paper focuses on the disarticulated human remains from late Iron Age and Roman Silchester ( Calleva Atrebatum ), noting the parts of the skeleton represented, their contexts, and whether there is evidence for curation or treatment post mortem . Twenty-one examples have been radiocarbon dated, enabling an assessment of changes in spatial patterning over time. An early and a late cluster are identified. The results from Silchester follow a review of comparable evidence from the major towns of Roman Britain. This reveals a broad similarity in patterning between Silchester and the Romano-British countryside. There are several urban parallels for Silchester’s late cluster, but only London for the early grouping.

title: Troy Story: The Ketton Mosaic, Aeschylus, and Greek Mythography in Late Roman Britain
authors: Jane Masséglia; Jennifer Browning; Jeremy Taylor; John Thomas
abstract: The Ketton Mosaic depicts the duel between Achilles and Hector, the dragging of Hector’s body and its ransom. Despite initial associations with the Iliad in the press, this article demonstrates that the Ketton mosaic does not illustrate scenes from Homer but an alternative variant of the narrative which originated with Aeschylus and remained popular in Late Antiquity. The composition also reveals its debt to a pattern repertoire shared by artists working in media such as painted pottery, coin dies and silverware, which had been circulating in the ancient Mediterranean for many centuries. Through its textual and visual allusions, the Ketton mosaic makes a strong case for the engagement of fourth-century Roman Britain with the cultural currency of the wider empire.

title: Fowl Play: A British ‘Fatal Charade’ at Brading Roman Villa
abstract: The rooster-headed man in a mosaic at Brading Roman Villa on the Isle of Wight is a mystery that has attracted a dizzying range of explanations since its discovery in 1879. Three broad theories have found favour — that he represents a deity, an exotic beast to be hunted, or a hunter either with a rooster-related name or mocking the emperor Constantius Gallus. In this article I outline the problems with these theories before offering an alternative explanation — that this figure is a damnatus , and the scene an imaginative execution, a so-called ‘fatal charade’. This suggestion both facilitates a more holistic interpretation of the mosaic, and rehabilitates earlier suggestions long summarily dismissed.

title: Assessing Defence in Late Antique North-eastern Gaul and the Germanic Provinces c. a.d . 250–500: Biases, Distribution and Chronology
abstract: The proliferation of fortification in north-western Europe during Late Antiquity marks an important shift from the first to early third centuries. The fortified cities and military installations were joined by new fortified towns and rural and hilltop defences. While these defences have been extensively studied, there has been little engagement with this transformation at a statistical level. This article provides an overview of defence in the region using data collected across northeastern Gaul and the provinces of Germania Secunda and Germania Prima . It will highlight biases, distributions and key variations in the dataset and demonstrate regional variations in defence on a large scale.

title: Establishing a Chronology for Roman and Post-Roman Stanwick, Northamptonshire
authors: Robin Fleming; Vicky Crosby; Alex Bayliss; Simon Mays; Christopher Bronk Ramsey; Elaine Dunbar; H.E.M. Cool; Angela Wardle
abstract: The programme of radiocarbon dating undertaken at Stanwick, Northamptonshire, demonstrates the value of scientific dating of Romano-British sites, including those with good pottery sequences and large numbers of datable coins and other finds. It has refined and clarified the chronology and phasing of the site, particularly in its final phase of occupation. It confirmed some of our original dating of the human burials, and showed other dates were significantly wrong. It also addresses issues relating to the calibration of radiocarbon dates and dietary isotopes in the period. This has enabled us to identify activities, material culture and burial practices current at Stanwick and elsewhere in the immediate post-Roman period.

title: Objects in Miniature: A Copper-Alloy Beneficiarius Spear-Shaped Mount from Inveresk
abstract: A copper-alloy spear-shaped mount, found during excavations at the extramural settlement at Inveresk Roman fort, represents a rare British example of a beneficiarius lance symbol. Stylistic parallels are found among a corpus of personal ornaments used by soldiers of the beneficiarii and are typically restricted to sites on the German limes . This paper discusses the style and function of this object and what its presence reveals about Inveresk and its role in the administration and control of Roman Scotland.

title: Further Details on the Roman Figure with a Circular Socket from West Keal, Lincolnshire*
abstract: A cast copper-alloy male figurine with a circular socket projecting from its head was discovered by a metal-detectorist in West Keal, Lincolnshire, and recorded via the Portable Antiquities Scheme (PAS) before inclusion in Britannia ’s 2020 roundup. Conservation by the finder revealed further decorative details, particularly on the tunic. This contribution examines these embellishments, their stylistic affinities and implications for dating. The identification of the figure as a servant opens discussion on the luxurious domestic settings of Roman Lincolnshire and high-status sites.

title: A Possible Roman Camp on the Wirral Peninsula
abstract: Satellite imagery in north-west Wirral shows a cropmark, plausibly representing the partial circuit of a Roman camp. On Wirral — that peninsula flanked by the rivers Mersey and Dee — the northern coast of which provided the only seaboard of the Cornovii tribe, Roman military sites are unknown. However, a fort has been posited 7 km to the north-north-west at Meols and a camp in its hinterland would not be unreasonable. This feature is therefore potentially significant and warrants description.

title: Spoon-Shaped Objects with Weapon Terminals from Western Britain
abstract: A small group of late Roman ‘spoon-shaped’ objects with weapon terminals and a westerly distribution add to the growing evidence of ‘regionality’ in material culture within Roman Britain. While their function remains uncertain, the presence of weapon-shaped terminals can be seen alongside the increasing numbers of model objects recorded from the province.

authors: Harry Manley; Paul Cheetham; Miles Russell; Dave Stewart
abstract: This brief note corrects an aspect of our 2024 paper looking at the evidence for the route of the Dorchester aqueduct in which we attributed a previously hypothesised route for the aqueduct to Christopher Sparey-Green.

title: III. Inscriptions
IV. Spotlight on New Research
abstract: This thesis aims to offer a new interpretation of the meanings Luke-Acts conveyed to its first audiences by imagining people from early Roman Britain encountering that text.As the events described in the New Testament were unfolding, the Romans invaded Britain (43 c.e.).By the time that invasion was complete (c.83 c.e.), the earliest books of the New Testament were in circulation.An understanding of early Roman Britain opens a window on to the world of the New Testament and its first audiences.The investigation of three archives from an urban, a military and a rural community draws on the methodology of archival ethnography.In these writings, traders and merchants, civilians and soldiers, town and country dwellers, slave and free, men and women come alive.People such as these are encountered in the New Testament and are among its first readers.The thesis uses first the Bloomberg tablets, to take the reader to passages to do with money and possessions, honour and shame, reciprocity and debt, patrons and clients, slaves and masters, the rich and the destitute, and Roman law and literacy.Second, it uses the Vindolanda tablets to examine passages concerning women of agency, the military and local people, Roman law, travel and identity, festivals and feasting, sickness and healing, honour and shame, patrons and clients, masters and slaves and the reversal of roles.Finally it uses the Uley curse tablets, examining passages to do with temples, ritual practice, cursing and praying.The resulting imagined reading of Luke-Acts is justified in the locations and with the writings chosen, informed by careful study of the data available, and warranted by close attention to the biblical text.It contributes to our understanding of the way the first readers of the New Testament negotiated life in the empire and understood Luke-Acts.

title: Proceedings of the Society for the Promotion of Roman Studies 2024–2025
Aurelius Lucius, Headhunting, and the Cult of Jupiter Optimus Maximus Tanarus at Chester
abstract: Connecting the altar of Jupiter Optimus Maximus Tanarus and the tombstone of Aurelius Lucius from the Roman fortress of Chester, it will be suggested that there was a distinct and localised religious cult at this Roman fortress promoting the practice and celebration of headhunting. This cult was likely introduced by Gallic soldiers but became an established part of the local micro-pantheon of gods at Chester, explaining both the altar and the depiction of a human head on the tombstone.

title: In the Footsteps of Trebellius Maximus: Finding the Rossett Roman Villa and its Implications
abstract: The discovery of a lead ingot near Wrexham in 2019 prompted an investigation into Roman activity in the surrounding area, leading to the identification of the first structurally attested Roman villa rustica in north Wales. In a region where evidence for rural settlement and agriculture has long been eclipsed by military and industrial remains, this find raises new questions about everyday life under Roman rule. This paper presents interim details of the discoveries, offering the first published account of the villa, and explores their significance for understanding rural settlement along Britannia’s western frontier. It outlines the fieldwork results, reviews existing evidence and identifies key research priorities and methodological recommendations for future study.

title: A Note on Roman Architectural Fragments from Tannery Cottages, Irthlingborough, Northamptonshire
abstract: The recovery from the Irthlingborough site of moulded architectural stone fragments from a plinth or cornice can be added to the earlier find of a sculptured slab in relief showing part of the marine thiasos , the retinue of followers of Oceanus, representing the realm of the sea. What structure this stonework was associated with is uncertain, but it may be paralleled by a similar but more extensive collection of sculptured and moulded stonework from the nearby villa site at Stanwick, where a funerary monument of some significance has been suggested. It may be that the Roman Nene valley landscape was punctuated by several structural markers reflecting the ‘ monumentum ’ of associated villa populations.

title: A Reused Bronze Age Barrow and Roman Religious Shrine Site at Red Lodge, Suffolk
abstract: Investigations at Red Lodge, Suffolk, recorded a multi-period site spanning the Neolithic through to the medieval period, focusing on remains of an isolated Early Bronze Age barrow. While no associated burials survived, the monument was later incorporated into a Roman-period religious complex, being enclosed within a ditched temenos , probably in the second century. A small building interpreted to be a shrine structure was subsequently constructed alongside the barrow, the ring-ditch of which was recut around this time, suggesting its active use within this religious place. A number of structured animal deposits occupied the religious enclosure, the most notable of which comprise distinctive pig ‘head-and-hoof’ deposits in close association with the shrine. Further probable votive material was found dispersed in deposits in the immediate vicinity of the shrine and barrow. A possible pond, well and oven structure hint at other activities carried out in the enclosure, presumably allied to its religious function which continued into the late fourth century. No subsequent early Medieval land use activity was identified, though a documentary source indicates the presence of a late Medieval gallows in this vicinity, perhaps on the barrow earthwork itself. A single medieval inhumation later inserted into the top of the temenos ditch is therefore speculated to constitute an execution victim.

title: Mobility and Roman Britannia
authors: David Roberts; Leah Reynolds; Rachèl Spros; Sophy Charlton; Richard Madgwick
abstract: This article reviews the evidence for mobility within, and into, the Roman province of Britannia, assesses the current state of the field and sets out how current approaches should be developed and improved. Mobility was foundational to the Roman empire and its provinces, and this paper demonstrates that Britannia provides a rich case study of the breadth, complexity and challenges of the datasets, methodologies and history of investigation of this central topic to understanding the Roman world. The review provides overviews of textual, epigraphic, material and bioarchaeological evidence and interpretive frameworks. Finally, it sets out a vision for holistic and ethical future archaeological research on this topic, especially in light of the bioarchaeological revolution in recent decades and rapidly developing datasets.

Brading Roman Villa: Evidence of a Late Roman Massacre?
abstract: Radiocarbon dating of disarticulated human remains from Brading Roman villa (Isle of Wight, UK) assigns them to a single event or multiple events within a short duration in the Late Roman period, c . 220/50–360/400. The evidence of the coins suggests the possibility of a brief abandonment of the villa following a potentially murderous event in the 340s or 350s, perhaps to be linked to reprisals taken by Constantius against supporters of Magnentius. This event may in turn coincide with a significant reorganisation of space in the west range of the villa.

title: Conflict in the Lake District: The Attack on Ambleside Roman Fort
authors: Manuel Fernández-Götz; John Henderson Reid; Stuart Campbell
abstract: Lead sling bullets ( glandes ) have been found for over a century at and around the Roman fort in Ambleside (Lake District). The glandes , together with the discovery of a remarkable inscription on a tombstone from the site, suggest the possibility of a conflict scenario. This article summarises the previous evidence and presents the results from a new research project that comprised two fieldwork campaigns (2021 and 2023) in the environs of the fort. The results confirm the hypothesis of a scatter of glandes to the north and east, which can be plausibly interpreted as the fort undergoing an external attack, during which the garrison troops defended themselves by shooting missiles outwards.

title: How Do We Make the River ‘Roman’? Changing Depositional Patterns in the Middle Thames Valley
abstract: This paper offers the first detailed examination of riverine depositional practice in the Roman Middle Thames, using a comprehensive, multi-period dataset of river finds. The study reveals an abrupt deviation from long-standing martial traditions, replaced largely by low-value coinage and coarse-ware pottery. Comparative analysis of two crossing sites, the urban Kingston bridge and the rural Goring ford, demonstrates that deposition was a highly structured, likely intentional practice. It is argued that this change reflects Imperial influence and ‘soft control’, alongside the conscious adoption of new material proxies to maintain the role of ritual deposition within the new socio-political landscape.

title: Where Are the Claudian Forts? A Review of the Evidence in South-eastern Britain, and an Alternative View of the Invasion Period
abstract: After more than 30 years of developer-led archaeology, the concept of ‘pacification’, the standard model of the invasion period in south-eastern Britain since the mid-twentieth century, can be reconsidered. The following is not about forts as such; it is about quality of evidence. It reviews proposed early forts south-east of the Fosse Way and concludes that few are genuine; some alternative functions are put forward. A broader explanation for the absence of early forts is offered in the context of friendly kingdoms: prior to the Claudian invasion, treaties may have been put in place between Rome and the polities of Verlamion and Silchester, which created a buffer zone to ensure the invasion’s success.

title: The Writings on the Wall: From Greek Alphabet to Painter’s Signature, The Inscriptions on the Roman Wall-paintings of the Liberty, Southwark, London
abstract: The excavations at Liberty Southwark (LDM21) carried out by Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) have yielded one of the largest assemblages of Roman wall-painted plaster in London. In the assessment and reassembling of the plasters, the building material specialist discovered two inscriptions unique to Roman Britain and likely to the study of Roman wall paintings in general. Pit (423) yielded what looks to be a signature by the painter while (135) produced a near-complete Greek alphabet scored into the plaster. Both inscriptions were analysed in the greater context of the Roman world in which comparisons of similar inscriptions were made.

title: An Iron Age Bloomery Iron-smelting Industry on the Mid Kent Downs
authors: Joanne Barker; David Dungworth; Grace Griffith
abstract: The recent discovery of a Middle to Late Iron Age bloomery iron-smelting site, revealed during archaeological works associated with the M2 Junction 5 improvement scheme in north-west Kent, has highlighted the possibility that the Stockbury Valley was the focus of a substantial ironworking industry during this period. Moreover, the waste slag assemblages recovered from the M2 Junction 5 scheme and several other sites around Stockbury appear to show an industry that employed elements of the prehistoric tradition (largely non-tapping) and the Roman tradition (tapping), producing tapped and non-tapped slag in the same smelt.

title: The Earliest Known Purposefully Collected Ichthyosaurian Fossil: A Vertebral Centrum from a Second-century a.d . Roman Pit in Colchester, Essex
authors: Patrick S. Spencer; Adam N. Wightman; Laura E.A. Pooley
abstract: This article discusses the noteworthy discovery of an ichthyosaur vertebral centrum from a Roman pit dating to the third quarter of the second century a.d . at the site of the former Essex County Hospital, Lexden Road, Colchester. The pit also yielded a toilet spoon ( ligula) and a potentially disparate associated animal bone group which could indicate the structured deposition of the centrum. The reason it was collected and then curated may have involved Greco-Roman folklore or mythology. Alternatively, it might have been a curio. The east Kent coast between Folkestone and Hythe is suggested as the most probable source of the fossil. This find represents the first ichthyosaur remains found in a Roman deposit and the earliest known instance of the deliberate acquisition of an ichthyosaur fossil.

title: Healthcare in Roman Colchester
authors: Nina Crummy; Glynn J. C. Davis; R. S. O. Tomlin; Peter Bray; Owen Humphreys; Kathryn Murphy; Keith Nyakubaya
abstract: Colchester Museums has collected Roman-period medical instruments from the town since the late nineteenth century. Brought together here, along with items from the town housed in other institutions, their typological links or differences are explored, along with their wide range of uses. They are set in a variety of contexts, including a conquest-period British Doctor’s kit from Stanway, near Colchester, the alloys used in their manufacture, their distribution across the town and its suburbs, the diseases evident from late Romano-British human remains in the town’s cemeteries, and herbal remedies and other treatments. Interpretation of a previously enigmatic collyrium stamp attests to an eye infection not previously recorded in Roman Britain.

title: Editorial
Re-Evaluating Subsistence Strategies During the Solutrean in the Cantabrian Region ( c. 22–19.5 ky cal BP )
authors: Rodrigo Portero; María José Fernández Gómez; Esteban Álvarez-Fernández
abstract: The Solutrean in the Cantabrian region is one of the periods in the Upper Palaeolithic with the highest number of faunal studies conducted in recent decades, which offer valuable insights into how human groups exploited their environment for survival. Here, the authors analyse twenty-four archaeological levels from twelve sites dated between c. 22 and 19.5 ky cal bp , focusing on the exploitation of large mammals through palaeoecological and palaeoeconomic approaches. Their examination of prey acquisition and transport, age profiles, seasonality, nutrition, and energy costs shows that hunting decisions were influenced not only by the economic profitability of prey but also by the environment, topography, climate, animal behaviour, and species abundance. This multifactorial perspective provides an updated view of subsistence strategies at the onset of the Last Glacial Maximum.

title: Faces in Places: Portable Clay Figurines from Åland and South-Western Finland in the Light of Chemical and Petrographic Analysis
authors: Jenni Lucenius; Torbjörn Brorsson; Niklas Stenbäck
abstract: This study of Neolithic Comb Ware and Pitted Ware clay figurines from south-western Finland and Åland focuses on their provenance, technological traits, and cultural significance. Using ICP-MA/ES chemical analysis and thin-section petrography, forty-two figurines were analysed to identify clay sources and preferences in fabrication techniques. The data indicate that the figurines, and thus the humans, moved between contemporaneous locations along the south-western Finnish coast and on Åland, suggesting regional connections between sites. Most figurines were crafted locally, but a significant number was non-local, signifying mobility within a cross-Baltic network. Distinct clay recipes included calcareous or plant-based tempers and the use of grog. The symbolic value of adding grog is seen as reinforcing connections to a place, indicating that portability and provenance, i.e. movement between places, was an important characteristic of the hunter-gatherer figurine tradition of the Neolithic in the northern Baltic.

title: The Aegean Meets Europe: Two Ornaments with Solar Motifs from Mycenaean Kefalonia (Greece)
abstract: This article presents an analysis of two sheet gold ornaments of the Mycenaean post-palatial period (twelfth–eleventh centuries bc ) found in two cemeteries on the island of Kefalonia. These unusual ornaments bear solar symbols of Nordic and central European type, the closest parallels being those on the contemporary gold discs from votive deposits on the Italian peninsula. The study considers the technological, morphological, and iconographic particularities of the Kefalonian ornaments and how they differ from each other and from other finds. The ornaments’ use in a funerary context is examined against Aegean practices, burial rites, and ideology. The examination of their iconographic and conceptual antecedents in the Aegean cultural sphere reveals that the exogenous input in their creation—linked to transcultural exchange within the Adriatic—was matched by indigenous engagement with aspects of cosmology.

title: The Late Iron Age Mound Raknehaugen in Norway: A Ritual Response to the Sixth-Century Crisis
abstract: This article challenges long-held assumptions that Raknehaugen, the largest prehistoric mound in Scandinavia, served as a high-status burial monument. While traditionally seen as reflecting elite power in the Late Iron Age, this interpretation is poorly supported by archaeological evidence, which has consistently failed to reveal any evidence of a burial. Instead, the author argues that the mound’s construction should be understood as a communal, ritual response to a catastrophic landslide that took place in the wake of the ad 536 ‘Dust Veil’ climatic crisis. Drawing on a relational landscape approach, recent LiDAR analysis, and dendrochronological data, the study situates Raknehaugen within a dynamic landscape and suggests that it functioned as a structure intended to restore the cosmological and social order. Reframing the mound as an active agent in a sacred landscape opens new avenues for interpreting Iron Age monumentality beyond elite-centric narratives, emphasizing landscape, materiality, and collective ritual practices.

title: Diet and Mobility in Byzantine Western Anatolia: Carbon and Nitrogen Isotopic Ratios and Ancient DNA Evidence from Barcın Höyük and Kadıkalesi Anaia
authors: Rana Özbal; Ali Metin Büyükkarakaya; Gülfem Uysal; Erge Bütün; Fokke Gerritsen; Ali Akbaba; N. Ezgi Altınışık; Mehmet Somel
abstract: This study presents the integrated results of stable carbon ( δ 13 C) and nitrogen ( δ 15 N) isotope and aDNA analyses, conducted to examine dietary and mobility practices in two mid- to late Byzantine communities in western Anatolia: the coastal cosmopolitan site of Kadıkalesi Anaia and the rural inland settlement of Barcın Höyük. Isotopic data from thirty-eight individuals indicate that both populations primarily consumed terrestrial C₃-based resources. At Kadıkalesi , δ 15 N values show greater variability, suggesting more differentiated access to animal protein sources, whereas the rural community at Barcın Höyük exhibits isotopic homogeneity, consistent with more uniform dietary practices and an equitable access to food. Kadıkalesi also shows intra-site dietary variation by age and sex, while Barcın is again more homogeneous. At Barcın, aDNA results indicate a predominant local genetic continuity, suggesting a stable population; a single instance of external ancestry is attested by a male individual with affinities to western populations, particularly from eastern Europe, in line with historical military resettlement patterns ( stratiotika ktemata ). By integrating isotopic and genomic evidence, this study demonstrates how ancestry and mobility shaped dietary habits, offering insights into the interplay of urbanism, mobility, and social organization in the Byzantine period.

title: Relationality and Economic Emergence: Ceramic Networks and Urban Assemblages in Medieval ( c. 1250–1400) England
abstract: This article presents an analysis of the relationship between urbanization as an ongoing process and economic development in medieval ( c. AD 1250–1400) southern and midland England. It is proposed that understanding the distribution of pottery through network analysis provides a means of comprehending the role played by affective material relations in these processes. Rather than seeing pottery distributions as reflecting an overarching economic context, the author investigates how relations with pottery, and between pottery and other commodities, generated distinctive and situated modes of urban life. He proposes that the medieval economy was a patchwork rather than a coherent system. The study draws on Deleuze’s concept of the ‘virtual’ to examine how economic emergence and urbanization are open-ended and difference-making processes.

A Child-Centred Approach to Cultural Hybridity: Weaning and Childhood Diets in the Greek Colony of Himera
authors: Laurie Reitsema; Abigail Shahar Gancz; Stefano Vassallo; Britney Kyle
abstract: During the Archaic and Classical periods, the establishment of Greek colonies in the Mediterranean region resulted in new, hybrid cultures. Weaning and early life diets reflect childhood experiences and cultural transmission. Here, the stable nitrogen and carbon isotopic ratios (δ 15 N, δ 13 C) from bone collagen of fifty-eight subadults and twenty-seven adult females from the Greek colony of Himera in Sicily are used to estimate the age of weaning and the nature of complementary foods. Bayesian analysis shows that weaning typically began at 3–4 months and was completed by 3.5–4 years. While a weaning ‘curve’ is detected at Himera, there is much variation, suggesting adherence to some shared norms but also individualized decisions about the diets of infants and children. This study expands our knowledge of Greek childhood and sheds light on the treatment of children within a culturally complex colonial setting.

An Inter-Civilizational Bronze Age System: International Relations, Diplomacy, and Narrative Sociability, 1700–1200 bc
abstract: Previous attempts at explaining how geographically distant and disparate Bronze Age polities, like the chiefdoms of northern Europe and the urban states of the Mediterranean, were connected have focused on exchange networks. By combining insights from political science with archaeology, this article sets out to do two things. First, to reintroduce system thinking to model interconnectivities in the Bronze Age world, using an old trope in international relations studies as a lens and analytical tool. Second, to argue that diplomacy and war must be treated on a par with trade as institutions of such a system, of major importance for understanding international relations during the Bronze Age. The authors discuss the so-called Amarna system’s scope in time and space, exploring whether and how Bronze Age polities in the far north of Europe, as outsiders, can be plausibly construed as constitutive ‘others’.

title: Life on a Hellenistic Construction Site: Stonemasons’ Marks on the Tauchira Gate at Ptolemais in Cyrenaica
abstract: The Tauchira Gate, the best-preserved part of the fortifications of Ptolemais in Cyrenaica (present-day Libya), has been studied by many researchers but the stonemasons’ marks have been largely overlooked. The documentation and analysis of 626 marks reveal valuable information about the chaîne opératoire employed in the gate’s construction. The author suggests that the marks reflect the way the stonecutters organized their work, which began with the extraction of the stone and continued at the construction site. The presence of marks in the letter-label system and monograms suggests that two different schemes of organizing and financing the work were used side by side, probably involving public tenders and private donations or contributions. The analysis established that the building had been completed relatively quickly, and the palaeographic features of the marks suggest that the Tauchira Gate is likely to have been erected during the reign of Ptolemy VIII.

A Tale of Three Towns: Local Conditions and the Commercialization of Farming in Nineteenth-Century New York, USA
abstract: The commercialization of agriculture in the nineteenth-century northern United States represents the foundational period for many rural American communities. It created the family-farm-as-business model that became the backbone of the agricultural economy for the next 100 years. However, it was not a monolithic movement. The timing, strategies, and causes varied between communities, and sometimes even between farms. Using archival, historical, and archaeological data, this work explores the interaction of community identities and values, environment, landscape, climate, and national economic trends in influencing when, how, and why farmers in Madison County, New York commercialized.

title: Mapping People, Labor, and Movement in the First Decades (1788–1825) of Colonial Parramatta, Australia, with Historical Spatial Data Infrastructure
abstract: In this article, we present a new research project in development that applies historical and archaeological methods to examine labor in colonial Parramatta, Australia. Established in November 1788, Parramatta is the third-oldest British colonial settlement in the former colony of New South Wales, Australia. Over 40 years of heritage research and large-scale archaeological excavations have documented much of Parramatta’s early history. However, due to the usual constraints of developer-funded projects, most of this work has remained focused on individual sites. Here, we examine some approaches for landscape-scale synthesis of evidence relating to colonial Parramatta. The research uses archival holdings to unravel the spatial networks of people and things that crossed lot boundaries, forming economic and relational webs that sustained the settler-colonial township (both convict and free). Informed by the relational approaches of both cultural (new) histories of capitalism and new materialism(s), this project functions at the scale of the town and its surrounding district. We seek to lay the foundations for further work using individuals to connect places within the landscape, to follow the movement of materials, and to trace the products and processes of labor.

title: Islands under Surveillance: Watch Towers, Gendered Schools, and the Emergence of Modernity in the Mangareva Islands, French Polynesia
authors: James Flexner; Emilie Perez; Moanatea Claret
abstract: Modern societies sought to control their populations through programs of mass education and surveillance. The origins of this practice had roots in Europe, but were quickly exported to colonial contexts around the world, including the Pacific Islands. While schooling and surveillance are currently often associated with state institutions, historically Christian missions were also critical to the spread of these phenomena in colonized territories. In the territory that became French Polynesia, the first permanent Catholic missionaries arrived in the Mangareva Islands beginning in 1834. Archaeological survey and excavations focusing on the building program of the missionaries has documented an extensive landscape of nineteenth-century stone buildings constructed both by missionary frères bâtisseurs (builder-brothers) and Mangarevan converts. Included among these buildings are several watch towers facing inward among the islands in the lagoon, and separate boys’ and girls’ school compounds in the islands of Aukena and Mangareva. The spatial organization and materiality of these spaces demonstrate the use of techniques of surveillance and schooling to attempt to control the Mangarevan population, including socializing male and female students for expected gendered roles in Christian society.

title: Exploring European Memory of the 1897 Lattimer Massacre with Predictive AI
abstract: Some historical archaeologists work in places colonized by countries whose language is other than that spoken by the researcher. Many of these projects have not consulted the relevant foreign-language literature, which could provide additional context for interpreting their findings. Predictive AI offers the unique advantage of rapidly accessing, translating, and synthesizing foreign language sources that may otherwise remain inaccessible due to language barriers. The following is an example of a little known international labor tragedy that occurred in northeastern Pennsylvania in 1897, when immigrant coal miners went on strike for better pay and working conditions. At least 19 men were killed and 38 wounded, and most of the victims were citizens of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Much of the incident and its aftermath have been reconstructed using English-language newspapers, court records, and oral histories. Due to language barriers, scholars have not examined how the victims' home countries recorded and perceived the incident. Using predictive AI enables researchers to create workable translations of these perspectives with a level of speed and scale previously unattainable, broadening the historical context of this incident. This approach provides an example for others whose work spans international boundaries and languages.

title: A Significant Period of Native American Pine Peeling in Joes Valley, Utah

Glass Artifacts in Plantation Contexts: Evidence from the Murutucu Site in the Amazon, Brazil
abstract: This study analyzes material evidence from the Murutucu Sugar Cane Mill in the Brazilian Amazon to clarify the socioeconomic structure of plantation life in the nineteenth century. By combining archaeological and historical sources, the research highlights pronounced differences in how glass objects were used by planters versus the enslaved individuals. Luxury items like wine bottles and decorative pieces were mainly linked to the planter class, demonstrating their wealth and status, while more utilitarian items appeared in the areas inhabited by enslaved individuals, reflecting restricted access to high-end goods. The work also addresses the repurposing of bottles, offering insights into consumption patterns and recycling practices of the era. Importantly, it presents a detailed examination of intentionally knapped tools from the slave quarters interior, especially the most complete example, as evidence of technological adaptation and resourcefulness among the enslaved. These findings enhance our understanding of plantation archaeology by shedding light on everyday life and social dynamics within this historical setting.

title: Multi-Isotope Analyses of Colonial Sheep from the Sydney Region, Australia: Implications for Husbandry Strategies
authors: Tanja Nussbaumer; Melanie Fillios; Renaud Joannes-Boyau; Matheus C. Carvalho
abstract: Stable isotope analyses of faunal remains have demonstrated significant potential to enhance understandings of human-animal relationships during periods of European colonization. Isotopic analyses enable reconstructions of historical livestock management practices, including diet, provenance, and mobility, while also providing insights into past climatic and environmental conditions. This study presents the first application of a multi-isotope approach to archaeological sheep tooth enamel in Australia, using bulk analysis of carbon (δ¹³C), oxygen (δ¹⁸O), and strontium (⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr) isotopes to reconstruct herd management strategies in colonial New South Wales. Isotopic data was obtained from the tooth enamel of 29 early to mid-nineteenth century sheep recovered from an archaeological context on Clarence and Kent Street, Sydney, and compared with two modern Merino sheep of known provenance and inferred diets. δ¹³C analyses indicate that the archaeological sheep consumed a predominantly C 3 plant-based diet, likely comprising both native and sown pastures, consistent with grazing in open woodland and bushy or grass-covered habitats. The wide range of δ¹⁸O values suggests that the sheep experienced diverse environmental conditions during early life, reflecting variation in local climate, altitude, water sources and seasonality. Sequential ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr enamel analyses reveal limited individual mobility but provide evidence for multiregional livestock sourcing. ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr values indicate at least three potential geological provenance zones, most likely within New South Wales, including regions beyond the Sydney Basin, although the possibility of overseas imports cannot be entirely excluded. These results contribute to broader understandings of livestock management, provisioning strategies, and environmental adaptation in early colonial Australia.

title: The Archaeology of the Transatlantic Trade in Peki, Ghana: Local Responses to Global Encounters in Atlantic West Africa
abstract: Archaeological studies of the transatlantic slave trade in West Africa have traditionally focused on coastal and discrete sites of slavery, leaving interior communities comparatively underexplored. This paper advances methodological frameworks for the archaeology of transatlantic trade that move beyond the search for direct material signatures of enslavement to examine the circulation, appropriation, social valuation, and consumption of imported trade goods, and how they shaped political and economic landscapes in Peki, an Ewe-speaking polity in southeastern Ghana. Drawing on archaeological data from sacred sites, burial contexts, and domestic middens, complemented by oral traditions and historical sources, we examine how participation in the Atlantic trade reshaped political authority, consumption practices, and everyday life between the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries. Archaeological materials from Peki, including liquor bottles, tobacco pipes, and European ceramics, demonstrate a shift from elite-controlled access to broader community consumption during the nineteenth century, coinciding with the transition from slave trading to “legitimate commerce.” By situating local material practices in Peki within wider Atlantic political economies, the paper shows how inland African communities actively navigated global economic forces and suggests that the Peki community be regarded as an important node in the network of places connected to heritage tourism and the UNESCO Slave Routes Projects related to the transatlantic trade in Ghana.
