Parapēgmata and poleis : astrometeorological calendars in the Hellenistic city
abstract: Between the fifth and first century BC, calendars that compiled astronomical and meteorological information, known as parapēgmata , came to be used throughout the Greek-speaking world. In the course of the Hellenistic period, numerous such almanacs attributed to scientific authorities who operated in different regions were circulating, some of which emphasized distinct atmospheric phenomena. By ca. 100 BC at the latest, individuals and communities began combining astrometeorological parapēgmata to produce their own, including inscribed public versions. I argue that politically active citizens and doctors would have benefited from the use of these calendars within the context of the Hellenistic polis because weather was believed to have a direct impact on the collective food supply and health of communities and such documents were perceived as an invaluable tool for anticipating important atmospheric changes, determining when meteorological thresholds were crossed and building consensus for communal action taken in response.

title: Philochoros, gifts of grain and the scrutiny of citizens in classical Athens
abstract: According to an account that Felix Jacoby published as Philochoros ( FGrH 328) F119, a gift of 30,000 medimnoi of grain was sent by Psammetichos from Egypt to Athens in the archonship of Lysimachides (445/4). When for its distribution a scrutiny ( diapsēphisis ) was held to check the citizen status of the claimants, 4,760 individuals appeared to be illegally listed as citizens, while 14,240 Athenians received a portion of grain. Brought together in this fragment, the events feature as a significant historical fact in studies of Pericles’ Citizenship Law, Athenian demography and the Athenian grain supply. However, in this article I argue that the account in F119 is not correct as it stands, but a conflation of historically disparate events into one episode. This confusing amalgam is not Philochoros’ mistake, but, with several possible causes, it must originate in the tradition between him and Plutarch, who incorporated it into his Life of Pericles (37). The most likely source of this conflated report for Plutarch’s version is the Alexandrian scholar Didymos. A major element in the confusion is the diapsēphisis of 346/5, when all male citizens scrutinized each other on their civic status, a one-off event that deeply affected Athenian society and its historical traditions.

title: Egyptian grain to Athens: contexts of Philochoros 328 F 119
abstract: Following on Josine Blok’s article (this volume), this note assesses the possible historical contexts for the gift of grain to Athens recorded in Philochoros FGrH 328 F119.

title: An inscribed decree from the Paros Museum and the Parian colonization of Pharos
authors: Peter Liddel; Christy Constantakopoulou; Yannos Kourayos
abstract: In this article we offer an editio princeps of a new inscription from the Cycladic island of Paros and discuss its implications for understanding Parian co-operation with Dionysiοs I of Syracuse in the Adriatic in the early fourth century BCE. We argue that the text throws light on the Parian colonization of Pharos, and is related to activities of the Parians in the Adriatic in what seems to be the result of local Parian strife and strong anti-Athenian affiliations on Paros. We explore possible interpretations of the inscribed decree and their implications for the relationship between the Parians and Dionysios.

title: Getting into ancient barbers’ hair: new perspectives on barbers in the Greek East
abstract: In Greek literature, the barber is always portrayed as a garrulous chatterbox and his shop as a central place for gossip and rumours. Apart from these numerous anecdotes, however, few scholars have investigated the concrete realities of the profession and the actual status of barbers in the Greek East (including Egypt). This paper seeks to fill this gap. It is based on a careful social and economic analysis of the profession, including barbers’ workspaces, their social recognition as skilled craftsmen, their funerary and religious practices, their relationships with their clients, as well as their income, wages and expenses. It attempts to re-place ancient barbers in their socio-professional and socio-economic environment, and to reconstruct some aspects of their daily lives that go beyond the statements of ancient authors and their elite discourse. By systematically cross-referencing all available historical data (literary texts, inscriptions, papyri, ostraca, iconographic and archaeological sources), the paper shows how their lives and status differ from their representation in the literary sources in order to bring these everyday workers out of the shadows and rehabilitate them as historical actors in Greek and Hellenized societies.

title: Sip, don’t suck: defining ‘Greek’ and ‘male’ via beer, wine and sex
abstract: This article re-examines archaic and classical treatment of beer drinking to argue, contra Nelson, that beer in archaic and classical Greek texts is not primarily feminine nor does it necessarily feminize its drinkers. Rather, a review of sympotic lyric, historiography, ethnography and Athenian drama demonstrates that beer is primarily an ethnic marker with no inherent gendered connotations. At the same time, in contexts where definitions of Greek masculinity are being constructed, beer can gain gendered connotations which enhance the ethnic otherness of the beverage and contribute to the definition of the Greek man. Any gendered implications of beer, furthermore, come not from the beverage itself but from the method of consumption, of sucking through a tube of sorts rather than sipping from a cup. This article thus argues that beer in the Archaic and Classical periods marks non-Greek status first and foremost and only secondarily effeminizes drinkers through associations with oral sex in contexts where ideas of masculinity are in play.

title: The delivery of Areus’ letter
abstract: The letters between Sparta and Judaea preserved in 1 Maccabees and Josephus’ Antiquities have generated considerable scholarly discussion. Only Josephus’ version of Areus’ letter to Onias includes information about its courier Demoteles, its ‘square’ script and the image on its seal. Comparison with contemporary Hellenistic epigraphical evidence suggests that these elements are archival metadata rather than parts of the original letter or Josephan inventions. Similar clauses attested in documents inscribed in several Hellenistic cities are remnants of archival processes, and the presence of such details in Josephus’ version of Areus’ letter suggests that it derives from an independent source and never underwent the translation process so evident in the Maccabean versions. This strengthens the case for authenticity.

title: When was Early Greece?
abstract: This article investigates the boundaries of the chronological-cultural unit of ‘Early Greece’, a phrase widely used in scholarship but which has little taxonomic meaning. I argue that the phrase, and the values that it encodes, continues to exist in a traditional evolutionary framework of cultural development within the Greek world. Through a bibliographical case study, I further demonstrate that there are different chronological understandings of ‘Early Greece’ within different subdisciplines, with material-based scholarship applying it predominantly to the Early Iron Age and text-based scholarship predominantly to the Archaic period. Following this, the article connects ‘Early Greece’ with protohistory, particularly through the lens of Homer references, and explores the ways in which the positionality of ‘Early Greece’ emphasizes the authority of textual sources over material ones and continues to articulate an under-defined vision of Greece centred on the fifth century BCE.

title: Professional and part-time potters and painters: modelling the production of Athenian black- and red-figure painted pottery
abstract: This article presents a comprehensive analysis of the production dynamics within the Kerameikos during the major period of black- and red-figure pottery production (600–350 BCE). Employing a statistical approach, this study explores the intricate interplay between the workflows of full-time and part-time painters and potters, and the nature of their respective tasks. By using Monte Carlo methods to estimate quantities, including the number of pots created annually and the hours required for painting, the statistical data generated not only support a complex and time-critical model for the potting industry, but the limits on the plausibility for some of these scenarios are also considered. These quantitative estimates are then situated within the context of the pottery-production chaîne opératoire to consider the seasonality of the various professions of pottery production. A case is made for the existence of permanent painters managing a backlog of pottery while part-time potters shifted between potting and painting (and other tasks), while the concept of project management is also discussed; it is suggested that a critical role of the κϵραμϵύς extended beyond mere craftsmanship to orchestrating workflows.

title: Curriculum uitarum : Homer and the many lives of Pythagoras and Empedocles
abstract: Pythagoras and Empedocles, the earliest pre-Socratic thinkers associated with the doctrine of metempsychosis, are both said to have accounted for their own previous incarnations. This article focuses on lists of their previous lives, here dubbed curriculum uitarum ( CVV ), and argues that they are revealing not only of the specifics of how metempsychosis is conceptualized by each thinker but also of the way in which they harness poetic authority. The article surveys all the surviving permutations of Pythagoras’ CVV across the tradition and identifies an interplay of different modes of enumeration within them: lists of named human individuals vs lists of life forms. The latter mode is what also defines Empedocles’ much-cited ‘epigram’ (B117 DK) on his past incarnations. Both CVV s are informed by strategic borrowings from Homer: while Empedocles’ list draws on the characterisation of the Iliad ’s Nestor and the Odyssey ’s Proteus, Pythagoras’ CVV is defined by the constant presence of the Trojan warrior Euphorbus. As is argued, this originates in the nexus of philosophical speculation and poetical exegesis which accrued around Euphorbus’ short-lived but memorable appearance in the Iliad . In-depth engagement with Homer and Homeric exegesis is thus shown to generate philosophical innovation and to form a strong link between the Pythagorean and Empedoclean teachings on metempsychosis.

title: Aesara on human nature: the tripartition of the soul revisited
abstract: The focus of this paper is a first-century pseudepigraphic treatise titled On Human Nature , preserved by Stobaeus and attributed to the Pythagorean Aesara. Whether the treatise is to be ascribed to a woman philosopher named Aesara or the Pythagorean man Aresas is a point of controversy. In what follows, we gloss over the question of the identity and gender of the author and turn to the philosophical content of the treatise. In the surviving fragment, Aesara analyses the structure of the human soul and the relationships among its parts. The human soul becomes a model of law and justice for both the city and the household. Thus, On Human Nature revisits well-known Platonic doctrines, such as the city-soul analogy, the tripartition of the soul and the definition of justice as harmony, providing novel insights into their political implications. In what follows, we argue that Aesara constructs an original psychological theory by supplementing Plato’s tripartite conception of the soul in the Republic with aspects from later dialogues. Specifically, Aesara employs the Laws to stress the political implications of the tripartition and the leading role of νοῦς, and the Timaeus to explain our psychological reactions through physiological phenomena.

title: Between images and concepts: Pherecydes of Syros and figuration in Archaic Greek thought
abstract: This article critically examines the frequent claim that Pherecydes of Syros deliberately composed his treatise to be read figuratively. More specifically, it is argued that mythopoeic images from the sixth century BCE ought to be distinguished from Classical and Hellenistic allegories lest later categories and distinctions be anachronistically projected onto an archaic thinker. Since this study shows how mythopoeic images are used to fill conceptual gaps in abstract discourse, and how philosophical vocabulary arises in the process of metaphorization, its findings might have implications beyond the context of Pherecydes’ contribution to the development of the allegorical tradition.

title: Miltiades the accursed: curses for moving sacred immovables in Greek religion
abstract: Herodotus’ depiction of Miltiades’ transgression in the sanctuary of Demeter Thesmophoros on Paros is marked by the intriguing phrase κινήσοντά τι τῶν ἀκινήτων (6.134.2). We examine this proverbial phrase, whose implications for Herodotus’ portrayal of Miltiades’ downfall have not yet been fully acknowledged. The article draws attention to the widespread concept of sacred immovables (ἀκίνητα) that were protected by imprecations, and suggests that Miltiades triggered a contingent curse protecting divine property. Herodotus configures the episode of Miltiades on Paros as a narrative of entrapment and steers his readers to view Miltiades’ fate as the consequence of a curse at work.

title: P.Oxy . 2456 and the chronology of Euripides
abstract: The list of Euripidean plays in P.Oxy. 2456, whose primary principle of arrangement is by alphabetical order of first letter, has a secondary principle of arrangement, namely chronology of first performance date. This discovery provides a relative dating, and/or termini ante vel post quos , for 15 plays. The ordering in the papyrus is compared to orderings of other ancient lists of classical dramas, including a list of Aristophanes’ comedies whose arrangement by the same combination of principles was identified by Wilamowitz. A source for this arrangement is proposed, namely Callimachus’ Pinakes .

title: Women in the ancient Greek world: history and historiography
abstract: This article examines some recent trends within the scholarship on ancient Greek women. The field of gender and women’s studies is vast, and so this review is necessarily selective; it is also historical in focus, though I have deliberately tried to include works that cover a broad chronological and geographical range, and those that draw on different kinds of source material. It is divided into three parts: part 1 examines questions concerning ‘real’ women, part 2 is on agency and part 3 draws some observations on the difficulties of, and opportunities for, writing histories of women.

title: Cognitive mapping and social cognition in ancient Greek narrative: novelistic couples
abstract: Although individual and collective minds in the ancient world have received considerable scholarly attention, the cognitive dynamics of social interaction itself – particularly the role of cognition in intimate relationships – remain largely unexplored. This article addresses this gap by introducing the concept of ‘cognitive mapping’ and applying it to couples in the five extant ancient Greek novels as a case study. Cognitive mapping offers a framework for analysing how novelistic couples alternate between alignment, in which partners share cognitive and emotional states, and misalignment, in which misunderstandings disrupt relational harmony. By tracing how lovers map one another’s emotions, intentions and desires through embodied processes and shared experiences, this study sheds new light on character interaction, plot development and reader engagement. It further demonstrates how novelistic narratives construct the couple as an interdependent cognitive system, in which lovers think, feel and respond as a single unit. This approach has broader implications for the study of personal identity, couples’ psychology and embodied interpersonal relations in the ancient world, as well as for ancient narrative theory and contemporary cognitive approaches to classical literature.

title: ‘And yet we that live remissly, undertake as great dangers as they’: Thucydides 2.39–40 and the reappropriation of anti-Athenian slurs
abstract: This paper argues that Thuc. 2.39–40 offers an ironic response to contemporary criticism of Athens by positively reframing the key terms associated with anti-Athenian slurs. It traces the use of aneimenōs , rhaithumia and related concepts in Thucydides and other Classical sources, showing how these terms were appropriated as part of ongoing debates about paideia in the Greek world and in the face of criticism of the Athenian lifestyle. It also examines the history of the interpretation of these passages by translators and commentators, starting with Lorenzo Valla and Thomas Hobbes, and suggests that this context helps explain both the passage’s resistance to straightforward translation and the tendency of modern translations to smooth out its evaluative language.

title: A Byzantine mock encomium inspired by Theocritus
abstract: Michael the Grammarian, an 11th-century teacher, wrote a comic and satirical masterpiece against an unnamed bishop of Philomelion, who received his position as a reward for procuring women for his ecclesiastical superior, the metropolitan of Amorion. This article argues that Michael’s poem is best understood as a mock encomium of the bishop’s origins, incompetence and vices, delivered by the bishop himself, in the spirit of Lucian’s Parasite and Teacher of Rhetoric . It is further argued that in composing this poem, Michael was inspired by Theocritus’ 11th idyll, consisting for the most part of Polyphemus’ desperate love song for the Nereid Galateia. It is possible that Michael understood the Cyclops’ self-description in this idyll as an ironic encomium as well. In addition to the allusion to Theocritus, Michael’s poem provides a rare witness to 11th-century familiarity with Euripides’ Cyclops . This article offers a detailed study of the poem, including its historical, literary and educational context. An Appendix provides the Greek text, English translation and notes.

title: Melodic repetition in the antistrophes of Greek tragedy
abstract: Scholarship on Greek metre routinely asserts that responding stanzas were sung to the same melody, but the ancient evidence for this practice is difficult and rarely discussed. In response to several recent studies proposing that Archaic and early Classical antistrophes did not feature melodic repetition, this paper offers a thorough investigation of the evidence for melodic repetition in responding stanzas. I conclude that the evidence strongly supports the view that responding stanzas did generally repeat the same melody, even if this overall pattern was subject to the variations and liberties characteristic of any artistic practice.

title: Power, agents and traders in the late Seleucid Empire ( ca. 125–64 BCE)
abstract: This article investigates the world of the late Seleucid Empire on the eve of Roman control of the Eastern Mediterranean. It introduces additional actors in first-century Syria and uses the local archaeology of Syria and the Levantine coast, and the spread of Eastern Sigillata A wares in particular, to interrogate rising consumption and disposable wealth in the region. By adding these unnamed traders and merchants as agents of power to our conventional method of studying the late Seleucid Empire, my approach encourages the separation of power from politics and moves away from a top-down interpretive lens. Instead, it emphasizes a multilayered explanation that views local traders and merchants as active participants. Such an approach suggests a much different set of causes for the events that led to the eventual Roman takeover in the first century and offers new avenues for further research on Seleucid history, the Hellenistic world and the collapse of ancient empires.

title: Herodotus on the death of Atys: an Anatolian heroic archetype
abstract: Herodotus’ story of the death of Atys, son of Croesus (1.34–45), has long been seen as an example of his willingness to embroider if not invent stories to give his narrative dramatic effect. Images on a distinctive class of funerary monuments from Anatolia demonstrate that the elements of the story of Atys derive from a tradition of commemorating noble rulers. Herodotus’ account is thus recognizable not as free invention, but as a reworking of a traditional memory of Atys, whose life was celebrated and death mourned according to what may be termed an Anatolian heroic archetype.

title: Philhellenism, mishellenism and classical reception in modern China
abstract: ‘Constantly commending Hellas’ is a metaphorical expression coined by Mao Zedong to label Soviet-backed party rivals as ‘philhellenic’ during the 1941 party purge, reinforcing his leadership under the guise of the Sinification of Marxism. Following the communist conquest of China in 1949, the metaphor remained central to debates over ‘Westernization versus Sinification’. It highlights tensions between philhellenism and mishellenism and provides a valuable lens to explore the intersection of classical reception and modern Chinese thought. This article traces ‘Hellenomania’ in China from the mid-19th-century colonial period to the post-Mao era and addresses issues of nationalism, ideological interpretation and intellectual autonomy. It argues that ‘Hellenomania’, which served as a historical resource for China’s transition from a dynastic empire to a nation-state, has its roots in the intellectual tendency to view Euro-American modernity as descended from classical antiquity. Through five case studies of phil- or mishellenists, including Liang Qichao (1873–1929), Mao Zedong (1893–1976), Xiao Jun (1907–1988), Gu Zhun (1915–1974) and Lin Zhichun (1910–2007), the article explores their roles within the frameworks of classical reception and intellectual history.

title: Roman conquest and Late Hellenistic resilience: the epigraphical case of Aemilius Paullus’ monument at Delphi (167–100 BC)
abstract: Building on recent studies of classical resilience, this article scrutinizes the second-century BC inscriptions on the monument of Aemilius Paullus at Delphi, erected in 167 BC. By analysing the epigraphic reuse of its surfaces, the article posits that the Roman pillar played a crucial political role in the second century BC. It functioned as a material device used by Delphi, the Amphictyony and pro-Roman Greek agents to consolidate their interstate authority and legitimacy amidst the intricate military dominance of Rome and the influence of the Greek leagues. These inscriptions reveal the interplay of new pro-Roman elites, interstate arbitrations, Greek memorialization and Roman provincialization, all converging to signify the rapid transformations of this era. Consequently, this study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of Greek ideological adaptations to Roman power during this period.

The Odeion of Pericles and the triumph of transience
abstract: Pericles’ Odeion, a renowned venue in Athens originally built in the second half of the fifth century BCE, accommodated poetic and musical competitions during the Panathenaia festival. Its design was said to mimic the military tent of the Persian king Xerxes. The present article offers a comprehensive, critical review of the Odeion’s cultural history. It traces how ancient authors described the building and how, since the 17th century, modern scholars have sought, excavated and interpreted it. In doing so, the article aims to show how, in the face of laconic and contradictory textual and archaeological records, the Odeion has received extraordinarily varied functions, reconstructions and interpretations. It argues that the building’s tent shape not only recalled the Greek defeat of the Persians, but also symbolized the triumph of transience.

title: The Parthenon frieze: a festive aesthetic
abstract: Since the early 19th century, the reception of the Parthenon frieze has enshrined its place among the canons of beauty in the modern Western world. This paper turns the question of beauty from the modern reception of the Parthenon frieze to its ancient manufacture and meaning. How, if at all, does the frieze relate to Classical Athenian notions of beauty? While many have linked the frieze to Athenian civic and political values, the relevance of Athenian aesthetic values for the frieze’s interpretation has been strangely neglected, despite their prominence in Classical Athenian texts. One area of life in Classical Athens in which ideas about beauty came to the fore was divine worship. The extensive textual evidence for beauty’s importance in Classical Athenian religion poses an untapped opportunity for looking at the Parthenon frieze in the light of Athenian religious and aesthetic attitudes. The paper argues that ideas about beauty were intrinsic to the frieze’s subject matter, formal execution, and the political and theological values it expressed.

title: Weights without looms: interpreting textile tools in storage contexts
abstract: While loom weights are ubiquitous in archaeological assemblages across the Mediterranean, few have been recovered in the exact locations where weaving was performed in antiquity. Rather, close analysis of textile tool publications reveals that most loom weights were deposited through various processes of reuse, loss, breakage, construction and storage. In this article, I argue that this final category of storage accounts for a far more significant proportion of archaeological loom weights than is usually recognized. I then explore three interrelated implications of this insight. First, I demonstrate that groups of weights left in storage contexts often only represent a small portion of the full range of tools typically owned by an ancient Greek household. Second, I show how storage offers a window into the decisions people made about what to leave behind in moments of duress. Finally, I assert that implicit in the act of storage is an expectation of retrieval, which in turn sheds light on circulation patterns within households. Altogether, these insights establish how a renewed focus on the storage of loom weights affords a more nuanced picture of the lives of ancient weavers.

title: Spartiates and Lakedaimonians: the language of identity in Archaic and Classical Sparta
abstract: In most modern translations of ancient Greek texts, the ‘Spartiates’ and the ‘Lakedaimonians’ have become inseparable and interchangeable. The term ‘Spartan’ is now routinely used as a generic, all-encompassing label, often for the sake of simplicity and accessibility. This interchangeability of the two terms is certainly not a modern phenomenon, with considerable conflation of the two occurring in Greek texts from the fifth century onwards. This begs the question, how would the ‘Spartans’ themselves wish to be identified? The purpose of the present paper is firstly to present the epigraphic evidence for use of the terms ‘Spartiate’ and ‘Lakedaimonian’ from the mid-sixth to the late fourth centuries BCE, the period of Spartan dominance and eventual decline. The fluctuating and developing usage of these two terms over time is then considered with regard to the evolution of Spartan self-presentation.

title: Exploring children’s use of domestic space in ancient Greece with material culture analyses
abstract: Without a comprehensive awareness of their material culture, it is easy to overlook children in household archaeology. This is particularly problematic since juveniles spend much of their time in domestic environments and did so in many ancient and historical contexts. In ancient Greece, literary evidence demonstrates the ideal was for children to remain in the house with female caregivers, at least until they started schooling (if male) or were married (if female). Failing to investigate evidence of children’s activities in excavated houses thus misses a significant opportunity to understand the lives of ancient Greek juveniles. An improved awareness of children’s material culture facilitates investigation of their activities in domestic contexts, through distribution analyses of their material culture in excavated houses. This article applies analyses to Classical houses in Attica, as well as to case studies from the Classical settlement at Olynthus, to develop an improved understanding of children’s lives and significance within their families and society across the fifth and fourth centuries BC in Greece.

title: The rhetoric of desperation: fables in Classical Greek oratory
abstract: This article reassesses the evidence for fables in the forensic and deliberative oratory of Classical Greece. With analyses of Aristophanes, Aristotle and the Attic orators, it challenges conventional assumptions about fables’ ubiquity in rhetoric of the Classical period. The study advances three arguments: first, attestations of the fable as a standard feature of rhetorical argumentation, or as having been told by the Classical orators, cannot be proven prior to the first century CE. Second, pre-Imperial testimonia on fable-telling in Classical oratory depict exceptional circumstances that deviate from normative rhetorical contexts. Third, to the extent that fables did appear in Classical oratory, they functioned as techniques of final recourse to persuade audiences when other arguments had failed or been forbidden. This article also reveals an association between rhetorical fables and death penalty cases.

Documenting Islamic Coin Finds in Conflict Zones: Provenance, Community, and the Syrian Case
abstract: This article presents a methodological framework for documenting and analysing Islamic coin finds in conflict-affected regions, arguing that for copper coinage (fulūs) provenance constitutes the primary source of historical value rather than a supplementary attribute. Using Syria as a case study, where excavation and institutional recording have been severely constrained since 2011, the article demonstrates how reliable numismatic data can still be generated under conditions of conflict. Based on fieldwork conducted between 2020 and 2023, the study integrates numismatic analysis with a purpose-built digital documentation system designed in an earlier project phase, alongside community-based reporting and ethnographic observation. The digital database, developed to be usable by non-specialists, allows consistent recording of typology, physical parameters, and findspot information under unstable field conditions. Particular attention is given to single finds reported by local communities, especially children, who are often the first discoverers of low-value copper coins whose significance lies in their findspots. Three case studies from al-Raḥba, Ḥalab, and Ḥimṣ demonstrate how securely documented finds can correct misattributions, refine mint histories, and reconstruct micro-regional circulation patterns absent from museum-based datasets. The article proposes a transferable, ethically grounded model for Islamic archaeology and heritage documentation in conflict zones. The study contributes to current debates on archaeological methodology and heritage protection by demonstrating how locally grounded documentation strategies can preserve contextual knowledge under conditions of conflict.

title: A Jewellery Hoard from Borsippa
abstract: In 1981, an assemblage of 44 artefacts was discovered at Tell Ibrahim al-Khalil within the ancient urban area of Borsippa, Iraq. The collection comprises a diverse range of objects, including gold and copper-alloy jewellery, beads, and other ornaments made from precious and semi-precious materials, found in close association with a ceramic vessel and textile fragments. The contextual evidence, including the absence of an identifiable settlement or burial setting, indicates an intentional deposition within medieval occupation layers. The hoard is characterised by considerable heterogeneity in material composition and manufacturing techniques. Technological and typo-chronological analyses indicate that the majority of the artefacts were produced between the 10th and 11th centuries AD, while some may date to the 12th century. Several objects display typological and stylistic features comparable to Fatimid jewellery traditions, with close parallels from Egypt, the southern Levant, Tunisia, Iran, and Syria, while others point to a broader range of regional traditions. The unusual combination of precious and base metals differs from patterns observed in certain Fatimid hoards and instead points to diverse practices of assembling and retaining valuables. As a rare medieval hoard, and currently the only assemblage of its kind known from the Babylon region, the find provides important insights into jewellery production, artisanal practices, and the circulation of materials, forms, and technologies across the medieval Islamic world. Rather than representing a single regional or workshop tradition, the assemblage brings together objects reflecting both local and supra-regional traditions. Its significance lies precisely in this combination, offering a rare glimpse into the material culture of the medieval Babylonian region and its wider connections. Although the precise circumstances and motivation of the deposition remain unclear, the religious significance of Borsippa offers an important interpretative context. The deliberate concealment of valuable objects may have involved personal, social, or symbolic considerations, while a pragmatic response to insecurity cannot be excluded. The hoard thus sheds light not only on the use and concealment of valuables, but also on the changing material and cultural landscape of Borsippa during the medieval period.

title: Filling the Gap: The Qasr al-Hallabat Wellhead and its Relevance to Establish a Chrono–Typological Sequence in the Transition from Classical Antiquity to Medieval Islamic Period
abstract: This paper presents the contribution made by the recently discovered Umayyad wellhead from Qasr al-Hallabat to the completion of a chrono-typological sequence of wellheads in the transition from Classical Antiquity to the Islamic period, specifically for types that use architectural elements to articulate their decoration. This recently discovered wellhead would fill a sequential gap between the well-defined Classical types, with a rather homogeneous evolution until Late Antiquity, and those developed later during the Islamic period in Al-Andalus, where we once again have a rather complete chrono-typological sequence from the 10th to the 15th century CE. In this paper, we will attempt to bridge these two distinct sequences by means of this new example with the diachronical approach of long durèe.

title: An Ayyubid Sgraffito Bowl from ʿAsqālan (Ashqelon, Israel): On the Evolution of Medieval Egyptian Glazed Wares and a Glimpse into the City’s Geopolitical Pendulum Swing between Muslims and Crusaders
abstract: This study discusses a rather unusual Ayyubid-period (late 12th century) glazed sgraffito-decorated bowl of Egyptian origin, which was found in ʿAsqālan (Ashqelon), on the southern Mediterranean coast of Israel. The ʿAsqālan bowl (and its few published counterparts) is chronologically and typologically placed between two major and much more renowned classes of Egyptian glazed wares—the Fustat Fatimid Sgraffito (FFS) and the Mamluk Barracks Sgraffito Ware—and it seems to constitute, respectively, a successor and a predecessor of these two wares. In addition, the study of the ʿAsqālan bowl against the local historical and archaeological background shows that this find provides a rare glimpse into the city’s Ayyubid past, a short but crucial phase in the mid-12th to mid-13th century geopolitical pendulum swing during which the city switched hands from Muslims to Crusaders and vice versa.

title: Revisiting Islamic Archaeology in the Malay World: With Special Attention to the Correct Date of Batu Aceh Permatang Pasir in Pahang
abstract: Islamic archaeology is a discipline largely underexplored by archaeologists in maritime Southeast Asia. Few specialists have directed sustained attention to the discipline, perhaps due to the perception that, as Islam continues to be a living tradition today, and Islamic history is relatively recent, compared to the likes of Srivijaya, Majapahit, or other Hindu-Buddhist traditions. Consequently, Islamic artefacts have often been misread or poorly dated, leading to chronological confusion and the proliferation of questionable historical narratives. In some cases, such errors are compounded by ideological motives or selective readings shaped by political or group interests. This study particularly focuses on one such artefact that has remained unresolved for over four decades—the Batu Aceh Permatang Pasir in Pahang. Some researchers claimed it dates to 419 AH/1028 AD, identifying it as the oldest Islamic tombstone in the Malay world. Despite ongoing suspicion surrounding its form and script, no one has yet provided a conclusive and convincing answer to the correct date of the artefact. This paper argues for the need to apply rigorous, methodologically grounded approaches to the dating of such artefacts, which, once put in place, could resolve many problems surrounding artefactual dates. Hence, this will result in a proper chronology and historical narrative that reflects what has truly occurred in reality in the past. This research finds that Batu Aceh Permatang Pasir, through detailed epigraphic analysis, comparative typology, and contextual palaeography, the correct date of the inscription is 914 AH, equivalent to 1508 AD. This is based on the outlined methodology and arguments. By situating the tombstone within a broader corpus of Islamic material culture in maritime Southeast Asia, this paper contributes to the ongoing debates on Islamisation, the standardisation of Islamic epigraphy, and the cultural dynamics of the Indian Ocean world.

title: Old devices, new meanings: The enduring materiality of outdated media and communication technologies
abstract: This article explores the enduring presence and shifting meanings of outdated media and communication technologies (MCTs) in everyday life. Based on 30 in-depth interviews conducted in Istanbul, it examines how individuals retain objects such as Walkmans, vinyl records, and early mobile phones – devices no longer widely used, yet still materially and emotionally significant. Rather than approaching these items as nostalgic collectibles, the study reframes retention as a materially mediated practice through which attachment, memory, and critique are enacted. Bringing material culture studies, science and technology studies, and domestication theory into conversation, the article argues that outdated MCTs act as mediators of identity and memory and enable alternative engagements with time, value, and media. Istanbul's urban ecology – marked by repair networks, second-hand circulation, and layered temporalities – further supports these practices. The article contributes to debates on materiality by showing how old devices persist as materially active participants in everyday urban life – culturally re-signified and affectively charged artefacts rather than passive remnants of past use.

title: Multiple and ordinary: The materialities of polycystic ovary syndrome
abstract: This article focuses on the everyday materialities of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) (currently being renamed to polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome). A PCOS is a combination of symptoms that vary from patient to patient, such as absent or irregular ovulation and menstruation, impaired glucose metabolism, excessive body hair or problems with fertility. This article adds to research on menstrual health and chronic disease, which has tended to prioritise tracking technologies and medical devices, by drawing attention to ordinary material objects. Drawing on Science and Technology Studies theorisations of disease and self-care, this article examines in-depth semi-structured interviews with people with PCOS to illuminate how materiality shapes everyday coping with this common yet diverse condition. The major finding of the analysis is that although medical professionals frame PCOS as a coherent whole, patients attend to their individual ‘packs’ of symptoms in their daily efforts to manage the condition.

title: Civilizational gene of knotting: The craftsmanship of the Uurga on the Mongolian Plateau and the material thinking of nomadic societies
abstract: This study examines the Uurga, a traditional Mongolian lasso pole used for capturing and managing livestock, exploring its material, social, and symbolic significance in nomadic societies. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork, this research traces how the Uurga has functioned not only as a practical instrument of domestication but also as a mediator of relationships between humans and animals. The study is organized into three parts. The first part clarifies the contexts of use and naming system of the Uurga. The second part provides a detailed account of Uurga-making, including pole-making, rope-making, and the intricate binding and knotting techniques. The third part explores the customs and beliefs associated with the Uurga. The study suggest that the Uurga represents a rich material culture, and as a primary technique for connecting different materials, knotting is its core method and may be foundational to the emergence and development of nomadic civilization. As such, the Uurga exemplifies the material thinking of nomadic societies, offering deep insights into the social, symbolic, and practical dimensions of life on the Mongolian Plateau.

title: The birth of the astronomical price: An ethnographic study of value and price in the Beijing art market
abstract: This ethnographic study examines the genesis of the astronomical price—known as tianjia —within the Beijing art market and aims to contribute empirically to anthropological debates on the value of art. Focusing on the dynamic interplay between abstract value and monetary price through the lens of practice, it traces how astronomical prices emerge through the coordinated labor of valuation, the discursive and embodied practices of auctioneers and bidders, and the ritual intensification of the auction event itself. By examining the concrete labor involved in the construction of value and the competitive escalation of bids at auction, the study argues that modern auctions are not merely sites where an object's value is formed and its ownership is transferred, but also ritualized stages on which archaic cosmology and modern calculative knowledge are brought into convergence through interpersonal interactions on the auction floor. It is through this convergence, the article suggests, that a form of collective effervescence is generated and astronomical prices come into being.

title: Unsettling collections, revitalizing culture: The work of art in Indigenous southeastern Australia
abstract: Situated in southeastern Australia, this article examines the pivotal work of Indigenous artists in revitalizing cultural practices and knowledge that colonial violence worked to erase. Our discussion tracks the material legacy of Kaawirn Kuunawarn (c.1820–1889), an important Ancestor of the Gunditjmara Nation and the maker of two greenstone axes held in Berlin's Ethnological Museum. We reassemble Kaawirn Kuunawarn's material record—dispersed across multiple collections and a distance of over 16,000 kilometers—and chart its legacy in the work of contemporary Indigenous artists. While our analysis offers a remarkable account of Gunditjmara cultural “survivance,” it also shows how Indigenous histories were obscured, rather than preserved, by global processes of museum collecting. In light of these erasures, cultural revitalization is highlighted as transformative political work: an affective, embodied mode of presencing the past that unsettles the colonial legacies of collecting, reconstituting archival objects and images as vital conduits of Indigenous social memory and identity.

title: Material imaginaries of the new iron curtain
authors: Natalia Magnani; Matthew Magnani; Anatolijs Venovcevs; Richard Fraser; Giuseppe Amatulli
abstract: The “social imaginary” has been critiqued for its overly deterministic qualities and resemblance to concepts of culture. Our article interrogates the materiality of the indeterminate at a time of heightened global uncertainty. Furthering a rapid response, material methodology in anthropology, we examine objects, animals, and infrastructures that disrupt and reinscribe border imaginaries in differential and unexpected ways in Sør-Varanger, on the Norwegian border with Russia, one month after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, amid emerging international sanctions and national border closures. We show how everyday engagements with various “materials"—souvenirs and monuments, surveyed and commodified species, industrial and transport infrastructures—foster a sense of uncertainty around the (im)permeability of an East-West border. The array of effects that they have on the imagination is unevenly and at times randomly shaped by their materiality. However, these differential effects are also patterned in their indeterminacy, as the scale and temporality of the materials’ movements affect their potential to transform border imaginaries. We thus rethink the material imaginary as simultaneously indeterminate and patterned in dialogue with scalar and temporal dimensions of mobility.

title: From traps to camps: Ghost fishing, plastic materialities and carceral entrapment
abstract: This article draws on ethnographic research with weavers and fishermen in Sardinia to explore emergent modalities of entrapment. Following fish traps from a Berlin museum collection to the bottom of the lagoon, and contrasting nasse traps made from plant material with synthetic ghost traps submerged in the Gulf of Oristano, I consider how synthetic materials exercise an indiscriminate, chronic agency that extends beyond single objects and designs. Combining material ecology with a critique of fossil capitalism, I develop the concept of carceral entrapment, or a modality of world-making that produces persistent harm beyond human control, in which the durability of plastics dissolves the dramatic nexus that Alfred Gell saw as constitutive of traps. Instead, carceral entrapment operates across scales and through ecological, economic, and corporeal relations, and generates enduring, unpredictable, and pervasive forms of harm. An anthropology of traps, I argue, must attend to these complex agentic relations and their uneven distributions.

title: Material noise at Cape Coast Castle: The costs of decolonizing heritage
abstract: Taking Cape Coast Castle as a case, this article asks how material remains sustain decolonial memory while unsettling the institutional arrangements that make it possible. Drawing on guided tours, local conversations, material observation, and institutional discussions, it shows how slavery memory is translated into controlled discomfort: powerful, recognizable, yet ordered enough to remain visitable and comfortable. The article argues that material remains are simultaneously docile and unruly: dampness, residues, corrosion, salt, microbial growth, and climatic weathering give emotional scripts sensory density, while the same traces become material noise when they demand cleaning, repair, conservation, funding, and responsibility. Digital heritage intensifies this tension as decolonial efforts to relieve material burdens risk reproducing coloniality through technological and donor dependency. Decolonization is therefore not the overcoming of pain, but a costly, unsettling, and unresolved struggle to live with material noise.

title: Thinking with material care
abstract: Engaging with care theories and perspectives arising from repair studies, this article proposes material care as a conceptual possibility to think with and to interpret material relations leading to overconsumption and wasting. We bring theoretical ideas on material care into conversation with empirical material from Finland, a country in which discarding is made easy with functioning waste management infrastructures. We use the material to gain understanding of what material care means in practice for people in their everyday life. With selected insights from the material gathered through object-centred dialogues, we reflect on care ethics in action, showing how material objects themselves influence people's choices on care and how avoiding care is part of the ethical considerations. We also discuss affective and embodied relations with things and meaning-making and creativity as crucial elements of material care. Our finding is that people do care about their things even though consumerism suggests otherwise, and we propose that this is because material care is significant to people's wellbeing in ways that are rarely addressed in present policy frameworks. The value of thinking with material care lies in the alternative visions for sustainability that it allows to nurture.

title: Geometric ornament as material knowledge: Ethnogeometric structures of spatial cognition
authors: Balnur Amantay; Manifa Sarkulova; İhsan Çapcıoğlu
abstract: This article proposes a method for analysing recurring geometric relationships in Chalcolithic Botai material culture in northern Kazakhstan. Ornamented artefacts, dwelling architecture and settlement layout are examined without assuming a single symbolic code or historical continuity. The methodology integrates ethnogeometry, Material Engagement Theory, the enactive signification hypothesis and Peircean and material semiotics. Analysis proceeds through four levels of inference, from observable material features to culturally specific interpretations. Results show that comparable geometric relationships are materialised differently through production, object orientation, bodily interaction, movement and spatial organisation. The unit of comparison is not a motif but a geometric relationship arising within a specific material practice. Formal similarity alone cannot establish ritual or cosmological meaning. Comparative cases from Sakha culture and Çatalhöyük are used asymmetrically to distinguish evidence-based conclusions from speculation. The article therefore treats geometric ornament as a form of embodied material knowledge while defining explicit evidential limits for archaeological interpretation.

title: Defining the Use of Cultic Space in the Early Iron Age: Tel Abel Beth Maacah as a Test Case
authors: Matthew Susnow; Nava Panitz-Cohen; Theo Kassebaum; Naama Yahalom-Mack
abstract: Numerous studies on the Late Bronze Age to Iron Age (IA) transition in the southern Levant have underscored how IA I (1190–980 BC) society displays evidence of both cultural continuity and discontinuity. This article investigates the role of cult in this process of transition, utilizing evidence revealed at Tel Abel Beth Maacah in the northern Hula Valley. Employing a methodology based on spatial analysis of artifacts, the article aims to establish the nature of cultic practices at the site, and comparison is made to contemporary IA I sites in the region to contextualize processes of continuity and change. A major break within cultic traditions during IA I is identified: groups were no longer beholden to the Bronze Age temple tradition of using demarcated spaces devoted exclusively to cult. Rather, a new type of space emerged, within which both cultic and quotidian activities were conducted. These spaces were neither standardized in their plans nor did they function like the region’s Bronze Age temples. Within them, familiar practices and symbols were utilized, but in new ways. This process is hypothesized to reflect new local authorities coalescing their status and power. The integration of cult into daily activities resulted in forms of democratization and inclusivity previously unknown in the region, serving as a link to developments in cultic practices of IA II.

title: Reassessing Hillforts in Central-Western Iberia: A Geospatial Approach to Hilltop Sites in the Alto Alentejo (Portugal) and Western Extremadura (Spain), Fourth to First Centuries BC
authors: Fernando Menéndez-Marsh; Tymon C.A De Haas; André Carneiro; Tesse D. Stek
abstract: This study proposes a formal geospatial approach to the contexts of fortified hilltop settlements that characterised the Iberian Peninsula during Iron Age (IA) II (fourth to first centuries BC), focusing on an area that encompasses Alto Alentejo in what is today Portugal and western Extremadura in Spain. Although the settlements here represent the most distinctive archaeological sites of this period, they remain poorly understood. The physical inaccessibility of hillforts has limited archaeological studies, while a reliance on Classical sources and ideological narratives of indigenous resistance to Rome promoted by the Iberian dictatorships in the 20th century have led to generic assumptions about the role of IA hillforts in these regions of the Iberian Peninsula. The study highlights their often overlooked diversity, with the goal of challenging generalised interpretations and resolving discrepancies in legacy data. By analysing a selection of hillforts through geospatial modelling, several locational factors can be quantified and used as proxies to associate cultural criteria with each hillfort. This makes it possible to bring out the heterogeneity of the hillforts and to identify two regional patterns in their locational characteristics. title: Stirrup Jars, Coastal Exchange, and Value in the Late Bronze Age Aegean (1470–1075 BC)
abstract: While it is generally assumed that transport stirrup jars functioned within a tightly monitored political economy in the Aegean during the Late Bronze Age, the many jars found outside palatial contexts unsettle this model. To explain the presence of these jars and their role outside the palatial sphere, this article provides a quantitative contextual analysis of transport stirrup jars in the LB II–IIIC period (1420–1075 BC). The data suggest that at least some stirrup jars circulated outside a palatial political economy and that their distribution can be attributed to the agency of merchants. Contrasting patterns of consumption of these jars are also apparent: at palatial sites they were more frequently stockpiled for use in commensal events, while those from non-palatial sites were deposited in ritual contexts. Thus, stirrup jars from palatial sites appear to have been valued for their contents, while those from non-palatial sites were valued as singular possessions. I suggest that this difference can be explained by the way that the meaning of these objects changed as they moved between social realms. Stirrup jars found outside palatial contexts testify to a broader network of exchange involving non-elite actors, as well as to differing sets of values that were actively contested through consumption practices.

title: New Approaches to Identifying Roman Libraries: Two Late Antique Examples from Stobi (North Macedonia) and Fuente Álamo (Spain)
authors: Antonio López García; Javier Martínez Jiménez; Eduardo Cerrato Casado
abstract: The identification of Roman libraries has long been the subject of debate, with architectural models, written sources and the archaeological record offering seemingly incompatible perspectives. Mamoli, however, has proposed a solution that deploys computational techniques for studying shape grammar to develop library grammar. This is a computational methodology that identifies minimal units of architectural meaning and the ways they may combine to determine if a built space has enough syntactic coherence to be defined securely as a library. In this paper, we use both traditional architectural analysis and the toolkit provided by shape grammar to analyse two Late Antique domestic spaces that have been identified as libraries: Room 7 in the so-called Theodosian Palace of Stobi (North Macedonia), the provincial capital of the province of Macedonia Salutaris; and Room 10 in the villa of Fuente Álamo (Puente Genil, Spain), a Roman site located along a road that connected the coastal cities of the Mediterranean and Corduba, the provincial capital of Baetica. These paired case studies demonstrate the utility of shape grammar as a method for identifying functional spaces in archaeological contexts.

title: The Pylos Hinterland Revisited: Survey Ceramics and Bottom-Up Approaches to Regional Organization of Late Bronze Age Greece
abstract: This paper presents a bottom-up perspective on the socioeconomic landscape of Mycenaean Pylos, based on the hitherto untapped potential of legacy survey data. Since the mid-20th century, intensive surface surveys have transformed our understanding of entire regions of the Mediterranean, yet interpretations relying primarily on site-size hierarchies impose a narrow view on the datasets, rendering peripheral sites into passive members of centralized political formations. Using functional analysis of Late Bronze Age ceramics (LH I–LH IIIB2, ca. 1600–1180 BC) collected by the Pylos Regional Archaeological Project (PRAP), this study compares assemblages from both large secondary centers and smaller rural sites within the palatial territory. The results show that communities differed not only in size but also in social status, economic practices, and access to goods, revealing a degree of local agency within the Pylian territory. While similar bottom-up approaches have been applied in other Mediterranean contexts, this study brings such perspectives into the discussion of Mycenaean states, underscoring the value of re-examining legacy survey data to explore regional patterns of social and economic organization.

title: A monumental apsidal building of the Roman Imperial period in Doliche
authors: Michael Blömer; Lennart Wouter Kruijer; Theresa Pommer
abstract: Excavations in the city center of the ancient city of Doliche in southeast Türkiye have brought to light the remains of a monumental apsidal building. Although the structure is poorly preserved due to looting and spoliation, the results of three seasons of excavation allow for an initial analysis and preliminary reconstruction. This article presents the building for the first time and discusses its importance in improving our understanding of monumental urban architecture in the region. The building is interpreted as a temple, and the article explores its potential links with apsidal temples in southern Syria and the Roman imperial cult.

Origins and features of Early Roman priesthoods: literary sources, images and material culture
authors: Francesco De Stefano; Francesca Fulminante; Jörg Rüpke
abstract: This paper examines three early Roman priesthoods, specifically, the Vestal virgins, the Salii, and the Flamines, through the lens of their visual and symbolic prerogatives, adopting a diachronic perspective based on literary sources, iconographic evidence, and archaeological data. The study highlights the deep historical roots of priestly paraphernalia in pre- and proto-historic funerary contexts, as well as a significant shift in gender dynamics. Prior to the 8th c. BCE, numerous male religious and martial figures are depicted with double shields and other distinctive attributes. From the 8th c. BCE to the Archaic period, both male and female religious figures appear, often equipped with knives, while double shields gradually disappear. This pattern suggests an expanding definition of religious and political prerogatives. By the 8th c. BCE, specialized male and female figures (identified by their knives) assume religious roles, whereas male warriors become kings ( reges ), holding political authority and often serving as Augurs as well. *

title: Situating a rock-born god: place, practice, and geologies of Mithras-worship at Močići (Croatia)
abstract: Contemporary accounts of Mithraism emphasize particular, shared modes of anthropogenic place-making: spaces laid out in distinctive, bench-lined arrangements, which may have been freighted with a surplus of cosmic symbolism that was actualized through the performance of ritual. Focusing on the site of Močići (Croatia), we argue that Mithraic place-making must instead be situated in a host of far more localized and material relationships that afford their own particular modes, experiences, and semiotics of worshipping the god. In the case of Močići, those relationships include local karstic geologies, particular lifeways and experiences of the landscape, and the ways that significances were woven around natural phenomena. The site encourages rethinking both contemporary conceptions of “Mithraism” and material- and place-based approaches to cult in antiquity.

title: Patronage and public amenities in Roman Epirus: the well of Junia Rufina at Butrint
abstract: The well of Junia Rufina has long been one of the main features of the archaeology of Roman Butrint. This paper aims at offering a chronological and cultural context for its dedication by inserting it into contemporary urban and historical developments. The monumentalization of the well in the 2nd c. CE illustrates how increased access to and architectural display of water was a main aspect of urban policy in the newly founded province of Epirus, in line with the rest of the Greek world. The role of Rufina, on the other hand, can be understood in the light of the cultural policies of the time, and as a manifestation of the power and prestige attached to female patronage in highly networked families throughout the Empire at the time of Hadrian.

title: The supply of metals in the later Roman Empire: framing the question
abstract: Whether the later Roman Empire ran short of precious or base metals, either at the level of the state or in private life, is a question that can only be answered in a tentative fashion. Surveying the period from the mid-2nd to the mid-7th c., this article weighs the difficulties presented by the full range of material and textual evidence, while attempting to establish a balance between all regions of the Roman world. It concludes by suggesting that there probably were indeed crises of metal production at certain periods, caused by the depletion of usable ores and hypothetically by a shortage of fuel.

title: Changing patterns of fineware consumption in Roman Mediterranean Gaul, ca. 225 BCE–100 CE
abstract: Widely found at archaeological sites across the Roman Empire, the appearance in the late 1st c. BCE onward of the red gloss ceramic referred to as terra sigillata signals important transformations in the socio-economic organization of production and consumption for provincial societies. Nonetheless, relatively few studies have explored diachronically the ways in which the appearance of terra sigillata may have impacted local lifeways compared with the uses of earlier ceramics. This article explores these issues in the context of Roman Mediterranean Gaul, focusing in particular on the region of eastern Languedoc, by comparing, in both discard and funerary contexts, the differential uses of black gloss ceramics from the 3rd to the 1st c. BCE with later terra sigillata vessels. The evidence discussed here suggests that the appearance of terra sigillata was important in reifying more individual-centered social relationships in dining and other aspects of daily life.

title: Not just a housekeeper: a new look at the work of the Roman vilica
abstract: The presence of the vilica or female supervisor at a Roman villa is attested across five centuries in varied texts, and her duties are detailed in an entire book of Columella’s On Agriculture . This paper challenges assumptions by modern scholars that her managerial functions were confined to those of a housekeeper, focused on food supplies for the household and the supervision of domestic labor inside the house. Through closer examination of textual, iconographic, and archaeological evidence, we can see that the vilica ’s principal role was to oversee not the domestic sphere, but rather a range of vital productive activities on the farm. In particular, she seems to have been responsible for wine and oil making and for important rituals linked to production. This has implications for our understanding of the roles of women within Roman farming and the Roman economy.

title: Working at worship, worshipping at work: approaching material, practice, and value
abstract: This article analyzes the intersections between work and worship in the ancient Mediterranean from an archaeological perspective and provides an introduction to this special section. The goal is to challenge and move beyond two conceptual frames that have been deeply persistent in scholarship on the ancient world: (1) the imposition of two distinct category-containers “religion” and “work,” which we contend have been constructed and held separate due to particular idealist, capitalist, and colonialist ways of conceptualizing the past; (2) notions of the “embeddedness” of ancient religion, which we argue rarely acknowledge the underlying Polanyian economic baggage. We propose taking an explicitly relational and praxeological approach, drawing on notions of “lived religion” that, unlike the prevalent model of “Lived Ancient Religion,” often consider the intersections of production and worship, and focusing on the ways practices, spaces, materials, persons, and divine powers articulate in particular constellations.

title: Chytra rituals in Athens
abstract: This essay examines the use of an ordinary household item – a chytra (stewpot) – to ritual effect. It focuses on Classical and Early Hellenistic deposits under the floors of a single room of the Classical Commercial Building, just north of the Athenian Agora. The plan of the building and workshop debris found in its floors identify it as a workplace, and the repeated appearance of the chytra and its orientation and relationship to the stratigraphy and other objects constitutes evidence of the ritual practices of those who worked there. Ancient texts and other chytra deposits, both in this building and elsewhere in the excavation, throw more light on these practices, constituting evidence for “religion-as-lived” in the Athenian workplace.

title: A Vesta’d interest: apotropaia and shrines as vernacular risk management strategies in Vesuvian bakeries
abstract: Pompeian commercial and industrial shrines are often cursorily lumped into the monolithic category of lararia , obfuscating their complexity. The shrines’ diverse combinations of deities, playful iconographies, and spatial placements suggest complex and dynamic strategies of appropriation and bricolage. Contextualized reassessment of assemblages and features reveals remnants of creative, “vernacular” ritual action. I argue that Pompeii’s pistrina proprietors prioritized familiar, locally invested deities alongside or even instead of the Lares to create a more personal, accessible space in their commercial ventures for reciprocal interaction with the divine – most notably, a variation of Vesta and her donkey. Spatial choices also indicate preferential construction of shrines in spaces that were particularly risky, with many closely associated with the mouth of the oven. But shrines were just one tool in a wider protective arsenal deployed around the volatile oven, which included amuletic and apotropaic interventions.

title: A fishy business at Pompeii: the House of the Sarno Lararium
abstract: The House of the Sarno Lararium at Pompeii (I.14.7) is known for the enigmatic scene painted on the lararium in its rear courtyard. Following a common practice in classical archaeology of identifying an artistic scene based on a reference in an ancient text, it has been interpreted as documenting the arrival of onions. This article proposes a novel interpretation. I argue that the scene represents a group of fishermen bringing their catch back to port, weighing it, and preparing it for distribution. To support this interpretation, I show how the imagery on the lararium can be linked to fishing and the pictured deity, Sarnus. Employing theoretical concepts of “taskscapes” and “lived religion,” I argue that this scene of non-elite fishermen indicates how household worship was entangled with daily labor, as well as how daily labor took place against the backdrop of a ritual landscape.

title: Wielding the axe, tending the priestly ornaments: religious labor in the emperor’s household
abstract: This paper investigates the ritual labor performed by the enslaved and freed members of the familia Caesaris who supported the emperor in his role as priest. Drawing on Roman art and funerary inscriptions, it contrasts elite and non-elite perspectives regarding religious work. Visual depictions – such as reliefs of the Ara Pacis and imperial sacrifice scenes – frame attendants as anonymous extensions of the emperor’s ritual authority, performing physical and sensory tasks that enhanced his prestige but denied their individuality. In contrast, inscriptions from the familia Caesaris record victimarii , musicians, and custodians of sacred implements who chose to highlight these roles in funerary commemoration. Their job-titles signaled skill, training, and membership in social networks that extended beyond imperial service, including participation in collegia and communal tombs. Examining these sources together reveals how ritual work was simultaneously devalued by elites and deeply meaningful to its practitioners, shaping identities, communities, and the lived experience of Roman religion.

title: The cult of Saturn in Africa under the Roman Empire
abstract: The title of this remarkable book may, in some respects, misrepresent the nature of its inquiry.It is not, in the strictest sense, an examination of how religion contributed to the making of Roman Africa.Rather, it offers a sweeping and deeply textured account of how the Roman Empire appropriated, reconfigured, and gradually transformed a preexisting cult (and perhaps local chthonic cults), centered originally on Saturn and deeply rooted in the African provinces, across centuries of imperial rule.What emerges is not a story of religion as a backdrop to empire, but of religion as a medium through which imperial power inscribed itself onto local landscapes and sensibilities.Or as the author eloquently puts it: "the Roman Empire left no relationshipamong persons, material signifiers, and interpretantsuntouched.Even a form of practice like stele-erection, or gods and iconographies that seem regionally distinct and continuous from the Iron Age through the Late Empire, became entangled with, reproduced, and naturalized those forms of relationship that constituted imperial hegemony" (23). 1 In Part I of the book (divided into two chapters) entitled "Colonial histories," McCarty investigates the impact of colonialism on the historiography of the Saturn cult.In many respects, he echoes the (uncited) perspective of Février, 2 who conceived of religion in Roman Africa not as a static reflection of belief, but as a contested and adaptive field, one in which imperial domination, local negotiation, and cultural integration were continually enacted.Far from being inert expressions of faith, religious institutions and practices functioned as critical instruments in the architecture of Roman power, legitimizing rule while mediating the complexities of provincial life.However, as McCarty astutely cautions, any attempt to uncover, much less fully grasp, the contours of Roman imperial hegemony in North Africa must begin with the critical unlearning of what he terms "essentializing idealism rooted in colonial archaeologies, overarching metanarratives, and the privileging of specific semiotic conventions" (23).His intervention gestures toward what Frantz Fanon more searingly described as the pervasive, ambient effects of colonialism on the mental, emotional, and spatial environment of the colonized.3

title: Paying up: Numidian peasants and the wider economy
abstract: In an important prolegomenon to her new book, Surviving Rome, Kim Bowes calls for a qualitative, microhistorical approach to Roman economic history, in order to build the large mosaic of the Roman economy from smaller, case-based tesserae.1 Such a bottom-up approach would contrast the large-scale, muscular models like those of Scheidel and Friesen, which take on the whole of the Roman economy, with more nuanced accounts of its separate parts.2 Paolo Tedesco's new book offers just such a microhistory: a detailed analysis of the world of the Albertini tablets, produced by the peasants who lived on the Fundus Tuletianos in southern Numidia at the end of the 5th c.CE.He then uses the vantage point established by this microhistory to examine a much longer chronology of the relationship between producers, landowners, and the state.The book begins with an overview of the settlement patterns of later Roman North Africa, starting with the extensive imperial properties, which were leased to members of the elite or farmed directly by conductores through tenants.The emperor owned between a quarter and a third of all the arable land, while most of the rest consisted of large, privately owned estates, the patrimony of Roman senators such as Symmachus, the Roman churches, and the provincial élites.Further down the scale, the curial class, and with them the African bishops, were always landowners.There is not much trace of smallholders; title: The gymnasium in Greece from the Hellenistic Period to late antiquity
