title: Earthen architecture and taskscapes in Neolithic northwestern Greece
abstract: This paper investigates earthen architecture in Neolithic northwestern Greece through the study of fire-hardened daub, a frequently overlooked category of archaeological material. Drawing on the concept of ‘taskscape’, the present approach challenges static and linear perspectives of technical practice, emphasizing instead its material and temporal entanglements. By turning the focus on the spatiotemporal context of the construction process, including the immanent temporalities of building materials and techniques, and their integration with the agrarian economy, this analysis sheds light on the lived experience of Neolithic architectural practice. The synthesis of macroscopic and microscopic data, deriving primarily from a handful of systematically studied sites, offers regional insights into the synchronization and synchorization of building activities with environmental rhythms and the agrarian calendar. The study concludes that daub assemblages constitute high-resolution archives, materializing the rhythmic pulses and complex choreographies of Neolithic life.

title: 5000 years of mudbrick at Arslantepe: ancient earthen architecture and modern sustainability
authors: Francesca Balossi Restelli; Elisa Biancifiori; Filippo Edoardo Capasso; Giuseppina Fazio; Giovanna Liberotti; Elisabetta Lulli; Lucia Mori
abstract: Arslantepe is a 5000-year-old mound in eastern Anatolia featuring early examples of advanced planning, skilled craftsmanship and durable earthen architecture. Over the last four decades, it has been preserved through minimal, reversible interventions and protective shelters. Comparison with surviving traditional mudbrick houses in nearby Orduzu shows enduring continuities in design, materials, and maintenance. The loss of this know-how and its exclusion from modern building codes contrast with archaeological evidence of mudbrick’s structural potential. Drawing on local heritage, the authors propose integrating traditional methods with modern engineering to create sustainable, earthquake-resistant earthen architecture for reconstruction. This case highlights how cultural continuity and environmental sustainability can guide future rural housing policies.

title: Building knowledge: anatomy of urban earthen architecture in the Pharaonic town of Elephantine
abstract: The incorporation of botanical additives into earthen building materials reflects not only practical construction techniques but also broader socioeconomic dynamics. At Elephantine, diachronic analysis of mudbricks, mortar, and plaster from Pharaonic Egypt reveals significant shifts in material recipes. These changes were shaped by evolving environmental conditions, agricultural strategies, and economic priorities, offering valuable insights into resource management practices in an urban context and the building knowledge of ancient workers. Tue selection and integration of plant temper demonstrate how construction methods aligned with the ecological and economic demands of ancient Egyptian society. This research highlights the interplay between material composition and resource use, providing a framework for understanding the adaptive strategies of past communities. Furthermore, the findings underscore the relevance of earthen architecture not only for sustainable building practices today but also for advancing the preservation of cultural heritage, emphasizing the enduring value of one of history’s most resilient architectural traditions.

title: ‘New settlers in new fashion’: earthen architecture as a cultural marker in the Phoenician foundation of Eivissa (Ibiza, Spain)
authors: Benjamín Cutillas-Victoria; Marta Lorenzon; Marco Aurelio Esquembre; Bernia Sanz Kite; Joan Ramon Torres
abstract: Phoenician colonization brought significant cultural and environmental challenges for displaced groups across the Mediterranean Sea. Establishing new settlements required adapting Levantine practices to unfamiliar environments and raw materials. A paradigmatic example of such a community establishment occurred on the island of Ibiza (Balearic Islands, Spain), where a distinctive building tradition emerged, characterized by the use of mudbrick architecture. This paper presents a geoarchaeological study of earthen building materials from Eivissa, the principal site that flourished in the 7th century BC and has remained inhabited to the present day. Our methodology – combining archaeological analysis with geochemical and petrographic characterization – allows us to identify different raw material sources and construction recipes, reflecting how Phoenicians could have adapted to Ibiza’s specific environmental conditions. The results shed light on the development of the island’s mudbrick architecture and the probable challenges faced by Phoenician communities in preserving their traditional building techniques.

title: Climate-responsive earthen architecture: multi-scale environmental analysis of passive house design in Classical Olynthos
abstract: This article presents the first quantitative analysis of the thermal performance of mud brick housing in Classical Greek cities. By integrating 3D architectural modelling with Rhinoceros 3D and the Ladybug and Honeybee environmental simulation toolsets, it introduces a novel methodological framework for studying ancient earthen architecture. Focusing on housing blocks at Olynthos, the study examines how architectural form, material properties, and house location shaped indoor climates. Results demonstrate that mud brick moderated temperature fluctuations, yet specific building forms and locations created perceptible differences in thermal comfort between rooms, storeys and house position within a city block. By moving beyond purely morphological or economic readings of domestic space, this research shows how earthen architecture shaped lived social experience and advances debates on the temporality of life, equality and standards of living in the Classical polis.

title: Earthen dialogues: the cosmopolitics of adobe architectural construction in the Jequetepeque Valley of Peru (600–1000 CE)
abstract: At the scale of the individual brick, adobe construction preserves a record of the decisions, labour, and political relationships through which it was made. This study compares Huaca Colorada and Tecapa, two neighbouring ceremonial centres in the Jequetepeque Valley, whose construction practices diverged markedly during the late Middle Horizon (600–1000 CE). Through morphological, grain-size, and pXRF analyses of over 1,600 bricks, distinct construction regimes emerge at each site: heterogeneous, inclusion-rich bricks and episodic building at Huaca Colorada reflect a decentralized process tied to ritual cycles and community labour, while standardized brick types and coordinated planning at Tecapa suggest a hierarchically organized regime consistent with highland building traditions. A discrete morphological and material convergence in Huaca Colorada’s final phase, concentrated in the east-facing platform oriented towards Tecapa, is interpreted as evidence of inter-site political negotiation, registered in the dimensions, sediment makeup, and geochemistry of individual bricks.

title: Tomb living: shaped-earth furniture in re-used tombs of Dra Abu el-Naga, Luxor
abstract: For much of the 19th and 20th centuries, Egypt’s Theban necropolis (Luxor) was a living palimpsest where ancient tombs mingled with modern mudbrick homes. The Qurnawis, the modern inhabitants of the necropolis, adapted pharaonic tombs, using earthen architecture to convert them into functional living spaces. Shaped-earth cupboards, shelves, troughs, ovens, and dovecotes were constructed both inside and outside the tomb-houses. This paper presents unpublished data from the Spanish archaeological mission at Dra Abu el-Naga North (Djehuty Project), documenting the surviving examples of modern earthen architecture within the Middle and New Kingdom tombs (2030–1070 BCE). The modern earthen architecture is possibly a continuation of an ancient tradition of the inhabitants of the necropolis, and of Egypt. Today, these earthen structures are nearly extinct, having been demolished, or replaced. Understanding and protecting these features offers invaluable insights into the daily life of Egypt’s modern inhabitants as well as their ancient counterparts.

title: Building one’s own prison: mudbrick production and embodied prisoner labour in Kazakhstan’s Soviet-era Gulags
abstract: One of the Soviet Gulag’s largest camp systems was Karlag, located in central Kazakhstan. The project, Central Asia’s Gulags, is the first to explore this expansive forced labour system from an archaeological perspective. Recent satellite and pedestrian surveys have identified annular pit features common to multiple camps. This study presents preliminary survey results from the site of Aktailak, a camp point within Karlag, with a focus on camp areas dense with annular pits. Data gathered from the targeted excavations of two barracks are used to calculate and humanize prisoner labour involved in mudbrick construction by focusing on embodied practices. Additionally, as unique features, annular pits have the potential to help identify unknown prison camps in the vast Kazakh Steppe.

title: Replica revolutions in rock art: from physical replicas to virtual reality libraries via contemporary art
abstract: Rock-art replicas generally are judged as more or less faithful substitutes for inaccessible originals. While previous studies have demonstrated the value of replicas for individual archaeological experiments, we reconceive them as persistent interdisciplinary research infrastructure. Drawing on reflections from original sites, we compare physical copies with virtual environments, developing criteria for evaluating replicas. Physical replicas preserve material, spatial and atmospheric relationships but constrain enquiry through fixed routes and authoritative narratives; VR replicas increase freedom, manipulation and perceptual experimentation but sacrifice embodied materiality. Neither currently supports cumulative research: observations disappear when the encounter ends. Central to this contribution is a two-directional account of indexicality: replicas point backwards to the caves and their makers, but also outwards to the scanners, artists, software, institutions and interpretive decisions that produce them. We therefore propose the perma-library as an infrastructure through which replicas can become comparable, revisitable, annotatable and capable of accumulating research over time.

title: Early large-scale petroglyphs in Central Scandinavia – the relevance of landscape and hunting contexts for implicit narrativity
authors: Tomas Persson; Peter Skoglund; Michael Ranta; Jan Magne Gjerde; Anna Cabak Rédei
abstract: Some of the earliest Scandinavian petroglyphs depict big game, such as elks and reindeer, dating from around 9000 to around 4000 BCE. These large images were represented as singular motifs, usually without any interaction with other figures, and without any explicit narrative appearance. However, involvement with the surrounding natural landscape and hunting contexts, particularly river rapids and straits, seems to have affected the placement of the images and likely given them narrative implications. This involvement may have given the earliest large-scale rock petroglyphs an implicit narrative functionality. Specifically, due to their size and visibility, especially from waterways, the images could have had an effective indexical function as ‘signposts’ at strategic hunting grounds related to water crossings. In order to corroborate these assumptions, examples from Sweden (Landverk, Gärde, and Duved) and Norway (Stykket) will be discussed, and contrasted with a later miniaturizing tradition.

title: Edible insects as heritage foods: towards an archaeology of alternative proteins for food sustainability
abstract: Insects and their secondary products form a persistent component of human diets from the Palaeolithic onwards, and entomophagy remains a common practice in many parts of the world. Coprolite analysis, biomarker and volatile organic compound (VOC) screening, ceramic and lithic residues, contextual caches, and isotopes provide direct and indirect evidence for entomophagy across diverse settings, supported by ethnographic and textual sources, but are rarely considered in wider archaeological narratives of subsistence. This article makes two arguments. First, the marginal place of insects in many archaeological syntheses reflects taphonomic filters, methodological priorities, and interpretive traditions rather than absence in the past. Second, archaeology is uniquely positioned to reframe insects as heritage foods in contemporary sustainability debates. By demonstrating that Western disgust is historically contingent and translating archaeological findings into accessible encounters, archaeology can help destigmatize entomophagy and support a shift to more diverse, resilient protein systems aligned with sustainable development goals.

title: Fire as spatial organizer: reconstructing the ritual grammar of a late Longshan ceremonial landscape at Yuhuicun, China
abstract: This paper investigates the spatial organization of fire-related deposits at Yuhuicun, a late Longshan period ceremonial complex in the Huai River Valley, China. Archaeological research has explored the role of fire in human adaptation, but less attention has been paid to how ritual fire was organized in space. Yuhuicun’s burnt sacrificial surface (BSS, ca. 90 m2) lies at the centre of a purpose-built platform surrounded by sacrificial pits, a trench containing nearly 18,000 sherds and diverse activity features. Drawing on theories of ritual materialization, structured deposition and elemental ontology, this study constructs a 126-feature spatial database and applies four complementary approaches: spatial association analysis, compositional patterning, functional clustering and co-occurrence network analysis. The results suggest that the fire at Yuhuicun played a central role in the site’s spatial organization, with the BSS as the focus of a ritual landscape consisting of two main areas linked by built features. The BSS preserves intense burning but no accumulated ash, while the adjacent trench is saturated with combustion residues, indicating deliberate redistribution.

title: From mountain flames to domestic smoke: rescaling ritual fire in the Gubbio valley from the Bronze Age to Imperial Rome
abstract: Archaeological accounts of religion in the Gubbio valley have often presented incorporation into the Roman world as a rupture, privileging public expressions of Roman religion. This leaves unresolved how locally embedded ritual practices changed across this transition. This paper investigates the changing scale and location of fire-related ritual from the Final Bronze Age to the Roman Imperial period. It combines contextual analysis of excavated evidence from Monte Ingino and Monte Ansciano with typological and GIS-based spatial analysis of lamps and incense burners recorded by the Gubbio Project. Burnt deposits and faunal assemblages indicate communal practices involving fire and feasting at elevated locations during the Final Bronze and Early Iron Ages. Sixth-century BCE construction and votive deposition at Monte Ansciano marked more explicitly defined collective ritual activity. Roman-period lamps and second-century CE incense burners reveal the dispersal of fire, light and smoke into household and rural settings, demonstrating the repeated rescaling and reformulation of ritual practice across changing contexts.

title: Carrying fire: containing sacred and profane flame in the Aegean Bronze Age
abstract: In this article, I explore the uses of fire in the Aegean Bronze Age, and specifically Minoan Crete. Despite a rich archaeological record with plentiful traces of burning, fire has received much less attention than might be expected. Particularly curious is the relative occlusion of fire in scholarship on Minoan buildings. I therefore propose a methodology that seeks to situate fire in relation to both its specific technicities and its architectural milieux. One important distinction is between fixed and portable hearths and their different functions. While the fixed hearth is in later periods often associated with the sacred, this connection is hard to make in the Minoan context. However, portable equipment for fire holds out more promise with both sacred and profane uses likely. The article further reflects on the implications of fire’s portability for our understanding of Minoan conceptions of interior space, architectural aesthetics and atmosphere.

title: Bridging morphometrics and Archaeogenetics: a non-destructive approach to species identification of sheep, goats and pigs based on bony labyrinth
authors: Agathe Guignet; Adeline Hemelsdaël; Daniel Gaspar; Áine Halpin; Valeria Mattiangeli; Vanessa Navarrete; Dani López-Reyes; Mireia Sabaté Balada; Gabriel de Prado; Jaume Noguera; Pau Menéndez Molist; Joan Bernabeu Aubán; Oreto García Puchol; Lluís Molina Balaguer; Alfredo Cortell-Nicolau; Renaud Lebrun; Cleia Detry; Ana Elisabete Pires; Daniel G. Bradley; Catarina Ginja; Silvia Valenzuela-Lamas; Allowen Evin
abstract: The petrous part of the temporal bone is a target for ancient DNA research due to its biomolecular preservation, yet destructive sampling risks losing valuable morphological information. Bony labyrinth morphology, captured by high-resolution 3D imaging, carries strong taxonomic and evolutionary signals, but its bioarchaeological application remains limited. We assessed the potential of bony labyrinth geometric morphometrics (GMM) for species identification of domestic animals by analysing 14 micro-CT-scanned archaeological petrosals from Spain alongside a dataset of 41 modern French and Spanish breeds of sheep and goats, as well as two pigs and two wild boars. Predictive discriminant analysis shows bony labyrinth shape reliably distinguishes these taxa, matching ancient genomic identification. Our findings demonstrate that bony labyrinth morphometrics is a robust, non-destructive approach for taxonomic identification of archaeological specimens, complementing other bioarchaeological proxies (e.g. ancient DNA, palaeoprotein). Integrated with palaeogenomic evidence, this framework enables comprehensive reconstructions of domestication processes and human-animal relationships.

title: Revealing archaeological olive diversity: insights from stone geometric morphometrics, experimental charring, and varietal identification (Port-la-Nautique, France, Roman period)
authors: Juliette Testas; Allowen Evin; Sarah Ivorra; Margaux Tillier; Corinne Sanchez; Nicolas Carayon; Patrick Andersch-Goodfellow; Mohammed Ater; Vincent Bonhomme; Laurent Bouby; Selhma Froul; Jalal Kassout; Hélène Lasserre; Bertrand Limier; Clément Lopes; Clémence Pagnoux; Christian Pinatel; Guillaume Besnard; Jean-Frédéric Terral
abstract: The cultivated olive tree, domesticated in the Levant by the mid-5th millennium BCE, spread westward across the Mediterranean to reach southern France by 600 BCE. Although geometric morphometrics applied to archaeological olive stones has provided insights into this diffusion, morphotype identification remains challenging, and the effects of charring, the most common preservation mode, are poorly understood. We compared ten morphometric approaches to determine the most effective method for discriminating wild and domesticated morphologies and distinguishing varieties. Controlled charring experiments assessed the effects of temperature, duration, and atmosphere on stone morphometry. The resulting methodology was applied to 261 olive stones from the Roman villa of Port-la-Nautique and the Capelles fishpond (Narbonne, France). Elliptic Fourier Transforms proved most effective for taxonomic discrimination, and charring up to 350°C did not prevent reliable classification against modern uncharred references. This approach enabled the identification, for the first time, of archaeological stones resembling present-day varieties, offering new insights into the evolution of olive agrobiodiversity.

title: Graded illumination as institutional practice: multi-nozzled lamps in public contexts across the Roman Mediterranean
abstract: This article examines multi-nozzled lamps recovered exclusively from public contexts across the Roman Mediterranean to investigate illumination as an institutional practice. Moving beyond typological description, it analyzes how variations in nozzle count and spatial deployment produce graded regimes of visibility within civic architecture. Drawing on a systematically assembled comparative dataset, the study identifies structured regional patterns in the distribution of enhanced lighting across agoras, bathhouses, palatial complexes, streets, and administrative buildings. The findings demonstrate that intensified illumination was neither randomly dispersed nor merely functional. Rather, lighting capacity was selectively embedded within architectural systems to organize attention, regulate movement, and reinforce hierarchies of presence. By integrating theories of space, visibility, infrastructure, and sensory experience, the article proposes that multi-nozzled lamps function as micro-infrastructural devices mediating institutional authority. Illumination is thus interpreted as a form of graded social materiality through which public consciousness and civic order were materially produced across the Roman Mediterranean.

title: Creation by fire: ritual burning and ancestor shrines in West Africa
abstract: Fire-hardened walls, burned floors and completely burned structures are common features of archaeological sites in central West Africa, often forming distinct strata in sites that developed into large mounds, or tells. Despite their ubiquity, the presence of burning on architectural remnants plays a very minor role in archaeological interpretations. We suggest that burned features are frequently the result of different forms of sacrificial burning that created durable ancestor shrines to anchor the past, living and future community. We contextualize ritualized burning within a broader cultural setting where fire is transformative and creative, with extensive religious dimensions that are both central to the important historic social status of blacksmiths and potters and fundamental to sacrificial practices more broadly. We argue that architectural burning is part of this broader corpus of transmutation by fire involving both divine power and extensions of the human soul that created material attachments critical to ancestral presence.

title: House-burning as a form of prehistoric potlatching
abstract: The potlatching practices of the First Nations of the Northwest Pacific Coast have been used as ethnographic analogies for Neolithic, Bronze Age and historic ceremonies. Its relevance in prehistory was aided by the often dramatic materialization of the potlatch’s accompanying ceremonies. What does potlatching have to do with house-burning in the European Neolithic? The experimental house-building and -burning programme in the Nebelivka Project, Kirovograd Oblast, Ukraine (2009–2017) confirmed earlier suggestions that much additional fuel over and above that contained in the original structure was required to achieve successful conflagration, supporting the explanation of deliberate burning. But this left a second problem – why should communities sacrifice such apparently solid, well-built and recently constructed structures? Here, the analogy with potlatching becomes more apparent, not only with the destruction of valuable objects but also the linkage of potlatches to the building or repair of a house in some Northwest Coast societies. We propose to use an informal Venn diagram approach to study these potential linkages. The results suggest that there is sufficient convergence between deliberate house-burning and potlatching to further our understanding of the former through insights from the latter.

title: The evolution of fire and ritual: a Durkheimian perspective
abstract: Durkheim envisioned the evolution of religion as an expression of the dialectical relationship between people living in society with the forces that emerge from this society. His evolutionary scenario was built on living and historic societies, primarily Aboriginal Australians, Biblical Jews, Catholics, and 19th Century cosmopolitan Europeans. This article explores the potential of applying Durkheim’s conceptual framework to the palaeoanthropological record with a focus on the potential role of fire in the emergence of ritual. This inquiry entails a consideration of the structure of evolutionary processes and the current archaeological record for the early engagement with fire.

title: Carved in stone and written as script. Material expressions of Bektashi identity in 19th c. Epirus (NW Greece)
abstract: Ottoman-era archaeology is gradually emerging in dialogue with art history and Ottoman studies. Yet aspects of material culture traditionally addressed by our discipline remain understudied and disjointed. This paper investigates stone carvings and Ottoman inscriptions from 19th-century Epirus, focusing on the town of Konitsa (NW Greece). We propose a synthetic approach that treats stone carvings and inscriptions as a distinct but complementary means of manifesting identity. Through a microhistorical comparative analysis of two neighbouring architectural complexes belonging to Bektashi-affiliated households, we use these media to illuminate the identities of local powerholders during an era of political upheaval and imperial reform. The contrast between vernacular, locally produced carvings and standardized, imported inscriptions reflects differing political orientations and strategies of cultural resilience in response to transformations within the Ottoman Empire.

title: Turn the light on: features related to the Roman lamps’ lighting
abstract: The relationship between lamps and fire has too often been taken for granted rather than critically examined. Research has largely focused on the morphology, iconography, epigraphy, production and trade of lamps, while paying less attention to their function and their relationship with fire. Yet classical literature provides valuable evidence for the association of lamp flames with both gods and humans in Antiquity, offering insights that the archaeological record alone rarely reveals. Understanding how people used, perceived and ritualised artificial light requires a multisource approach that integrates textual, archaeological and iconographic evidence. Artificial light was far more than a practical necessity. In the Roman world, fire permeated nearly every domain of life, serving both everyday activities and religious practice. Lamp flames embodied a striking duality: they could sustain life or cause destruction, illuminate domestic spaces or accompany the divine, acting as both witnesses and agents of human experience. Their light was simultaneously functional, symbolic and protective. Recognising this complexity broadens our understanding of lamps beyond their material form, reminding us that these artefacts cannot be separated from the flames they once held. When we study lamps, we are also studying the light that illuminated the gods and people in Antiquity.

title: Multidisciplinary analyses of Gotlandic picture stones: a case study of fragments from Martebo and Stenkyrka
authors: Hannah Strehlau; Patrick Hänsel; Laila Kitzler Åhfeldt; Magnus Källström; Michael Fergusson; Sigmund Oehrl
abstract: The Gotlandic picture stones are an unparalleled monumental art in Scandinavia whose rich imagery offers a glimpse into pre-Christian belief systems. Their fragmented condition and reuse in secondary contexts, however, has challenged our understanding of their original use. Against this background, this article matches the two Migration Period picture stones GP 268 Martebo kyrka I and GP 428 Stenkyrka kyrka 46 which were previously considered separate monuments. Because the fragments lack matching fracture edges and display apparent inconsistencies in their decoration, we conducted a multidisciplinary investigation using photogrammetry, groove analysis, runology, and isotope analysis. The results demonstrate that the stones share the same width, possess complementing decorative elements, and originate from the same geological rock layer on Gotland. Groove analysis further indicates that the majority of the decoration expresses the same carving characteristics. The runic inscription was likely added to GP 268 Martebo kyrka I during the Migration Period as part of the original decoration. Taken together, these findings support the affiliation of GP 268 Martebo kyrka I and GP 428 Stenkyrka kyrka 46, identifying them as a single monument and a key monument of phase A Gotlandic picture stones (400–550 CE).

title: The Northern Tradition rock art of western Norway: from archaeological relativism to iconographic relevance under Late Mesolithic demographic change
abstract: The paper argues that more holistic and theoretically informed approaches to contextualizing the Northern Tradition rock art of Scandinavia have significantly expanded the interpretive potential of its iconography. By integrating archaeological excavations, independent scientific analyses, and extensive radiocarbon dating procedures, a more robust chronological framework has emerged, situating the production of Northern tradition rock art firmly to the end of the Late Mesolithic. This chronological anchoring has enabled a reconceptualization of the imagery not merely as isolated symbolic expressions, but as practices embedded within contemporaneous material, social, and perhaps even ecological transformations. The demonstrated synchrony between iconographic themes and demographic shifts at the term of the Late Mesolithic further suggests that the imagery may be read as an active engagement with – and representation of – structures and features once part of prehistoric dynamics. The paper also critiques prevailing interpretive models shaped by modern Western utilitarian and consumption-based assumptions, arguing that such frameworks still constrain our ability to access alternative ontological premises. Instead, it advocates theoretical approaches inspired by multispecies perspectives, relational ontologies, and broader anthropological debates on animism and posthumanism, to reconstruct past premises. From this standpoint, the Northern Tradition iconography may be understood as preserving traces of Late Mesolithic worldviews in which humans, animals, landscapes, and non-human entities were entangled within shared social and cosmological fields. This perspective not only opens new interpretive pathways for understanding the epistemic content encoded in the imagery and tentatively helps to explain the sudden appearance of rock art, but also provides a more expansive foundation for revisiting and recontextualising the wider corpus of Northern Tradition rock art.

title: Joining hands: cross-cultural analysis of decorated handprints
authors: Barbara Oosterwijk; Linda Hurcombe; Jamie Hampson; José Iriarte
abstract: Hand depictions are among the most widespread motifs in global rock art, appearing from the Pleistocene to the present and often representing some of the earliest symbolic practices. At Cerro Azul and Paredones del Potrero in Amazonian Colombia, red handprints feature diverse decorations – including spirals, braided lines and geometric infill – whose production and significance remain little understood. This study presents the first detailed typological classification of thirteen decorated handprint types from these sites. Quantitative and spatial analyses are integrated with ethnographic and Indigenous perspectives, together with cross-cultural comparisons from regions including Brazil, Borneo and Australia, to explore how decorated hands may have functioned as embodied gestures, markers of identity and elements of cosmological landscapes. By combining fine-grained local documentation with a global comparative framework, the study demonstrates the potential of decorated handprints to illuminate the interplay of body, material and place in the creation of enduring social and symbolic relationships.

title: Carved stone in Mesolithic Cornwall: portable art, Mesolithic magic or mundane markings. Extraordinary new discoveries from southwest Britain
authors: Chris Carey; Andy M. Jones; Anna Lawson-Jones; Jo May; Laura Ratcliffe-Warren; Sean Taylor
abstract: Shaped and carved stone is a fundamental component of the archaeological record from the Mesolithic period across the UK. Whilst flint is the central element of this archaeological record, there is also a significant non-flint lithic component to many British Mesolithic sites that has been somewhat understudied. Within Cornwall, south-west Britain, research into this non-flint lithic component, partially retrieved through innovative methods of whole ‘earth’ sampling of Mesolithic land-surfaces, has revealed a significant collection of Mesolithic carved stones. A selection of these stones is presented and consideration is given to whether these pieces were created from their use as tools or whether these pieces of stone have longer biographies, potentially eventually becoming mnemonic devices. Parallels are drawn to other Mesolithic carvings from across the UK, with some symbols such as the ‘X’s and parallel lines, evident over a wide area and across the long time period of the Mesolithic.This paper is dedicated to our dear friend and colleague Andy Jones.

title: Stone workshops between petrography and iconography: a preliminary study on Iron Age basalt carvings
authors: Cristiana Biancalani; Marina Pucci; Chiara Colombo; Maria Catrambone; Antonio Sansonetti
abstract: The flourishing of sculptural series on orthostats, protomes and statues, which decorated the so-called Syro-Hittite city-state citadels, represents a unique phenomenon in stone production during the pre-classical period (12th-7th centuries BC) in the Syro-Anatolian region. Since the first discoveries of these sculptural cycles, archaeological and art-historical research has primarily focused on problems related to style, dating and production, mostly through an iconographic approach. However, the matter of the workshops (from quarrymen to sculptors) has not been fully explored, nor has the integration of geological aspects (such as the identification of quarries) and the production process. This article presents preliminary results from a broader project that addresses this issue through iconographic and petrographic analysis of basalt samples from sculptures found at Syro-Hittites sites. This study aims to introduce an interdisciplinary approach, seeking to bridge the existing gap between workshops, quarries and the Syro-Hittites political entities that commissioned these monumental artworks.

title: The persistence of memory: reuse and resignification of prehistoric petroglyphs in historical times. Two case studies from Malagón (La Mancha, Spain)
authors: Álvaro Ibero; Luis Benítez de Lugo Enrich; Álvaro Guzmán Sil
abstract: This paper presents two unpublished petroglyph sites from Malagón (La Mancha, inner Iberia) as case studies in the long-term cultural reuse and reinterpretation of prehistoric rock art. Through a diachronic-biographical approach that combines archaeological, historical, and ethnographic sources, our research has identified several graphic phases spanning from Late Prehistory to the 19th century. These include cup-marks, schematic motifs, inscriptions, Christian iconography, and modern imagery. Moreover, interviews with locals indicate that these sites have remained in use through to the present day. Consequently, both sites represent an ideal scenario to explore how different human communities have persistently engaged with these sites throughout millennia, attributing new meanings aligned with changing worldviews. Thus, rather than conceiving archaeological sites as static relics, the study emphasizes their dynamic role in the construction of collective memory and identity. Ultimately, all this supports the notion that integrating traditional knowledge into archaeological interpretation can result in a more inclusive and socially grounded approach to heritage preservation.

title: Beyond context: a productive approach to Iberian sculpture
abstract: Iberian sculpture poses major interpretive challenges due to the frequent loss of primary archaeological contexts. Traditionally approached through typological and stylistic frameworks, these works are often recovered in secondary settings or have been reused, making their original functions difficult to determine. This article adopts a biographical and productive perspective, tracing Iberian carved stone from quarrying and carving to reuse and final deposition. By focusing on material processes and labour, rather than solely on form or symbolism, it reframes sculpture as a product embedded in social and economic relations. The paper also reflects on the interpretive consequences of context loss and transformation, contributing to broader discussions on the biography of carved stone and the challenges of reconstructing meaning from displaced materials.

title: Stone panopticum: rethinking on the monumental stone sculpture of the Iron Age Histri
abstract: Stone as a durable and symbolic material played a central role in the visual culture and social practices of Histrian communities during the last millennium BCE. This paper examines the fragmented stone sculpture from Nesactium (Croatia), focussing on its meaning, function and cultural context. Using the concepts of material agency and object biography, it shows how these monuments, in addition to their monumentality, structured space and belonging, shaped collective memory and social identities as well as ideological forms of expression and representation. Nesactium sculpture thus emerges as a visually articulated social practice with a multi-layered and multifunctional role within the community. Their production testifies to a high level of artisanship and strong links to the Italo-Adriatic cultural sphere.

title: Lapidarian liturgies: mark making as ritual practice and technological process in Graeco-Roman magical gems
abstract: ‘Magical gems’ form a specific corpus of the larger category of glyptic art from Graeco-Roman antiquity. Decorated in rich iconography and text, they are important markers of more personal forms of religious practice. This paper argues that it is not only their iconography or text which bestows them with their magical properties but also the process by which they are crafted. Through exploring methods of production and the relationship between carving, engraving, and mark making, this paper explores the thinking, cognition, and ritual action that may have been involved. The paper concludes that through a process of mark making, gems became actively charged agents, which embodied religious and magical properties. These, in turn, were mediated through visual and haptic encounters which were central to their use and ability to function.

title: Flames of creation: rituals of fire, sacrifice, and renewal in the ancient Andes
authors: Edward Swenson; Ellen Pacheco; John P. Warner
abstract: The distinctive materiality (qualia) of fire can account for its near universal sacred status, including in past Andean societies. As a brilliant manifestation of destructive-creation, fire epitomizes a highly-motivated, non-arbitrary sign, thus explaining its intimate link with sacrifice, beginnings, endings, life, and empowering transformation. In the context of a select survey of global traditions, we mobilize a case study from the Moche temple of Huaca Colorada (700–900 CE) in the Jequetepeque Valley of northern Peru to demonstrate that fire served as an important medium in rituals of sacrificial consumption essential for metabolic creation and growth, and by extension, social and cosmic reproduction. The immolation of ceremonial constructions in rededication rites and the sacrifice and interment of individuals associated with intense burning events at the temple support this argument. We further contend that fire-based rites complemented pyro-technologies widely practiced at Huaca Colorada, and cooking and craft industries formed part of integrated religious liturgies. Ultimately, a comparison of Huaca Colorada with the neighbouring ceremonial centre of Huaca Dos Cruces (1000–1350 CE) reveals that despite fire’s inherent material-semiotic properties, its meaning and ritual efficacy varied historically and appears to have changed in the post-Moche period in the Jequetepeque Valley.

title: Flat white or with a round character? New light on stone funerary slabs and orbs from south Sweden
abstract: Stone funerary orbs with carved ornamentation, along with similarly decorated stones, but in the form of slabs, are a distinctive yet underexplored category of archaeological objects from Late Iron Age Sweden. These carved stones are originally found in burial contexts from the Migration Period (c. 400–550 CE) and at times early Vendel Period (c. 550–800 CE). In later centuries, they are known to have been removed from their original context, and re-used for other purposes. This paper discusses stone funerary orbs and slabs from the Mälar Valley, south Sweden, and sheds light on their different object itineraries throughout time. In doing so, it focusses on the making of their ornamentation, and its (desired) affects and effects, as well as the possible qualities that were associated with the stone itself (e.g. form, colour, descent) and how these aspects may have played pivotal roles in their removal from burial contexts to new ontological realms.

title: Shape analyses and the human skeleton
abstract: One key theme running through human skeletal research from early studies in the 18th century to today is a focus on shape. Unfortunately, early research fell prey to racist ideas about human biology. But thankfully, over the last 100 years, there has been a refocus on how to interpret the shape of human bones and what we can learn from it. We now answer a variety of questions using shape, ranging from how and why certain anatomical traits evolved to constructing a biological profile of an individual. Advancements in the methods used to capture and analyse shape also enable archiving and sharing of large amounts of digital data. This paper reviews how shape has been used to study the human skeleton, outline advancements, and reflect on trajectories for future research. It also presents ethical considerations of shape analyses and open science within human skeletal research from a global perspective.

title: Getting into shape: computing continua of Middle Stone Age prepared core technology
abstract: Levallois technology is a particularly skilful and cognitively intensive lithic technology where preparatory core shaping is aimed at producing predetermined flake blanks. It has significant implications for hominin evolution and dispersals, yet remains notoriously difficult to define relative to other prepared cores. Significant variability in prepared core techno-morphology is often rendered into a handful of rarely agreed upon discrete categories. We ask whether existing classifications of cores are immutable, discrete groups, or whether there are unbroken continua of prepared core variability. With a bespoke set of 3D computational methods, we directly quantify the criteria used to define Levallois technology. Applied to a diverse sample of prepared cores from five African MSA sites, these methods establish continua of prepared core preparation, recurrence and exhaustion. Quantifying this continuous variability in how blanks are removed from cores can help holistically address past hominin technological decision making, investment and flexibility.

title: On the historical mode of existence of rock art: making, chaîne opératoire, and history
abstract: This paper discusses a theoretical and methodological approach to exploring the historical dimension of rock art from a post-representational perspective. We propose that by making and experiencing rock art, a field of historical relations among humans, non-humans, materials, and places was woven, allowing the emergence of the affective properties of rock art and its historical mode of existence. This field of relations can be traced by reconstructing the chaîne opératoire of rock art, considering the intertwining of four sequences (images, instruments, pigmentary material, performativity of bodies) and four analytical dimensions (material, visual, spatial, temporal). Finally, these ideas are briefly discussed by comparing the rock art of hunter-gatherers and agrarian groups in central-north Chile

title: The punctuated itineraries of purple porphyry
abstract: Porphyry is a reddish-purple, white-speckled stone that was quarried in Egypt’s Eastern Desert under Roman rule. This distinctive stone has been frequently re-carved, reused, and imitated from antiquity to the present. The Tracing Purple Porphyry Project (TPPP) traces temporal, spatial, and contextual patterns in porphyry reuse to understand the stone’s changing meaning and value. Drawing on data from the TPPP, this article employs the concept of ‘punctuated itineraries’ – rooted in scholarship on object biographies – to understand how episodes of physical transformation have reignited earlier meanings of porphyry for new audiences. We introduce two notable kinds of punctuations, embellishment and miniaturization. These are exemplified here by a Roman amphora adorned with the appendages of an eagle in the medieval period and a miniature porphyry obelisk carved in eighteenth-century Rome. Ultimately, they demonstrate how punctuations can activate the stone’s enduring associations with Rome’s imperial and Christian legacies and its exoticizing Egyptian origins.

title: Revisiting Creswell Crags: applying digital methods to reassess the northernmost examples of Upper Palaeolithic cave art
authors: Izzy Wisher; Lisa-Elen Meyering; Barbara Oosterwijk
abstract: The engraved parietal art of Creswell Crags, discovered in 2003, remains the only example of Palaeolithic cave art in the U.K. and represents the northernmost signature of Upper Palaeolithic artistic behaviour. Despite its unique nature and significant advances in digital techniques used to evaluate parietal art, it has received limited academic attention in the past two decades since its discovery. We utilized a suite of digital modelling techniques (high-resolution photography, close-range photogrammetry, Reflectance Transformation Imaging) to reassess the art. Our results demonstrate the potential of such techniques to revise the original interpretations of the art and provide tentative, yet accessible, evidence of previously unidentified engravings. Our work also produced an accessible digital repository with vast potential for future research into this important site.

title: 北海道における細石刃石器群の展開と気候変動

abstract: 만경강 유역권의 청동기시대 연구는 익산의 청동기문화 연구에서 비롯되었다. 그리고 전북혁신도시 일원의 발굴조사를 계기로 독자적인 고고학의 영역으로 전환될 수 있었다. 이러한 배경을 바탕으로 북쪽의 미륵산에서 남쪽의 모악산 사이에 펼쳐져 있는 분지형 공간을 ‘만경강 유역 문화권’으로 설정할 수 있게 된 것은 고고학적으로 의미가 작지 않다.만경강은 전북 지역을 남과 북으로 가르며, 여러 지류들은 세분된 지역권을 만들어준다. 상류권인 동쪽의 고산권을 비롯하여, 북쪽은 봉동권·왕궁권·익산권·서수-황등권·군산권으로, 남쪽은 용진권·건지산권·황방산권· 백구권·김제권으로 구분할 수 있다. 북쪽은 익산권에, 남쪽은 황방산권과 건지산권에 유적이 집중적으로 분포하는 특징을 보인다.이러한 유적의 분포를 배경으로 청동기시대는 전기-중기-후기의 체계로 구분된다. 전기에는 늦은 시기의 미사리유형·가락동유형 및 흔암리유형 단계 유적의 존재, 익산권에 전기∼중기 단계 어느 시점에 요령식동검문화의 존재를 살필 수 있다. 중기에는 황방산권이 중추적인 문화중심지로 성장, 거점취락의 존재와 지역연계망의 구축, 지석묘와 송국리형 묘제의 다양한 조합, 체계적인 취락설계와 사회적 위계체계 형성 등을 추출할 수 있다. 후기에는 소수의 유적을 통해 대규모이거나 체계적인 취락의 보편성 부재를 엿볼 수 있다.한편 중상위 규모/체제의 취락들에서는 집체적 성격의 제의행위가가 존재하였다. 전기에는 환구와 수혈을, 중기에는 광장에서 수혈이나 입대목(立大木)을 활용하였다. 이러한 문화 전통은 후기 단계 취락으로 전승되는데, 문화 집단 간 복합관계를 설명해주는 근거가 된다.

abstract: 본고는 영산강유역에서 확인되는 이른바 ‘빈무덤’ 현상의 유구 사례를 대상으로 그 기능과 성격을 규명하는 데 목적이 있다. 이를 위해 매장 목적의 고분과 구별되는 비고분적 특징에 주목하였으며, 해당 사례를 ‘분구상성토물(墳 丘狀盛土物)’로 개념화하여 검토하였다.검토 결과, 분구상성토물 사례는 담양에서 해남에 이르는 영산강유역 곳곳에서 확인된다. 주요 특징으로는 중심매장시설의 부재를 비롯하여 다장을 전제하지 않는 고정형 분구, 구릉 능선상의 입지, 독립적인 공간 점유, 주구시설의 미비, 그리고 입대목·입석·계단시설 등 특정 경관시설의 수반을 들 수 있다. 또한 이들 상당수는 고분군 내에 병존하면서 형태·기술·상징성을 공유하고 있으며, 기능적으로는 매장보다 의례·기념적 성격을 보다 강하게 드러낸다. 공간적으로는 해양과 내륙을 잇는 주요 교통로상의 고개마루나 취락의 초입부에 독립적으로 조성되거나, 묘역 내 특정 지점에 배치됨으로써 고분과 차별화되는 독자적인 기능을 수행한 것으로 판단된다.분구상성토물은 분구 자체에 상징성이 부여된 고총고분과 동일한 사회적 맥락 속에서 그 축조 배경을 찾을 수 있으며, 지역사회의 권력 구조와 집단의 정체성을 가시적으로 완성시킨 의례·기념물로 기능하였다. 특히 동시기 신라·가야·일본열도 등 여타 지역에서는 찾을 수 없는 마한 고유의 정신문화적 산물로서, 마한인들의 관념적 기반과 의례체계를 복원할 수 있는 중요한 고고자료로 평가된다. 나아가 이러한 전통이 공주 송산리고분군 능역에서도 확인된다는 사실은 백제가 마한의 정신문화를 배척하지 않고 일정 부분 수용·계승하였음을 재확인시켜주는 자료라는 점에서 의의가 크다.향후에는 개별 유구의 축조 맥락과 행위 흔적에 대한 정밀한 분석을 토대로 고분과 구별되는 의례 공간으로서의 위상을 보다 구체화할 필요가 있다. 그동안 분구상성토물이 충분히 조명되지 못한 배경에는 물질자료 중심의 해석경향과 기존의 관성적인 인식 틀이 일정 부분 작용했던 것으로 보인다. 앞으로의 연구에서는 이를 신중하게 검토하여 유사한 해석상의 오류가 반복되지 않기를 기대한다.

journal: 호남고고학보 (Journal of the Honam Archaeological Society)
title: The Distribution and Significance of Wa-Type Archaeological Remains in the Hanseong Period Baekje Region
abstract: 한성기 백제권에서 출토된 왜계 고고자료가 시기별로 어떤 분포상의 특징을 보이는지, 그리고 그 의미가 무엇인지를 고분 부장유물을 중심으로 살펴보았다.왜계 고고자료는 4세기 말~5세기 초부터 무기류를 중심으로 서남해안 지역에 유입되기 시작한다. 5세기 중반부터는 왜계 토기가 급격하게 유입된다. 백제와 왜의 교섭이 활성화되면서 토착 세력과 외부 세력의 접촉면이 넓어지는 양상을 보이며, 특히 영산강 유역권에서 왜계 토기의 밀도가 압도적으로 높게 나타난다. 이는 이 일대가 왜와의 교류에 특화된 지역이었을 가능성을 시사한다. 아울러 그 배후에는 백제의 정치적 의도도 작용하고 있었던 것으로 보인다. 한편 중부 내륙의 천안 지역에는 서남해안과 유사한 구조의 왜계 고분이 조영된다. 당시 교통로는 왜계 고고자료의 분포양상으로 보아, 낙동강 하구를 기점으로 남원 아영 분지를 거쳐 북상하는 육로가 있었던 것으로 추정된다. 이와 함께 연안 항로와 육로를 연계하는 방식도 활용되었다. 도성으로 진입하기 위한 중부 내륙의 거점지역인 천안·연기·청주일대에는 왜계 무기류의 밀도가 높고, 왜계 고분도 조영되는 것으로 보아 백제 중앙을 방비하기 위한 목적으로서 왜인의 활동 가능성을 상정할 수 있다.결론적으로 한성기 백제는 왜와의 교류 과정에서 교통로를 다변화하고, 점차 토착 세력과의 접촉면을 넓혀 가면서 영향력을 확대해 나가고 있었다. 이 과정에서 영산강 유역권뿐만 아니라 도성에 인접한 내륙 거점지역에서도 왜인을 군사적 목적으로 이용한 것으로 판단된다.

journal: 호남고고학보 (Journal of the Honam Archaeological Society)
title: A Reexamination of the Evolution of Burial Mounds and Tomb-Building Groups on the Haenam Peninsula (3rd-6th Centuries)
abstract: 본 연구는 3세기부터 6세기에 이르는 해남반도 고분의 변천과정을 재검토하고, 이를 바탕으로 고분 축조세력과 왜계고분의 성격을 재검토하는 데 목적이 있다. 기존 연구에서는 5세기를 기점으로 백포만권역에서 도암만권역으로 중심지가 이동한 것으로 인식되어 왔다. 이러한 해석은 5세기에 도암만권역에서 왜계요소를 포함한 고분이 집중적으로 등장하고 백포만권역 고분이 상대적으로 감소하는 현상에 근거한 것이었다. 그러나 최근 발굴조사 성과를 반영할 경우, 이러한 변화는 단순한 중심지 이동으로 설명하기 어려워 보인다.이에 본 연구에서는 해남반도를 4개의 권역으로 구분한 후, 각 권역별 고분의 입지·분형·매장시설을 검토하고 부장토기를 근거로 편년을 설정하였다. 그 결과 해남반도 고분은 제형 분구와 토광이 중심을 이루는 초기 단계에서 원형분구와 석곽이 등장하는 단계, 그리고 횡혈식석실과 전방후원형 분구가 나타나는 단계로 변화하는 양상을 확인하였다. 또한 이러한 변화는 부장토기의 편년과도 대체로 일치하며, 고분의 분포와 전개 양상이 권역별로 차이를 보인다는 점도 파악하였다.따라서 해남반도 고분문화는 특정 권역에서 일방적으로 확산된 것이 아니라, 각 권역 재지세력의 지속과 변동 속에서 전개된 것으로 이해할 수 있다. 특히 5세기 이후 나타나는 왜계요소는 외래집단이 직접 이주한 결과라기보다 재지세력의 선택적 수용과 해상교류를 기반으로 한 집단의 활동이 복합적으로 반영된 결과로 볼 수 있다. 따라서 해남반도 고분문화의 전개는 중심지 이동의 관점이 아니라, 권역별 발전 과정과 외래요소 수용 방식의 차이라는 관점에서 설명하는 것이 타당하다.

journal: 호남고고학보 (Journal of the Honam Archaeological Society)
title: Change and Significance of Three Kingdoms Period Pottery in the Goheung Region
abstract: 본고에서는 최근 조사된 동호덕고분, 장덕리 산81번지유적 토기가마 출토 토기를 포함시켜 고흥지역 삼국시대토기의 변천 양상을 북부와 남부로 나누어 살펴본 후, 이를 해남, 장흥 등 인근지역과 비교하면서 고분과 함께 토기변천에 반영된 의미를 파악해 보았다.고흥지역의 삼국시대 토기는 가야, 왜, 영산강유역 토기와 비교하거나 사비기의 고분 연구성과를 포함시켜 10기(4세기 후엽~7세기 중엽)로 구분하였다. 북부지역은 4세기 후엽부터 김해지역 등의 금관가야계 토기가 보이다가 5 세기 대에는 진주지역 등과 관련되며 주로 소가야계 토기가 나타난다. 이와 달리 남부지역은 4세기 후엽에 가야계토기가 나타나 5세기 대까지 이어지는데 이는 주로 함안, 창원, 김해 등의 낙동강중·하류지역과 관련된다. 5세기중엽에는 창녕지역 토기도 추가된다. 인근지역 중 고흥 남부지역과 비슷한 토기 양상을 보이는 곳은 해남 현산면 일대이며, 장흥지역은 고흥 남부와 북부의 양상이 혼재된 모습이다. 고흥 남부지역에서는 5세기 전엽부터 왜계 자료도 나타나고, 5세기 후엽부터 백제 기종이 늘어나는데 웅진기 후반에는 왜계, 가야계와 신라계 토기가 반입뿐 아니라 모방도 이루어지고, 지역형식의 개배도 나타난다. 일부 외래계 토기 기종은 사비기 고분 출토 토기에 이어진다.고흥지역은 토기와 고분의 변천 양상으로 보아 4세기 후엽부터 가야계 토기와 고분이 나타나 5세기 전·중엽까지 이어지고, 남부지역에는 왜계고분도 공존하였다. 이로 보아 고흥 남부와 북부에는 서로 다른 재지세력이 존재했고, 백제 근초고왕 남정 후 가야와 적극적으로 교류하면서 해상세력으로 성장한 것으로 추정된다. 5세기 중엽 이후북부와 남부에서 영산강유역을 포함한 백제 토기가 늘어나고 토기 생산도 이루어지기 시작한 것은 안동고분의 백제계 위세품 사여와 관련될 것이다. 안동고분의 피장자는 왜인일 가능성이 있으며 한성기 백제의 군사적 활동 지원을계기로 들어와 고흥 남부지역에 정착한 것으로 추정된다. 웅진기에도 고흥 남부지역에는 고총 조영이 이어지는데, 6세기 중엽 이른시기에 조영된 동호덕고분이 그 양상을 잘 보여준다. 이 고분은 가야계 분구와 석실묘, 호석(추정), 왜계 즙석, 다양한 외래계 유물(반입, 모방 토기 등)과 함께 백제의 토기, 관고리 목관 사용 등의 매장관습도 확인된다. 이 고분의 다양한 외래계 요소는 5세기를 전후한 시기에 낙동강중·하류지역의 가야 문물을 적극 수용하며 성장했던 고흥 남부의 재지세력이 왜인집단의 정착으로 혼재하면서, 이전 시기에 이어 신라화되어가는 가야지역과 교류를 지속한 결과로 추정된다. 동호덕고분의 규모, 조영 시기로 보아 고흥 남부의 재지세력은 백제의 섬진강유역 진출후 백제 해상세력으로써 군사적 활동을 하였고, 인근 사비기 고분과 토기에도 일부 요소가 이어지는 점에서 사비기방군성제도 하에서도 그러한 활동을 이어나갔던 것으로 추정된다.

journal: 호남고고학보 (Journal of the Honam Archaeological Society)
title: A Study of Funerary Practices of 5th and 6th Centuries Tombs in the Yeongsan River Basin
abstract: 이 글은 영산강유역 5~6세기 고분을 대상으로 장송의례 전개 과정을 복원하는 데 목적이 있다. 이를 위해 고분의주요 공간을 정지층과 기반층, 묘광과 매장시설, 분구 성토층, 분구 위, 주구로 나누고 각 장소에서 나타나는 의례흔적을 종합적으로 분석하였다.영산강유역 장송의례는 고분 축조 단계와 연동되며 각 장소로 구분되는 의례를 수행하였다. 정지층과 기반층에서는 기물을 매개로 지신을 향한 의례가 수행되었다. 매장시설에서는 기물 매납, 주칠, 음식물 공헌 등을 통해 피장자의 승천과 안녕을 염원하는 의례가 이루어졌다. 분구 성토층에서는 폐쇄의례, 고분 완성, 고분의 안정을 기원하는 의례가 행해졌다. 분구 위와 주구에서는 기물 훼기, 동물 희생 등 죽음과 현세를 분리하는 의례가 이루어졌다.토광묘, 목관(곽)묘, 옹관묘, 석곽묘는 정지층과 기반층 의례 → 매장시설 축조 의례 → 시신 안치와 기물 부장 → 안치시설 외부에서 의례 → 분구 성토층 의례 → 주구 의례로 이어지는 일련의 흐름을 갖는다. 반면, 석실묘는 축조후 일정 시간이 지나고 납관이 이루어지는 흐름으로 인해 분구 성토층과 매장시설 축조 의례 → 시신 안치와 기물부장 의례 → 폐쇄의례→ 성토층 의례 → 분구 위 의례, 주구 의례의 과정을 가진다. 주구에서의 의례는 고분 완성 이후에 국한되지 않고 고분을 축조하는 여러 시점과 단계에서 의례가 수행된 것으로 추정된다. 영산강유역의 장송의례는 고분의 장소와 묘제별로 독립적으로 수행되면서도 전반적으로 축조-안치-폐쇄-폐기라는 절차에서 수행되었다.매장시설 외부에 뚜껑과 토기를 함께 매납하는 외부 부장 의례가 영산강유역 모든 묘제에서 공통적으로 나타난다. 이는 묘제의 변화 속에서 현지 세력의 고유한 장송 관념이 지속되었음을 알 수 있다. 시각적으로 피장자가 보이지 않거나 매장시설을 최종적으로 덮기 직전의 위치에서 토기가 확인되는 것으로 보아 매장시설의 마지막 단계에 수행된 의례로 이해된다. 주로 석재나 토기로 막음한 상태로 출토되며, 내부에 음식물을 담았을 것으로 생각된다.따라서 영산강유역의 매장시설에서 피장자를 향한 마지막 의례로 음식물 공헌이 이루어졌던 것으로 추정된다.이러한 연구 결과는 마한사회 유적의 복원에서 유물과 유구의 재현을 넘어, 장송의례를 통해 정신문화와 의미까지 복원할 때 비로소 완성됨을 설명하는 것이다. 이는 고고자료에서 물질이 과거의 행위를 드러내는 한편, 의례는 그 의미와 가치를 해석하는 핵심 단서로 기능하기 때문이다.

journal: 호서고고학 (Journal of the Hoseo Archaeological Society)
title: An Archaeological Understanding of (Prehistoric) Social Structure
authors: The hoseo Archaeological Society; Bumcheol Kim
abstract: The concept of social structure has long occupied a central position in archaeological interpretations of past societies. Since the early twentieth century, when structural-functionalism provided a dominant theoretical framework, archaeology has increasingly incorporated perspectives from modern sociology that emphasize the role of social actors, thereby enabling more dynamic explanations of social change in the past. Meanwhile, archaeology has engaged with significant methodological and theoretical issues relevant to proper understanding of diachronic/synchronic variation of social structures. These include efforts to identify social complexity through material remains, to account for inconsistencies between social principles reconstructed from different lines of archaeological evidence, and to adopt multi-scalar approaches to social transformation. In Korean archaeology, such developments have been actively employed to interpret the rapidly growing body of archaeological data since the 2000s. Nevertheless, it remains questionable whether these concepts have been consistently and rigorously applied, and whether the social structures of Korean prehistory have been sufficiently theorized in a productive and systematic manner.

journal: 호서고고학 (Journal of the Hoseo Archaeological Society)
title: A Preliminary Study on Reconstructing the Social Dynamics of Paleolithic and Neolithic Societies in Korea
authors: The hoseo Archaeological Society; Minkoo Kim
abstract: This paper focuses on the dynamics between factors that generate hierarchy among members of society and egalitarian mechanisms that suppress such hierarchy, in order to supplement the perspective that dichotomizes prehistoric societies into egalitarian and inegalitarian ones. To this end, it examines the limitations of neo-evolutionary classifications and considers the processes through which hierarchy emerges, as well as the mechanisms by which it is controlled by the majority of social members, through examples from great apes and hunter-gatherer societies. Social hierarchization and counter-hierarchization interact with various factors, including population growth, surplus production, exchange, communal labor, and intergroup conflict, and their specific manifestations vary according to the social and environmental conditions faced by a given group. Therefore, the Paleolithic and Neolithic periods cannot be defined as consistently egalitarian or inegalitarian societies. An analysis of the Korean Neolithic period, particularly the Unseo-dong site in Incheon, shows that although some signs of hierarchization appeared in large-scale Neolithic settlements, the development into a hierarchical society was ultimately limited by restraining mechanisms such as group fission. Prehistoric societies on the Korean Peninsula should therefore be understood not as having a fixed character, but as fluid and complex structures in which the power of a minority oriented toward hierarchy coexisted with the power of the majority seeking to maintain equality.

journal: 호서고고학 (Journal of the Hoseo Archaeological Society)
title: Various Issues in the Discussion on the Emergence of Regional Social Organizations in the Bronze Age
authors: The hoseo Archaeological Society; Dongseok Kang
abstract: This paper examines the problems and limitations of theories regarding the emergence of large-scale social organizations during the Bronze Age and proposes several approaches to overcome them. Previous studies have sought to reconstruct large-scale social organizations —in which social complexity began to increase— based on evidence such as the restructuring of the Bronze Age economy around agriculture, the emergence of large-scale settlements, wealth inequality, and the circulation of prestige goods. This was primarily explained as a fixed, unidirectional, vertical settlement system. However, this approach had the limitation of failing to comprehensively address the multifaceted patterns of emergence of social organizations that would have unfolded dynamically during the process of social complexity. To overcome this, three approaches were proposed. First, an approach based on the heterarchy perspective is necessary. The heterarchy approach, which defines settlement relationships through a complex system where hierarchical relationships and horizontal interactions intersect, can explain the diverse patterns of emergence of social organizations. Second, it is necessary to develop the discussion of social organization from the perspective of strategies for expanding political power. Leaders who emerge during the process of social complexity attempt to expand political power through the control of labor, the distribution of goods, and the manipulation of ideology; these actions serve as both the source of power and the backdrop for the formation of social organizations. The relationship between these leaders’ power expansion strategies and the formation of social organizations can be explained through the settlement density in the Hoseo region and the distribution networks of prestige goods in the Namgang River basin. Third, we need a multi-scalar approach that moves beyond the limitation of viewing settlements as fixed entities and instead understands them as multi-layered spatial relationships that overlap, combine, and interconnect across various scales. By reconstructing settlement patterns from a dialectical socio-spatial perspective, we can provide a more comprehensive explanation of the emergence of early complex social organizations.

journal: 호서고고학 (Journal of the Hoseo Archaeological Society)
title: Decline and Resilience of the Songguk-ri Culture: future research prospects
authors: The hoseo Archaeological Society; Heejin Lee
abstract: This paper reviews an approach to interpreting social change from an ecological perspective and reviews previous studies on the correlation between social continuity and environmental change during the Bronze Age. Furthermore, it explores key considerations for advancing future research on the prosperity and decline of Bronze Age culture. Although previous studies regarding the climate of the Korean Bronze Age are limited, they can be summarized as follows: The impact of cooling trend on social structure has been discussed in connection with the onset of the Bronze Age, the development of agriculture during the Early Bronze Age, the expansion of arable land and rice cultivation due to alluvial developments, and the decline of the Songguk-ri culture. Additionally, pilot studies have applied models such as the Panarchy Adaptive Cycle to understand climate change not merely as a physical phenomenon but within a socio-economic context. Meanwhile, this paper examines the necessary steps to further research social change in the Bronze Age from an ecological perspective. It emphasizes that, alongside efforts to specify the actual ripple effects of climate change, a prior understanding of the complexity of Bronze Age social systems —which determines human response mechanisms to external variables— is essential. Specifically, this paper suggests the need for a review of the functioning of the overall economic system (including the production, distribution, and consumption of economic surplus) and the formation and operation of cultural resilience as observed in rituals and other crisis-response mechanisms.

journal: 호서고고학 (Journal of the Hoseo Archaeological Society)
title: A New Approach to Understanding Social Structure in Prehistoric Korea through Dietary Analysis: Stable Isotope Evidence from Human Remains
authors: The hoseo Archaeological Society; Kyungcheol Choy; Juyoung Park
abstract: Recent studies of Prehistoric social structures have suggested new interpretive possibilities through bioarchaeological approaches. Bioarchaeological methods are used to infer social relationships such as social status, gendered divisions of labor, and hierarchical organization by examining differences in health conditions and labor intensity reflected in human skeletal remains. Accordingly, bioarchaeology is a useful tool for understanding prehistoric social structures and social differentiation by linking individual life histories with their broader social contexts. This study applies stable isotope analysis to human remains from archaeological sites to investigate dietary patterns and social classification in Prehistoric Korea. By examining differences in dietary patterns according to sex, age, and individuals, this research explores social differentiation reflected in dietary practices. Furthermore, the results of this analysis are considered alongside previous studies that have examined social structures through the multidimensional analysis of factors such as human remains, burial structures, and associated grave artifacts. By combining the analysis of dietary patterns with burial systems, this study aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of patterns of social differentiation in prehistoric societies. Stable isotopic studies on dietary patterns suggest that there was no clear social stratification based on sex or age during the Neolithic and Bronze Ages. Distinct dietary differences associated with social status or gender become more clearly visible only during the Three Kingdom period. In contrast, researches on burial practices indicate that the formation of social hierarchies and increasing horizontal segmentation within communities began as early as the Bronze Age. This discrepancy between the two approaches to social differentiation may suggest that the social hierarchies expressed through mortuary practices were not directly reflected in the daily dietary practices of individuals. In other words, dietary patterns tend to be relatively stable and conservative. Even when drastic changes occur in subsistence economies or social stratification, these shifts are not immediately reflected in diet; rather, clear dietary differences tend to emerge only when social stratification and hierarchical differentiation become more pronounced and well-established.

journal: 호서고고학 (Journal of the Hoseo Archaeological Society)
title: Core Sites and Linkage Strategies of the Jungwon Historical and Cultural Zone: A Case Study of Chungju City
authors: The hoseo Archaeological Society; Sieun Yang; Shinyeong Park
abstract: This study aims to re-examine the characteristics of major archaeological and cultural heritage sites in Chungju, the core area of the Jungwon Historical and Cultural Zone, and to propose linkage strategies for systematic conservation, management, and utilization at the regional scale. This discussion is situated within the context of the enforcement of the Special Act on the Maintenance of Historical and Cultural Zones. The Jungwon Historical and Cultural Zone is not the cultural sphere of a single political entity, but a integrative cultural space in which multiple historical and cultural layers from Mahan to Unified Silla overlapped through the Namhan River waterway and inland transportation networks. However, the zone still suffers from low public recognition and an abstractly perceived identity. Therefore, identifying core sites that can concretely demonstrate its historical value and establishing linkage strategies among these sites are essential tasks. This study identifies three core zones in Chungju: the Jungangtap-myeon area, the Tangeumdae area, and the Chungju-eupseong area. The Jungangtap-myeon area, where numerous sites from the Tappyeong-ri settlement to the Tappyeong-ri Seven-story Stone Pagoda are concentrated, clearly demonstrates the layered historical and cultural strata of Baekje, Goguryeo, Silla, and Unified Silla. The Tangeumdae area, centered on the Chilgeum-dong iron production site and Tangeumdae earthen fortress, represents a space where iron production, the Namhan River waterway, and Baekje’s local governance intersected. The Chungju-eupseong area illustrates the historical continuity from the ancient administrative center of Jungwon-gyeong to the medieval and early modern historical city of Chungju. To organically connect these three zones, this study proposes three major strategies: integrated management based on the Historic Urban Landscape approach, strengthening the identity and public recognition of the Jungwon Historical and Cultural Zone, and establishing community-driven heritage utilization models. This approach moves beyond the preservation of individual heritage sites and seeks to restore a regional historical and cultural environment in which heritage, space, and people interact. Ultimately, it can contribute to building a sustainable, citizen-centered model for the conservation, management, and utilization of historical and cultural zones.

journal: 호서고고학 (Journal of the Hoseo Archaeological Society)
title: A Web-Based Archaeological Terrain Analysis System and AI-Assisted Report Writing Methodology
authors: The hoseo Archaeological Society; Uihaeng Heo; Khujin Oh
abstract: This study presents the development background, process, and methodological application of ArchaeoGIS Pro, an archaeology-specific geographic information system (GIS) that operates entirely within a web browser without requiring dedicated software installation or server infrastructure. Current archaeological GIS practice faces three representative challenges: dependence on expensive commercial software, insufficient reflection of Korea-specific archaeological contexts, and a persistent gap between spatial analysis outputs and written report narratives. To address these issues, a terrain analysis system named ArchaeoGIS Pro was developed. The system derives archaeologically meaningful terrain information from digital elevation models (DEMs)—including slope, aspect, hillshade, curvature, and the Topographic Wetness Index (TWI)—and incorporates a criteria-based exploratory overlay analysis module for assessing site suitability, along with spatial analysis functionality. The analytical results are integrated with a large language model (LLM) to explore the feasibility of generating draft natural environment descriptions conforming to the format of Korean buried cultural heritage excavation reports. Numerical comparison with established commercial GIS software confirmed high agreement across major analytical parameters. The system can be accessed and tested at https://www.archaeology.kr/Archaeo_GIS.html, allowing independent verification of the analytical functions described in this paper. The LLM-assisted report drafting function represents a preliminary attempt to bridge the gap between GIS analysis outputs and written archaeological narratives. At this stage, objective evaluation criteria for assessing the quality of AI-generated drafts have not yet been fully established, and systematic comparison with actual excavation reports is identified as a future research objective. The study also acknowledges limitations including the lack of sufficient field application cases, the need for validation of site suitability criteria across different periods and site types, and the requirement for archaeology-specific AI training data. Despite these limitations, the system demonstrates the potential of integrating web-based GIS terrain analysis with AI-assisted reporting as a practical auxiliary tool for archaeological research.

journal: 호서고고학 (Journal of the Hoseo Archaeological Society)
title: Issues and Improvement Measures Concerning the Buried Heritage System under the National Heritage Impact Assessment Act
authors: The hoseo Archaeological Society; Doheon Kim
abstract: With the recent introduction of the national heritage impact assessment system, impact assessments for buried heritage are now being conducted. Although the national heritage impact assessment system has many administrative advantages in that it integrates several pre-existing systems, the provisions concerning buried heritage have largely retained the problems of the previous system. Moreover, there has thus far been little substantive discussion of the buried heritage system itself. Based on this awareness of the problem, this study examines the issues inherent in the buried heritage system. The review suggests that the buried heritage system has the following problems. First, although the law formally advocates preventive investigation, prediction, and assessment, the subordinate regulations in practice operate only within limited parameters, focusing on areas presumed to contain buried heritage, previously investigated areas, projects of 30,000 square meters or more, and areas publicly designated by local governments. In addition, although surface surveys occupy an important position within the buried heritage system, there are insufficient mechanisms to compensate for their methodological limitations. In other words, the current system risks being reduced to one that manages only areas that are already known or that meet certain formal criteria, rather than one that broadly investigates areas where buried heritage may potentially exist. To address these problems, it is first necessary to strengthen investigations of land surrounding areas presumed to contain buried heritage. In addition, alongside zones publicly designated by the heads of local governments, surface surveys should also be permitted, as in the past, when the head of a local government deems them necessary. This study also argues that monitoring surveys should be excluded from preservation measures and that such surveys should instead be made mandatory when construction is carried out after a surface survey. Furthermore, it would be appropriate to operate an organization such as a committee to review surface survey reports and related materials; once this system is firmly established, cases in which authority is delegated to local governments could also be eliminated. Finally, from a long-term perspective, this study argues that it would be desirable to adopt investigation methods that involve actual excavation to verify buried remains, such as sample surveys or trial excavations, rather than relying on surface surveys.
